Following his release, he lived in exile in France, where he died of meningitis in 1900.
pope-francis: Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio on December 17, 1936, served as the 266th pope of the Catholic Church from 2013 to 2025 (1936–2025). Born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, he worked as a chemical technologist before entering the Society of Jesus in 1958. He was ordained a Catholic priest in 1969 and later served as the Archbishop of Buenos Aires from 1998 until his papal election. Created a cardinal by Pope John Paul II in 2001, he was elected supreme pontiff in March 2013, becoming the first Jesuit pope, the first from the Americas, and the first from the Southern Hemisphere. Throughout his pontificate, Francis was recognized for his humility, emphasis on God's mercy, concern for the poor, and commitment to interfaith dialogue. He championed environmental stewardship in his encyclical Laudato si' and initiated significant structural reforms within the Vatican bureaucracy.
lord-byron: George Gordon Byron, 6th Baron Byron, better known simply as Lord Byron, was a leading English Romantic poet and lyricist. Born in London in 1788, Byron became one of the most famous and influential figures of the Romantic movement. His major works include the long narrative poems Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and Don Juan, as well as shorter lyrics like She Walks in Beauty. Byron's writing helped popularize the Byronic hero, an idealized yet flawed character marked by passion, cynicism, and rebellion. Beyond his literary achievements, he was famous for his aristocratic lifestyle, numerous romantic affairs, and substantial debts, which led him to leave England in 1816. Byron spent his remaining years traveling across Europe, particularly in Italy and Greece. In 1823, he joined the Greek War of Independence to support the campaign against the Ottoman Empire. He died of a fever in Missolonghi, Greece, in 1824 at age thirty-six.
charles-de-gaulle: Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle was a French military general and statesman who led France through pivotal twentieth century crises. Born in Lille in 1890, he served as an army officer during World War I. Following the defeat of France by Nazi Germany in 1940, de Gaulle fled to London and established the Free French Forces, broadcasting a famous appeal for resistance and organizing wartime opposition. After the liberation of Paris in 1944, he chaired the Provisional Government of the French Republic until resigning in 1946. De Gaulle returned to power in 1958 amid the Algerian Crisis, overseeing the creation of a new constitution that established the Fifth Republic. Serving as President from 1959 to 1969, he pursued an independent foreign policy, granting independence to Algeria, developing a sovereign nuclear deterrent, and withdrawing France from NATO's integrated military command. He died in 1970.
basshunter: Jonas Erik Altberg, professionally known as Basshunter, is a Swedish singer, record producer, and DJ born on December 22, 1984, in Halmstad, Sweden. He began producing music in his teens using digital audio workstations and initially released his tracks independently online. Basshunter gained international prominence in 2006 with the release of the Swedish-language single Boten Anna, which topped music charts across Europe. He followed this success with the popular track Vi sitter i Ventrilo och spelar DotA. In late 2007, he released an English version of Boten Anna titled Now You're Gone, featuring re-recorded vocals and lyrics, which reached number one on the UK Singles Chart for five consecutive weeks. His major-label studio album, Now You're Gone – The Album, was released in 2008 and achieved commercial success worldwide. Over his career, Basshunter has released multiple albums and established himself as a prominent figure in Eurodance and electronic music.
neil-armstrong: Neil Alden Armstrong was an American astronaut, naval aviator, and test pilot who became internationally known as the first person to walk on the Moon. Born on August 5, 1930, near Wapakoneta, Ohio, Armstrong developed an early passion for aviation. He served as a U.S. Navy pilot during the Korean War before joining the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, later NASA, as a research test pilot. In 1962, he was selected for NASA's second astronaut group. Armstrong made his first spaceflight in 1966 as command pilot of Gemini 8, performing the first successful space docking of two spacecraft. On July 20, 1969, as commander of the Apollo 11 mission, Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface, famously declaring the event a giant leap for mankind. After leaving NASA in 1971, he taught aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati and served on several presidential commissions. Armstrong died on August 25, 2012.
carl-linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus, later ennobled as Carl von Linné, was a Swedish botanist, physician, and zoologist born in 1707 and died in 1778. Often referred to as the father of modern taxonomy, he is internationally known for formalizing binomial nomenclature, the standardized system of naming organisms using a two-part scientific name indicating genus and species. Educated at Lund University and Uppsala University, he pursued a career in medicine and natural history, eventually becoming a professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala. Linnaeus conducted extensive botanical expeditions, including a notable journey through Lapland. His monumental publications, such as Systema Naturae in 1735 and Species Plantarum in 1753, categorized thousands of plant and animal species into hierarchical groups based on shared physical characteristics. His system provided a practical, universal framework that fundamentally transformed biological classification and laid the foundation for modern ecology and evolutionary studies.
nikola-tesla: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was a renowned Serbian-American engineer and inventor internationally known for his pioneering contributions to the development of alternating current electricity systems. Born in Smiljan in the Austrian Empire, Tesla studied engineering and physics before emigrating to the United States in 1884. He briefly worked for Thomas Edison before establishing his own laboratories to pursue independent research. Tesla patented the induction motor and related alternating current technologies, licensing them to entrepreneur George Westinghouse. This technology became the global standard for long-distance power distribution. Throughout his career, Tesla made significant advances in electromagnetism, high-voltage experiments, radio communications, and wireless energy transmission, notably inventing the Tesla coil. Despite obtaining over three hundred patents worldwide and gaining widespread fame for his visionary concepts, Tesla faced financial difficulties in his later years. He spent his final decades living in New York City, where he passed away in 1943.
elvis-presley: Elvis Aaron Presley was an American singer and actor who became one of the most significant cultural icons of the twentieth century, internationally known as the King of Rock and Roll. Born on January 8, 1935, in Tupelo, Mississippi, Presley moved to Memphis, Tennessee, in 1948. He began his music career in 1954 at Sun Records, blending rhythm and blues, country, and gospel genres. Signing with RCA Victor in 1955, his single Heartbreak Hotel achieved national success in 1956. Presley's energetic performance style and televised appearances brought him rapid fame and wide influence. He served in the United States Army from 1958 to 1960. Presley also pursued an acting career, starring in over thirty feature films, including Love Me Tender and Viva Las Vegas. Following a return to live music in 1968, he maintained a heavy concert schedule and a Las Vegas residency. Presley died in Memphis on August 16, 1977.
ernest-hemingway: Ernest Miller Hemingway was an influential American author and journalist whose understated writing style profoundly shaped twentieth-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, on July 21, 1899, he began his career as a newspaper reporter before serving as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy during World War I. His wartime experiences heavily inspired his early literary works, including the novel A Farewell to Arms published in 1929. Throughout the 1920s, Hemingway lived in Paris as part of the Lost Generation of expatriate writers, producing acclaimed works such as The Sun Also Rises. He later reported on the Spanish Civil War and World War II, experiences reflected in his 1940 novel For Whom the Bell Tolls. Renowned for his sparse prose, he earned the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1953 for The Old Man and the Sea and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954. Hemingway died in Ketchum, Idaho, on July 2, 1961.
fidel-castro: Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was a Cuban politician, author, and revolutionary who governed Cuba for nearly five decades. Born in Birán in 1926, he studied law at the University of Havana and engaged in political activism. In 1953, he led a failed attack on the Moncada Barracks, resulting in his imprisonment and exile to Mexico. There, he formed the 26th of July Movement with Che Guevara and his brother Raúl Castro. Returning to Cuba, his guerrilla movement successfully overthrew the regime of Fulgencio Batista in 1959. Castro subsequently served as Prime Minister and President, transforming Cuba into a single-party socialist state. His government aligned closely with the Soviet Union, leading to major Cold War confrontations including the Bay of Pigs Invasion and the Cuban Missile Crisis. His administration implemented widespread healthcare and literacy programs while suppressing political opposition and civil liberties. Citing health issues, Castro transferred power to Raúl in 2008 and died in 2016.
benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was an internationally known American polymath and statesman who played a pivotal role in shaping the early United States. Born in Boston, Massachusetts, Franklin achieved initial commercial success as a printer, publisher, and writer, gaining widespread fame through Poor Richard's Almanack. As a scientist and inventor, he earned international acclaim for his pioneering research in electricity, discovering the principle of conservation of charge and inventing the lightning rod, bifocals, and the Franklin stove. In public service, he was a key Founding Father who helped draft and sign the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the United States Constitution. Serving as the American minister to France, his diplomatic skill secured crucial military and financial support during the Revolutionary War. Franklin also established fundamental civic institutions, including the University of Pennsylvania, leaving an enduring global legacy across science, literature, and governance.
benedict-xvi: Benedict XVI, born Joseph Aloisius Ratzinger on April 16, 1927, in Marktl, Germany, was an influential German theologian who served as the 265th pope of the Catholic Church from 2005 to 2013. Ordained a priest in 1951, he established a distinguished academic career, teaching theology at various German universities. In 1977, he was appointed Archbishop of Munich and Freising and created a cardinal. Pope John Paul II named him Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1981, a position he held for over two decades, gaining a reputation for staunch theological conservatism. Following the death of John Paul II, Ratzinger was elected pope in April 2005. During his pontificate, Benedict XVI emphasized traditional Christian values and sought to revitalize European faith. In February 2013, citing advanced age and declining health, he became the first pope to resign in nearly six centuries, assuming the title of Pope Emeritus until his death on December 31, 2022.
george-orwell: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, an internationally known British novelist, essayist, journalist, and critic who lived from 1903 to 1950. Born in Motihari, India, Blair was educated in England at Eton College before serving with the Indian Imperial Police in Burma. He later returned to Europe, adopting his pseudonym in 1933 to publish his early autobiographical and fictional works. His writing was characterized by lucid prose, social criticism, and opposition to totalitarianism, as well as a commitment to democratic socialism. Orwell's experiences in the Spanish Civil War informed his account in Homage to Catalonia. He achieved worldwide acclaim with his political allegory Animal Farm, published in 1945, and the dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949. Orwell died of tuberculosis in London at age forty-six, leaving a profound impact on modern culture and language.
stephen-hawking: Stephen William Hawking (1942–2018) was a British theoretical physicist, cosmologist, and author who achieved international recognition for his scientific work and public engagement. Born in Oxford, England, Hawking studied physics at the University of Oxford before earning his doctorate in applied mathematics and theoretical physics at the University of Cambridge. In 1963, he was diagnosed with motor neuron disease, a condition that gradually paralyzed him, requiring the use of a speech-generating device. Despite his illness, Hawking spent decades as a professor at Cambridge, serving as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics from 1979 to 2009. His groundbreaking theoretical contributions merged general relativity with quantum mechanics. He worked alongside Roger Penrose on gravitational singularity theorems and predicted that black holes emit subatomic particles, a phenomenon termed Hawking radiation. Additionally, Hawking popularized astrophysics through bestselling books, including A Brief History of Time, published in 1988. He died in Cambridge in 2018.
margaret-thatcher: Margaret Hilda Thatcher, born Margaret Hilda Roberts, was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990 and Leader of the Conservative Party from 1975 to 1990. Born on October 13, 1925, in Grantham, Lincolnshire, she studied chemistry at Oxford University before qualifying as a barrister. Elected to Parliament in 1959, she served as Secretary of State for Education and Science from 1970 to 1974. As Britain's first female prime minister and the longest-serving prime minister of the twentieth century, she implemented free market economic policies including deregulation, the privatization of state-owned enterprises, and the reduction of trade union influence. Abroad, she maintained a strong alliance with United States President Ronald Reagan, led the country during the 1982 Falklands War, and was dubbed the Iron Lady for her firm political stance. She resigned in 1990 following party opposition over domestic tax policies and European integration, and died on April 8, 2013.
walt-disney: Walter Elias Disney (1901–1966) was an internationally known American animator, film producer, director, screenwriter, voice actor, and entrepreneur. As a pioneer of the American animation industry, he co-founded the Disney Brothers Studio, which eventually became The Walt Disney Company. Disney introduced several iconic cartoon characters, most notably Mickey Mouse, whom he originally voiced. In 1937, he produced Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length animated feature film, revolutionizing the film industry. Over his career, Disney expanded his entertainment empire into television and live-action cinema, and he developed Disneyland, a groundbreaking theme park that opened in California in 1955. Recognized worldwide for his cultural impact, Disney earned 22 Academy Awards from 59 nominations, holding the record for the most individual Oscars won. He remained an influential figure in entertainment until his death from lung cancer in 1966, leaving behind a global legacy in animation, film, and themed entertainment.
john-paul-ii: Pope John Paul II, born Karol Józef Wojtyła on May 18, 1920, in Wadowice, Poland, served as the 264th pope of the Catholic Church from 1978 until his death in 2005. Elected at age 58, he was the first non-Italian pope in 455 years and became one of the most influential global leaders of the twentieth century. Prior to his papacy, Wojtyła served as the Archbishop of Kraków. During his pontificate, he traveled extensively, visiting 129 countries to engage with believers and world leaders. He played a key role in supporting the Solidarity movement in Poland, contributing to the fall of communism in Eastern Europe. John Paul II emphasized interfaith dialogue, visited synagogues and mosques, and advocated for human rights. After surviving an assassination attempt in 1981, he continued his active ministry despite declining health in his final years. He died on April 2, 2005, and was canonized in 2014.
nicolaus-copernicus: Nicolaus Copernicus was a Polish mathematician and astronomer who lived from 1473 to 1543. His full name in Polish was Mikolaj Kopernik, but he is globally recognized by his Latinized name, Nicolaus Copernicus. He is internationally known for formulating a comprehensive heliocentric model of the universe, which positioned the Sun, rather than the Earth, at the center of the solar system. This theory fundamentally disrupted the prevailing geocentric system that had dominated Western thought since antiquity. Copernicus presented his mathematical proofs and astronomical theories in his landmark book, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, published in 1543, shortly before his death. His work demonstrated that Earth rotates daily on its axis and revolves annually around the Sun. This breakthrough initiated the Copernican Revolution, laying the crucial groundwork for modern astronomy and triggering a broader scientific revolution across Europe. In addition to astronomy, Copernicus was a church canon, physician, translator, and economist.
albert-camus: Albert Camus was an internationally known French philosopher, author, and journalist born on November 7, 1913, in Mondovi, French Algeria. He gained renown for his literary and philosophical works exploring morality, the human condition, and absurdism. Raised by a working class family, Camus studied philosophy at the University of Algiers before beginning his writing career. During World War II, he joined the French Resistance and edited the underground newspaper Combat. Camus authored acclaimed literary works, including the novels The Stranger and The Plague, alongside influential philosophical essays such as The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel. Although frequently categorized as an existentialist, he rejected the label, framing his thought around the absurd conflict between humanity's search for meaning and an indifferent world. In 1957, he received the Nobel Prize in Literature. Albert Camus died in an automobile accident in France on January 4, 1960.
volodymyr-zelenskyy: Volodymyr Oleksandrovych Zelenskyy is a Ukrainian politician, actor, and comedian who has served as the President of Ukraine since May 2019. Born on January 25, 1978, in Kryvyi Rih, he earned a law degree from the Kryvyi Rih Institute of Economics but pursued a career in entertainment. He co-founded the production company Kvartal 95, which produced films, cartoons, and television shows. Zelenskyy achieved widespread national fame starring in the satirical television series Servant of the People, playing a high school teacher elected president after a viral video. Leveraging his popularity, he entered politics and won the 2019 presidential election by a landslide on an anti-corruption platform. During his presidency, Zelenskyy faced severe domestic and geopolitical challenges, culminating in the February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia. His refusal to evacuate Kyiv and his subsequent communication strategy earned him international recognition as a wartime leader coordinating defense and foreign military aid.
mikhail-gorbachev: Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev was a Soviet politician who served as the final leader of the Soviet Union from 1985 until its dissolution in 1991. Born on March 2, 1931, in Privolnoye, Russian SFSR, he rose through the Communist Party ranks and became General Secretary in 1985. Gorbachev introduced sweeping domestic reforms known as perestroika, aimed at economic restructuring, and glasnost, which expanded freedom of speech and political openness. Internationally, he sought to ease Cold War tensions through historic disarmament summits with United States President Ronald Reagan and withdrew Soviet troops from Afghanistan. His refusal to intervene in the 1989 Eastern European revolutions contributed to the collapse of the Eastern Bloc. Gorbachev was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990 for his role in ending the Cold War. After surviving a failed coup attempt in August 1991, he resigned as President of the Soviet Union on December 25, 1991. He died on August 30, 2022.
sung-jae-gi: Sung Jae-gi was a South Korean anti-feminist and men's rights activist who founded the organization Association of Korean Male in 2008, later known as Man of Korea. Born on September 11, 1967, in Daegu, he became a prominent figure in South Korea's masculism movement during the early twenty-first century. Sung actively campaigned against government policies he viewed as favoring women over men, strongly advocating for the abolition of the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family. He argued that South Korean men faced systemic discrimination, particularly regarding compulsory military service and social expectations. Throughout his activist career, Sung organized numerous public protests, media campaigns, and legal challenges to champion men's rights. On July 26, 2013, Sung jumped off the Mapo Bridge in Seoul as a demonstration aimed at raising funds for his struggling organization and drawing national attention to men's rights. His body was recovered three days later, confirming his death at forty-five.
lionel-messi: Lionel Andrés Messi, born on June 24, 1987, in Rosario, Argentina, is an internationally known Argentine association football player widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He began his professional career with FC Barcelona, joining the club's youth academy before making his senior debut in 2004. During his seventeen seasons with Barcelona, Messi won ten La Liga titles, four UEFA Champions League trophies, and seven Copa del Rey titles. In 2021, he transferred to Paris Saint-Germain, where he secured two Ligue 1 titles, before joining Major League Soccer club Inter Miami in 2023. Internationally, Messi represents the Argentina national team, serving as captain. He led his country to victory in the 2021 Copa América and the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Throughout his career, Messi has earned numerous individual honors, including a record eight Ballon d'Or awards, establishing an extraordinary legacy in global football.
louis-pasteur: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist who lived from December 27, 1822, to September 28, 1895. Internationally known for his discoveries in vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization, he is regarded as a primary founder of modern bacteriology. Early in his career, Pasteur made significant contributions to chemistry, particularly regarding the molecular asymmetry of crystals. He later turned his attention to biological sciences, disproving the doctrine of spontaneous generation through rigorous experimentation. His research demonstrated that microorganisms cause both fermentation and disease, providing vital support for the germ theory of disease. To prevent spoilage in food and beverages, he developed pasteurization, a process involving mild heating. Pasteur also created the first effective vaccines for rabies and anthrax, transforming medical treatment and public health. In 1887, he established the Pasteur Institute in Paris, serving as its director until his death.
james-joyce: James Augustine Aloysius Joyce was an acclaimed Irish novelist and poet who lived from 1882 to 1941. Recognized as one of the most influential figures of the modernist avant-garde movement, he revolutionized narrative technique through his pioneering use of stream of consciousness. Although Joyce spent most of his adult life living abroad in self-imposed exile in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris, his literary works remained intensely focused on his native Dublin. His major publications began with the short story collection Dubliners in 1914, followed by the semi-autobiographical novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in 1916. His masterpiece, Ulysses, published in 1922, paralleled Homer's Odyssey in a detailed exploration of a single day in Dublin. Joyce spent his final working years composing the avant-garde, linguistically complex novel Finnegans Wake, published in 1939. He died in Zurich in 1941, leaving a profound legacy in twentieth-century literature.
gabriel-garc-a-m-rquez: Gabriel José de la Concordia García Márquez was a prominent Colombian novelist, journalist, and screenwriter. Born on March 6, 1927, in Aracataca, Colombia, he began his career in journalism before achieving international literary fame. García Márquez is widely celebrated for popularizing magical realism, a narrative style combining fantastical elements with realistic settings. His masterpiece, One Hundred Years of Solitude, published in 1967, earned global acclaim and became a cornerstone of the Latin American Boom literary movement. His other notable works include The Autumn of the Patriarch, Chronicle of a Death Foretold, and Love in the Time of Cholera. In 1982, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Beyond his fiction, he maintained a lifelong commitment to journalism and political commentary. He spent much of his later life in Mexico City, where he died on April 17, 2014, leaving an influential cultural legacy.
richard-wagner: Wilhelm Richard Wagner was a German composer, theatre director, and conductor who lived from May 22, 1813, to February 13, 1883. He is best known for his influential operas, or music dramas, which revolutionized Western classical music. Unlike most opera composers, Wagner wrote both the libretto and the music for each of his stage works. He pioneered the concept of the Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art, seeking to synthesize poetic, visual, musical, and dramatic arts. His compositions are famous for their complex textures, rich harmonies, and elaborate use of leitmotifs, which are musical themes associated with specific characters or ideas. Among his most celebrated works are the monumental four-opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, Tristan und Isolde, and Parsifal. Wagner also oversaw the construction of the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, an opera house designed specifically to stage his works. His musical innovations profoundly shaped the development of late Romantic and modern classical music.
nicolas-sarkozy: Nicolas Paul Stéphane Sarközy de Nagy-Bocsa, born on January 28, 1955, in Paris, is a French politician who served as the 23rd president of the French Republic from 2007 to 2012. Before his presidency, Sarkozy held several high-profile cabinet positions, including Minister of the Interior and Minister of Finances, and served as the leader of the center-right Union for a Popular Movement party. During his term as president, his administration responded to the 2008 global financial crisis, negotiated key European Union treaties, and authorized French military participation in the 2011 international intervention in Libya. Domestic policy under his tenure emphasized economic deregulation and labor reforms. Sarkozy ran for reelection in 2012 but was defeated by Socialist candidate François Hollande. Following his presidency, he remained an influential figure in French conservative politics until his formal retirement from elected office. In subsequent years, Sarkozy faced several legal investigations and convictions regarding campaign finance violations and corruption.
naruhito: Naruhito, whose full birth name and title is Prince Hiro Naruhito, is the 126th Emperor of Japan, reigning since May 1, 2019. Born in Tokyo on February 23, 1960, he is the eldest son of Emperor Emeritus Akihito and Empress Emerita Michiko. Naruhito studied history at Gakushuin University before attending Merton College, Oxford, where he researched historical water transport systems, making him the first direct heir to the Japanese throne to study abroad. In 1993, he married diplomat Masako Owada, and the couple has one daughter, Princess Aiko. Naruhito officially became Crown Prince in 1991 and acceded to the Chrysanthemum Throne following his father's historical abdication, initiating Japan's Reiwa era. As head of state under Japan's constitutional monarchy, his duties are strictly symbolic and ceremonial. Throughout his life, Naruhito has actively advocated for global water conservation, environmental protection, and international cultural exchange, maintaining Japan's imperial traditions while engaging with contemporary global issues.
yuri-gagarin: Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was a Soviet air force pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into outer space. Born on March 9, 1934, in Klushino, Gagarin joined the Soviet Air Force before being selected for the space program in 1960. On April 12, 1961, he boarded the Vostok 1 spacecraft and completed a single orbit around Earth, lasting 108 minutes. This historic achievement made him an international celebrity and earned him the title Hero of the Soviet Union, the nation's highest honor. Following his flight, Gagarin toured internationally as a cultural ambassador and continued serving in the Soviet space program, helping train future cosmonauts and working as a test pilot. On March 27, 1968, Gagarin died at age thirty-four when the MiG-15 jet he was piloting crashed during a routine training flight near Kirzhach. His legacy remains a major milestone in human spaceflight history.
marlene-dietrich: Marie Magdalene Dietrich, known professionally as Marlene Dietrich, was an internationally known German and American actress and singer who lived from 1901 to 1992. Born in Berlin on December 27, 1901, she achieved global fame through her breakthrough role as Lola in the film The Blue Angel in 1930. Moving to Hollywood under contract with Paramount Pictures, she starred in acclaimed films such as Morocco, Shanghai Express, and Destry Rides Again. Renowned for her glamour, distinctive singing voice, and sophisticated androgynous style, Dietrich became one of the top earning performers of her era. During World War II, she strongly opposed the Nazi regime, became a citizen of the United States in 1939, and spent years entertaining Allied troops on the front lines. After her movie career slowed, she toured world stages extensively as a concert and cabaret artist from the 1950s into the 1970s. Dietrich died in Paris on May 6, 1992.
henry-ford: Henry Ford was an American business magnate and industrialist who lived from July 30, 1863, to April 7, 1947. Born in Springwells Township, Michigan, he showed an early interest in mechanics. In 1903, he established the Ford Motor Company, which revolutionized the automotive industry. Ford introduced the Model T in 1908, an affordable automobile that made motor travel accessible to the general public. To meet high demand, he pioneered the moving assembly line for mass production in 1913. This innovation dramatically reduced manufacturing costs and time, transforming modern industrial manufacturing practices, a concept often referred to as Fordism. He also introduced the five dollar daily wage, which doubled his workers' pay and helped build a robust middle class consumer base. Through his technological and commercial innovations, Ford became one of the most famous and wealthiest figures in the world, leaving a lasting impact on global transportation and manufacturing.
george-h-w-bush: George Herbert Walker Bush was an American politician and businessman who served as the forty-first president of the United States from 1989 to 1993. Born in Milton, Massachusetts, in 1924, he was a decorated World War II naval aviator before graduating from Yale University and entering the Texas oil industry. A member of the Republican Party, Bush held several high-level government positions prior to his presidency, including U.S. representative from Texas, ambassador to the United Nations, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, and vice president under Ronald Reagan from 1981 to 1989. During his presidency, Bush navigated significant international developments, including the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the reunification of Germany, and the military victory in the 1990 to 1991 Gulf War. Domestically, he signed landmark legislation such as the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990. Bush passed away in 2018 at the age of ninety-four.
friedrich-engels: Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, sociologist, and economist who played a foundational role in the development of modern socialism and communism. Born in Barmen, Prussia, in 1820 to a wealthy textile manufacturer, Engels developed a strong interest in radical politics and economic conditions during his youth. In 1845, he published The Condition of the Working Class in England, a seminal study based on his firsthand observations of industrial life in Manchester. Engels is best known for his close intellectual and political partnership with Karl Marx. Together, they co-authored The Communist Manifesto in 1848, outlining the principles of scientific socialism. Beyond co-writing major political texts, Engels financially supported Marx and later edited and published the second and third volumes of Das Kapital following Marx's death in 1883. Throughout his life, Engels contributed extensively to Marxist theory before passing away in London in 1895.
jane-austen: Jane Austen was an internationally renowned English novelist whose full name was Jane Austen. Born on December 16, 1775, in Steventon, Hampshire, she grew up in a supportive, literary family. Austen wrote six major novels that critically examined the British landed gentry of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Her works, including Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park, and Emma, were published anonymously during her lifetime. Two additional novels, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, were published posthumously. Austen’s writing is celebrated for its sharp irony, social realism, and commentary on women's economic dependence on marriage. Despite modest fame during her lifetime, her critical standing grew immensely after her death. She never married and spent her final years living in Chawton before dying on July 18, 1817, in Winchester, England. Today, she remains an enduring global icon of classic English literature.
j-r-r-tolkien: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic who lived from 1892 to 1973. Born in Bloemfontein, South Africa, he was raised in England from early childhood. Tolkien studied at Exeter College, Oxford, served in World War I, and subsequently built a distinguished academic career. He held professorships at the University of Oxford, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon and later as the Merton Professor of English Language and Literature. An expert in Germanic philology and Old English, he made lasting contributions to academic scholarship. Tolkien achieved worldwide recognition through his fiction, particularly the 1937 children's novel The Hobbit and the high fantasy epic The Lord of the Rings, published in 1954 and 1955. His broader legendarium, including The Silmarillion, was edited and published posthumously by his son Christopher. Renowned for his elaborate world-building and invented languages, Tolkien remains a central figure in modern fantasy literature.
cristiano-ronaldo: Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro is a Portuguese association football player who is internationally recognized as one of the most successful figures in modern sports. Born on February 5, 1985, in Funchal, Madeira, he began his senior career with Sporting CP before signing with Manchester United in 2003. Ronaldo achieved widespread success during his first stint at Manchester United and later at Real Madrid, where he became the club's all-time leading goalscorer. He subsequently played for Juventus and returned briefly to Manchester United before joining the Saudi club Al Nassr in 2023. As captain of the Portugal national team, he led his country to victory at the 2016 UEFA European Championship and the 2019 Nations League. Recognized for his athleticism, goal-scoring prowess, and longevity, Ronaldo holds several records, including the most international goals scored in men's football history, and has won five Ballon d'Or awards.
hillary-clinton: Hillary Diane Rodham Clinton, born October 26, 1947, is an American politician, diplomat, and lawyer who served as the 67th United States Secretary of State from 2009 to 2013. Raised in Park Ridge, Illinois, she graduated from Wellesley College and Yale Law School. She married Bill Clinton in 1975 and served as First Lady of Arkansas before becoming First Lady of the United States from 1993 to 2001. As First Lady, she advocated for healthcare reform and children's rights. Clinton was elected as the first female U.S. Senator from New York in 2000, serving from 2001 until 2009. President Barack Obama subsequently appointed her Secretary of State, a role in which she directed American foreign policy during his first term. In 2016, she made history as the first woman to secure a major American political party's presidential nomination. Although she won the popular vote, she lost the Electoral College vote to Donald Trump.
harry-s-truman: Harry S. Truman was an American politician who served as the 33rd president of the United States from 1945 to 1953. Born on May 8, 1884, in Lamar, Missouri, he rose through local politics before representing Missouri in the United States Senate from 1935 to 1945. Truman became vice president under Franklin D. Roosevelt in January 1945 and succeeded to the presidency following Roosevelt's death in April. Shortly after taking office, he authorized the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, concluding World War II. His presidency marked the beginning of the Cold War, defined by the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, and the formation of NATO. Domestic accomplishments included ordering the desegregation of the United States Armed Forces. He also led the country through much of the Korean War. Truman left office in 1953 and died on December 26, 1972.
fr-d-ric-chopin: Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin, internationally known as Frédéric François Chopin, was a renowned Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic era. Born on March 1, 1810, in Żelazowa Wola, Poland, he published his first composition at a young age and gained early acclaim as a child prodigy in Warsaw. In 1831, Chopin settled in Paris, where he maintained a career as a composer, performer, and sought-after music teacher. Unlike many contemporaries, he preferred intimate salon performances over large public concerts. Chopin composed almost exclusively for solo piano, producing iconic works including nocturnes, mazurkas, waltzes, polonaises, ballades, and preludes. His music is celebrated for its technical complexity, harmonic innovation, and deep poetic expressiveness, often incorporating elements of Polish folk music. Throughout his life, Chopin suffered from frail health. He died of tuberculosis in Paris on October 17, 1849, at the age of thirty-nine.
jean-paul-sartre: Jean-Paul Charles Aymard Sartre was an internationally known French existentialist philosopher, playwright, novelist, screenwriter, and political activist who lived from 1905 to 1980. Born in Paris, he became one of the leading figures in twentieth-century French philosophy and Marxism. Sartre studied at the École Normale Supérieure and later taught philosophy. His seminal philosophical work, Being and Nothingness, published in 1943, explored concepts of human freedom, responsibility, and existential angst. Beyond technical philosophy, he achieved literary fame with his 1938 novel Nausea and his 1944 play No Exit. Sartre maintained a lifelong intellectual and romantic partnership with the feminist philosopher Simone de Beauvoir. In 1964, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, but he famously refused the honor, arguing that a writer should not allow himself to be transformed into an official institution. He remained dedicated to leftist political causes and social critique until his death in Paris in 1980.
lady-gaga: Lady Gaga, born Stefani Joanne Angelina Germanotta on March 28, 1986, is an American singer, songwriter, and actress. She rose to international prominence with her debut studio album, The Fame, in 2008, which produced hit singles such as Just Dance and Poker Face. Known for her musical versatility and visual transformations, she followed this with albums including The Fame Monster, Born This Way, Artpop, and Chromatica. Beyond music, she achieved recognition in acting, winning a Golden Globe Award for her role in the television series American Horror Story: Hotel. She gained further acclaim starring in the film A Star Is Born in 2018, receiving an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress and winning Best Original Song for Shallow. Throughout her career, she has accumulated numerous accolades, including multiple Grammy Awards, establishing herself as one of the world's best-selling music artists.
madonna: Madonna Louise Ciccone, born August 16, 1958, is an American singer, songwriter, and actress often referred to as the Queen of Pop. Raised in Michigan, she moved to New York City in 1978 to pursue a career in modern dance. After performing as a drummer and vocalist in music groups, she achieved solo success with her self-titled debut album in 1983. She followed it with critically and commercially acclaimed records such as Like a Virgin, Like a Prayer, and Ray of Light. Renowned for her continual reinvention and versatility in music production, songwriting, and visual presentation, she has pushed boundaries in artistic expression within mainstream music. As an actress, she starred in films such as Desperately Seeking Susan and won a Golden Globe Award for Best Actress for her role in Evita. Recognized as the best-selling female recording artist of all time by Guinness World Records, Madonna remains an influential cultural figure.
mother-teresa: Mother Teresa, born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, was an Albanian-Indian Roman Catholic nun and missionary. Born in Skopje in 1910, then part of the Ottoman Empire, she moved to Ireland in 1928 to join the Sisters of Loreto, before relocating to India in 1929. In 1950, she founded the Missionaries of Charity, a religious congregation that grew to manage homes, hospices, and centers for people with HIV/AIDS, leprosy, and tuberculosis, primarily in Kolkata. Renowned for her humanitarian work among the impoverished and dying, she expanded her congregation globally over the following decades. Her efforts earned her numerous accolades, most notably the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. Mother Teresa died in Kolkata on September 5, 1997, at the age of eighty-seven. She was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 2003 and canonized as Saint Teresa of Calcutta by Pope Francis in 2016.
theodore-roosevelt: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was an American statesman, conservationist, historian, and writer who served as the 26th president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. Born in New York City in 1858, he overcame childhood ill health to pursue a strenuous public and personal life. After attending Harvard College, he held various political offices, served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy, led the Rough Riders during the Spanish-American War, and became governor of New York. In March 1901, he assumed the vice presidency, ascending to the presidency six months later following the assassination of President William McKinley. As chief executive, Roosevelt implemented his Square Deal domestic agenda, which targeted large corporations, protected consumers, and vastly expanded national parks, forests, and wildlife refuges. In foreign affairs, he brokered the peace ending the Russo-Japanese War, winning the Nobel Peace Prize, and initiated construction of the Panama Canal. Roosevelt died in 1919.
agatha-christie: Dame Agatha Mary Clarissa Christie was an English mystery author born on September 15, 1890, in Torquay, Devon. Internationally renowned as the Queen of Crime, she wrote 66 detective novels, 14 short story collections, and six romantic novels under the pseudonym Mary Westmacott. Christie gained widespread fame for creating memorable fictional detectives, most notably the Belgian investigator Hercule Poirot and the amateur sleuth Miss Jane Marple. Her debut novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, introduced Poirot in 1920. Christie also authored The Mousetrap, the world's longest-running play, which premiered in London in 1952. During the First World War, she worked as a nurse and pharmacy dispenser, gaining detailed knowledge of poisons that frequently informed her literary plots. She was appointed a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1971 for her contributions to literature. Christie died on January 12, 1976, leaving a legacy as the best-selling fiction writer in history.
sarah-bernhardt: Sarah Bernhardt, born Henriette-Rosine Bernard, was an internationally acclaimed French stage actress, painter, and sculptor who lived from 1844 to 1923. Renowned as one of the most famous performers of her era, she gained global prominence during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Bernhardt began her professional acting career at the Comédie-Française in Paris before establishing herself as a leading figure in French theater. She achieved widespread acclaim for her roles in classic tragedies and contemporary dramas, including Jean Racine’s Phèdre, Victor Hugo’s Ruy Blas, and Edmond Rostand’s L'Aiglon. In addition to her theatrical success, she managed several Paris venues, including the Théâtre Sarah-Bernhardt. Beyond the stage, Bernhardt was a skilled artist whose sculptures and paintings were exhibited at the prestigious Paris Salon. Her extensive international tours across Europe, North America, and South America solidified her status as one of the world's first global celebrity performers.
alfred-nobel: Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, and businessman who lived from 1833 to 1896. Born in Stockholm, he was educated in Russia and the United States, developing a strong expertise in chemical engineering and explosives. Nobel is best known for inventing dynamite in 1867, a controllable explosive that revolutionized construction, mining, and engineering worldwide. Over his lifetime, he accumulated 355 patents for various chemical and mechanical innovations, including ballistite and gelignite. He also acquired the Swedish armaments company Bofors, transforming it into a major manufacturer of steel and artillery. Despite his immense fortune derived from weapons and explosives manufacturing, Nobel expressed a deep interest in literature and peace. Upon his death in San Remo, Italy, his final will stipulated that the majority of his vast estate be used to institute five annual awards. These became the prestigious Nobel Prizes, recognizing outstanding achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace.
dwight-d-eisenhower: Dwight David Eisenhower, who lived from 1890 to 1969, was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. Born in Denison, Texas, he graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1915. During World War II, Eisenhower achieved the rank of five-star general and served as Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe. In this capacity, he directed the 1944 Allied invasion of Normandy, which contributed significantly to the defeat of Nazi Germany. Following the war, he served as the military governor of the American zone in occupied Germany and became the first Supreme Allied Commander of NATO in 1951. As president, Eisenhower managed Cold War tensions with the Soviet Union, ended the Korean War, authorized the Interstate Highway System, established NASA, and enforced desegregation in Little Rock, Arkansas. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1969.
jorge-luis-borges: Jorge Francisco Isidoro Luis Borges Acevedo was an internationally known Argentine writer, essayist, poet, and translator who lived from 1899 to 1986. Born in Buenos Aires, he spent much of his youth in Switzerland and Spain, where he engaged with avant-garde literary movements before returning to Argentina in 1921. Borges gained global renown for his intricate short stories, particularly the collections Ficciones and The Aleph, which explored complex themes such as labyrinths, mirrors, infinity, dreams, and philosophical concepts. His pioneering work profoundly influenced Latin American literature and international postmodern fiction. In addition to his creative writing, he served as the director of the National Library of Argentina and taught literature at the University of Buenos Aires. Despite suffering from progressive blindness that rendered him completely blind by his fifties, he continued to compose works orally until his death in Geneva in 1986.
hugo-ch-vez: Hugo Rafael Chávez Frías was a Venezuelan politician and military officer who served as the 56th president of Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013. Born in Sabaneta in 1954, Chávez pursued a military career before co-founding the clandestine Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200. After leading a failed military coup attempt in 1992, he was imprisoned and later pardoned. He transitioned to electoral politics, founding the Fifth Republic Movement and winning the 1998 presidential election. Internationally known as a prominent socialist leader and vocal critic of United States foreign policy, Chávez instituted the Bolivarian Revolution in Venezuela. This movement introduced a new constitution, expansive state-funded social programs, and the nationalization of key economic sectors utilizing the country's oil wealth. Re-elected multiple times, he maintained significant influence over Latin American regional affairs until dying from cancer on March 5, 2013, in Caracas at age fifty-eight.
le-corbusier: Charles-Édouard Jeanneret-Gris, internationally known by his pseudonym Le Corbusier, was an influential Swiss-French architect, designer, urbanist, and writer who lived from 1887 to 1965. As a key pioneer of modern architecture and the International Style, he revolutionized design by developing the five points of a new architecture, which promoted reinforced concrete, support columns called pilotis, open interior spaces, roof gardens, and horizontal ribbon windows. His celebrated structural masterpieces include the Villa Savoye in Poissy, the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille, and the pilgrimage chapel of Notre-Dame du Haut in Ronchamp. In urban planning, Le Corbusier advocated for high-density, highly organized urban centers through theoretical projects like the Radiant City and designed the master plan for Chandigarh in India. A prolific writer, his seminal book Toward an Architecture famously characterized the home as a machine for living in. He also created enduring modernist furniture designs.
woodrow-wilson: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was an American academic and politician who served as the twenty-eighth president of the United States from 1913 to 1921. Born in Staunton, Virginia, he earned a doctorate in political science from Johns Hopkins University and later became the president of Princeton University and governor of New Jersey. As president, Wilson enacted progressive legislative reforms under his New Freedom program, establishing the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Trade Commission, and child labor laws. Internationally, Wilson initially maintained American neutrality during World War I before leading the nation into the conflict in 1917. Following the war, he authored the Fourteen Points peace proposal and championed the creation of the League of Nations to promote global stability, an effort that earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919. Suffering a debilitating stroke in 1919 while campaigning for treaty ratification, Wilson completed his term and died in 1924.
jules-verne: Jules Gabriel Verne was an internationally known French writer born in Nantes on February 8, 1828, and who died in Amiens on March 24, 1905. Best remembered for his pioneering adventure novels and early contributions to the science fiction genre, he initially studied law in Paris before committing fully to literature. Verne achieved great commercial success collaborating with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel to create the celebrated series Extraordinary Voyages, a sequence of fifty-four novels. Among his most famous works are Journey to the Center of the Earth, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, and Around the World in Eighty Days. His imaginative narrative style often anticipated major modern technological advancements, such as submarines, space travel, and airships. Today, Verne remains the second most-translated individual author in the world, widely recognized for his profound impact on global literature and popular culture.
rudyard-kipling: Joseph Rudyard Kipling was an internationally known English writer and poet who lived from 1865 to 1936. Born in Bombay, British India, his early childhood experiences in Asia deeply shaped his creative work. After completing his formal education in England, Kipling returned to India in 1882 to work as a journalist, where he began writing popular short stories. He rapidly achieved global fame for his imaginative fiction and verse. His most famous works include the children's classic short story collection The Jungle Book, the espionage novel Kim, and celebrated poems such as If and Mandalay. In 1907, Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, making him the first English language author to receive the honor. While his works remain celebrated worldwide for their narrative craft, his legacy also reflects the complex political context of British imperialism. He died in London in 1936 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
jimmy-carter: James Earl Carter Jr. lived from 1924 to 2024 and was an American politician and humanitarian who served as the thirty-ninth president of the United States from 1977 to 1981. Raised in Plains, Georgia, Carter graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1946 and served in the Navy's submarine force. After returning to Georgia to manage his family's peanut business, he entered public service as a state senator before serving as governor of Georgia. As president, he prioritized human rights, negotiated the Camp David Accords, signed the Panama Canal Treaties, and established executive departments for energy and education. His administration faced economic stagflation, an energy crisis, and the Iran hostage crisis. Following his presidency, Carter founded the Carter Center in 1982 to promote human rights, democracy, and global public health. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002 for his international humanitarian work.
frida-kahlo: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón was a Mexican painter known internationally for her uncompromising and vividly colored self-portraits. Born on July 6, 1907, in Coyoacán, Mexico City, Kahlo suffered from polio as a child and survived a devastating bus accident in 1925. The severe injuries left her with chronic pain and required numerous surgeries throughout her life. During her recovery, she began painting, often using a mirror mounted above her bed. Her works incorporated elements of traditional Mexican folk culture, surrealism, and symbolism, exploring themes of identity, pain, mortality, and the human body. In 1929, Kahlo married the prominent Mexican muralist Diego Rivera, a volatile relationship marked by mutual artistic influence and personal tumult. Kahlo was also politically active, maintaining ties to the Mexican Communist Party. She died on July 13, 1954, at the age of forty-seven. Posthumously, Kahlo achieved widespread acclaim, becoming a celebrated figure in modern art and feminist history.
emmanuel-macron: Emmanuel Jean-Michel Frédéric Macron is a French politician who has served as the president of France and ex officio Co-Prince of Andorra since May 2017. Born on December 21, 1977, in Amiens, Macron studied philosophy and public affairs before graduating from the École nationale d'administration in 2004. He worked as a senior civil servant and later became an investment banker at Rothschild & Co. Entering politics, Macron served as Deputy Secretary-General to President François Hollande and was appointed Minister of Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs in 2014. In 2016, he founded the centrist political movement En Marche! and resigned from government to run for president. Winning the 2017 election at thirty-nine, he became the youngest president in French history. His tenure has focused on labor reforms, economic modernization, and strengthening European integration. Macron was re-elected to a second term in April 2022.
bertrand-russell: Bertrand Arthur William Russell was an influential British philosopher, logician, mathematician, and public intellectual. Born in Monmouthshire, Wales, into an aristocratic family, he became one of the leading figures in the development of analytic philosophy in the early twentieth century. Russell made foundational contributions to mathematical logic, most notably through his work on set theory and Russell's paradox. Alongside Alfred North Whitehead, he co-authored the monumental three-volume Principia Mathematica, which attempted to ground mathematics on logical principles. Throughout his long career, Russell wrote extensively on epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, and political theory. Beyond academia, he was a prominent social critic, advocate for free thought, and anti-war activist. He was imprisoned for his pacifist stance during World War I and later campaigned vigorously against nuclear armament. In 1950, Russell was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for his varied writings championing humanitarian ideals. He died in 1970 at the age of ninety-seven.
raphael: Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino, universally known as Raphael, was an Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance. Born in Urbino in 1483, he received early artistic training from his father, Giovanni Santi, and later worked under Pietro Perugino. By 1504, Raphael had moved to Florence, where he produced numerous influential works, particularly depictions of the Madonna. In 1508, Pope Julius II invited him to Rome, where he executed monumental fresco cycles in the Vatican Palace, including The School of Athens. Alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, Raphael formed the traditional trinity of High Renaissance masters. Beyond painting, he was appointed chief architect of Saint Peter's Basilica in 1514. Known for his clarity of form, compositional harmony, and visual poise, Raphael ran an unusually large and productive workshop. He died prematurely in Rome on April 6, 1520, at the age of thirty-seven, leaving behind a profound artistic legacy.
richard-nixon: Richard Milhous Nixon (1913–1994) was an American politician who served as the 37th president of the United States from 1969 to 1974. A member of the Republican Party, he previously served as a U.S. representative and senator from California, and as the 36th vice president under Dwight D. Eisenhower from 1953 to 1961. Nixon's presidency was marked by significant foreign policy achievements, including opening diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, signing the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with the Soviet Union, and ending direct U.S. military involvement in the Vietnam War. Domestically, his administration established the Environmental Protection Agency and enforced desegregation of Southern schools. However, his second term was overwhelmed by the Watergate scandal, a political crisis involving a break-in at Democratic headquarters and a subsequent cover-up. Facing impeachment, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, becoming the only American president to resign from office.
alan-turing: Alan Mathison Turing was an English mathematician, computer scientist, logician, and cryptanalyst, born on June 23, 1912, and deceased on June 7, 1954. Highly influential in the development of theoretical computer science, he provided a formalization of the concepts of algorithm and computation through the theoretical model known as the Turing machine. During the Second World War, Turing worked at Bletchley Park, Britain's main codebreaking center. There, he played a crucial role in cracking intercepted ciphers, most notably those produced by the German Enigma machine, which significantly aided the Allied effort. After the war, he contributed to early computer architecture by designing the Automatic Computing Engine and devised the Turing test to evaluate artificial intelligence. In 1952, Turing was convicted of gross indecency for homosexual acts, undergoing chemical castration. He died two years later from cyanide poisoning. In 2013, he received a posthumous royal pardon.
arthur-conan-doyle: Sir Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle was a British writer and physician who lived from 1859 to 1930. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, he studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh Medical School before establishing a medical practice. Doyle began writing stories during his time as a doctor. He gained international renown as the creator of the fictional detective Sherlock Holmes and his companion, Dr. John Watson. Holmes first appeared in the 1887 novel A Study in Scarlet, eventually featuring in four novels and fifty-six short stories. Beyond his detective fiction, Doyle was a prolific author who wrote historical novels, science fiction tales such as The Lost World, poetry, and non-fiction. He was knighted in 1902 for his service to the nation, which included writing pamphlets supporting Britain's position in the Boer War. Later in life, Doyle became a prominent advocate for Spiritualism. He died of a heart attack at his home in Sussex at age seventy-one.
marcel-proust: Valentin Louis Georges Eugène Marcel Proust was a prominent French novelist, critic, and essayist born in Paris on July 10, 1871. Raised in a wealthy, bourgeois family, Proust suffered from severe asthma from childhood, an illness that profoundly affected his life and career. He initially frequented Parisian literary salons and wrote short stories, articles, and critical essays, including early works such as Pleasures and Days and his posthumously published essay collection Against Sainte-Beuve. Proust is internationally best known for his monumental novel In Search of Lost Time, published in seven volumes between 1913 and 1927. The masterpiece explores themes of involuntary memory, art, society, and time, leaving a lasting legacy on modern literature. In his final years, Proust lived as a recluse, working tirelessly in his famous cork-lined bedroom to complete his life's work. He died of pneumonia in Paris on November 18, 1922.
muhammad-ali: Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. on January 17, 1942, was an American professional boxer and activist widely regarded as one of the greatest heavyweight fighters in sports history. He won a light heavyweight gold medal at the 1960 Rome Olympics before turning professional. In 1964, after defeating Sonny Liston to win the world heavyweight championship, he converted to Islam and changed his name to Muhammad Ali. In 1967, Ali refused military induction during the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs, which led to a draft evasion conviction, the loss of his boxing license, and the stripping of his title. After his conviction was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1971, Ali returned to the ring, ultimately becoming the first three-time lineal heavyweight champion. He retired from boxing in 1981 and focused on humanitarian causes until his death on June 3, 2016.
george-bernard-shaw: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic, and polemicist whose influence extended deeply into Western culture. Born in Dublin on July 26, 1856, he moved to London in 1876, where he established himself as an influential music and theater critic. Shaw became an ardent socialist and a leading member of the Fabian Society, using his writing to promote social reform, women's rights, and economic equality. Over his career, he wrote more than sixty plays, blending comedic wit with incisive social commentary. His most famous works include Pygmalion, Major Barbara, Man and Superman, and Saint Joan. Through these works, Shaw challenged Victorian morality and transformed modern drama. In 1925, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, and he later won an Academy Award in 1938 for the screenplay adaptation of Pygmalion. Shaw remained active as a writer and public figure until his death on November 2, 1950.
john-lennon: John Winston Lennon was an English musician, singer, songwriter, and peace activist who achieved worldwide fame as a founder, co-lead vocalist, and rhythm guitarist of the Beatles. Born in Liverpool in 1940, Lennon demonstrated an early interest in music, forming his first band, the Quarrymen, in 1956. This group eventually evolved into the Beatles in 1960. Alongside Paul McCartney, Lennon formed one of the most successful songwriting partnerships in music history, contributing to the band's critical and commercial success throughout the 1960s. Following the dissolution of the Beatles in 1970, Lennon embarked on a solo career, producing renowned albums such as Plastic Ono Band and Imagine, as well as famous political anthems. He married artist Yoko Ono in 1969, and together they engaged in prominent peace activism. Lennon temporarily retired from music in 1975 to raise his son before returning with Double Fantasy in 1980. On December 8, 1980, he was fatally shot in New York City.
recep-tayyip-erdo-an: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is a Turkish politician who has served as the President of Turkey since August 2014. Born on February 26, 1954, in Istanbul, he began his political career in student groups during the 1970s and later served as the Mayor of Istanbul from 1994 to 1998. In 2001, he co-founded the Justice and Development Party, leading it to a major parliamentary victory the following year. Erdoğan served as Prime Minister of Turkey from 2003 to 2014 before assuming the presidency. During his leadership, he oversaw significant infrastructure expansion, initial economic growth, and a central transformation of Turkey's governance from a parliamentary system to an executive presidency following a 2017 constitutional referendum. His tenure has been marked by an active regional foreign policy and expanded diplomatic engagement. Erdoğan secured re-election to the presidency in 2018 and 2023, maintaining his position as a central figure in modern Turkish history.
bob-dylan: Bob Dylan, born Robert Allen Zimmerman on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota, is an American singer-songwriter who is widely considered one of the most influential figures in modern popular culture. Emerging in the early 1960s through the Greenwich Village folk music scene in New York City, he achieved widespread recognition with songs such as Blowin in the Wind and The Times They Are a-Changin. Dylan transformed popular songwriting by blending literary quality and social commentary with various musical styles, including folk, blues, rock, and country. His groundbreaking mid-1960s transition to electric instrumentation yielded historic rock albums like Highway 61 Revisited and Blonde on Blonde. With a career spanning over six decades, he has released over thirty studio albums and toured continuously. Dylan's artistic achievements have earned him ten Grammy Awards, an Academy Award, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature.
charles-baudelaire: Charles Pierre Baudelaire was an internationally acclaimed French poet, art critic, and translator whose work profoundly influenced the development of modern European literature. Born in Paris on April 9, 1821, Baudelaire became a pivotal figure in nineteenth-century culture. His landmark 1857 poetry collection, Les Fleurs du mal, explored themes of modern industrial life, urban spleen, sensuality, and existential despair. Though initially prosecuted for offending public morals, the volume revolutionized poetic form and aesthetic sensibility, establishing him as a chief forerunner of Symbolism and modernist literature. Beyond his original poetry, Baudelaire was an insightful art critic who championed painters like Eugène Delacroix and formulated influential ideas on modern art and urban dandyism. He was also instrumental in introducing American writer Edgar Allan Poe to French readers through his acclaimed translations. Plagued by financial difficulties and declining health, Baudelaire died in Paris on August 31, 1867, leaving a lasting literary legacy.
leon-trotsky: Leon Trotsky, born Lev Davidovich Bronstein in 1879, was a Russian Marxist revolutionary, political theorist, and key Soviet politician. He initially aligned with the Mensheviks before joining Vladimir Lenin and the Bolsheviks prior to the 1917 October Revolution. Trotsky played a pivotal role in the Bolshevik rise to power, serving as the first People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs and organizing the Red Army as the People's Commissar for Military and Naval Affairs during the Russian Civil War. Following Lenin's death in 1924, Trotsky emerged as the leader of the Left Opposition, advocating for permanent revolution and opposing Joseph Stalin's rise to power and doctrine of socialism in one country. Defeated in the political struggle, Trotsky was expelled from the Communist Party in 1927 and deported from the Soviet Union in 1929. He continued writing and criticizing Stalinism while living in exile, ultimately settling in Mexico, where he was assassinated by a Soviet agent in 1940.
john-adams: John Adams was an American statesman, attorney, diplomat, writer, and Founding Father who served as the second president of the United States from 1797 to 1801. Born on October 30, 1735, in Braintree, Massachusetts, he was educated at Harvard College and established a successful legal career. Adams emerged as a key leader of the American Revolution. In the Continental Congress, he advocated for independence and assisted Thomas Jefferson in drafting the Declaration of Independence in 1776. During the Revolutionary War, he represented the nation on diplomatic missions in Europe, helping negotiate the 1783 Treaty of Paris. Adams served as the nation's first vice president under George Washington from 1789 to 1797. His presidential term was marked by foreign policy challenges, including the Quasi-War with France, and the passage of the Alien and Sedition Acts. After his presidency, he retired to Massachusetts, where he died on July 4, 1826.
rosa-luxemburg: Rozalia Luxemburg, internationally known as Rosa Luxemburg, was a Polish-German Marxist theorist, philosopher, economist, and revolutionary socialist who lived from 1871 to 1919. Born in Zamość, Congress Poland, she became a central figure in the European socialist movement. She co-founded the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania before relocating to Germany, where she joined the Social Democratic Party of Germany. Luxemburg critically analyzed capitalism and imperialism, developing influential theories on mass strikes and democratic socialism. A staunch opponent of World War I, she left her party to co-found the anti-war Spartacus League alongside Karl Liebknecht. This organization later evolved into the Communist Party of Germany. Following the failed Spartacist Uprising in Berlin, Luxemburg was captured and extrajudicially executed by right-wing Freikorps paramilitary forces on January 15, 1919. Today, she remains an influential figure in socialist thought and international political theory.
noam-chomsky: Avram Noam Chomsky, born December 7, 1928, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an American linguist, philosopher, cognitive scientist, and political activist. Often called the father of modern linguistics, he revolutionized the field in the 1950s by introducing the concept of generative grammar, which posited that the ability to learn language is an innate human capability. His work significantly influenced cognitive science, psychology, and computer science. Beyond academia, Chomsky became a prominent political figure and social critic starting in the 1960s with his opposition to the Vietnam War. He has authored dozens of books critiquing American foreign policy, global capitalism, and mass media, co-writing the seminal media analysis work Manufacturing Consent. As an institute professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and laureate professor at the University of Arizona, Chomsky remains one of the most cited scholars in modern history and a major intellectual voice in global political discourse.
alfred-hitchcock: Sir Alfred Joseph Hitchcock was an internationally known British filmmaker whose career spanned six decades. Born on August 13, 1899, in London, he began his career in the British film industry during the silent era, directing acclaimed works such as The Lodger and Blackmail. In 1939, Hitchcock relocated to Hollywood, where he achieved immense critical and commercial success. Renowned as the Master of Suspense, he pioneered innovative cinematic techniques, including complex camera movements, precise editing, and distinctive point-of-view shots. His filmography includes iconic psychological thrillers and suspense films such as Rebecca, Rear Window, Vertigo, North by Northwest, Psycho, and The Birds. Beyond feature films, he achieved widespread popularity hosting the television series Alfred Hitchcock Presents. He received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award in 1967 and was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in early 1980. Hitchcock died in Los Angeles on April 29, 1980.
elon-musk: Elon Reeve Musk is an internationally known American businessman and investor born on June 28, 1971, in Pretoria, South Africa. He gained early prominence after co-founding the online mapping software company Zip2 and the digital payments system PayPal. In 2002, Musk founded Space Exploration Technologies Corp., known as SpaceX, an aerospace manufacturer and space transport services company where he serves as chief executive officer. He joined the electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla Motors, Inc. in 2004 as an early investor and chairman, later becoming its chief executive officer and primary product architect. Musk also co-founded Neuralink, a neurotechnology enterprise, and founded The Boring Company, an infrastructure construction service. In 2022, he purchased the global social media platform Twitter, which he subsequently rebranded as X. Musk is recognized globally for his leadership in technology, sustainable energy, commercial spaceflight, and digital communications, making him one of the most prominent figures in modern business history.
maxim-gorky: Maxim Gorky, whose full name was Alexei Maximovich Peshkov, was an internationally known Russian and Soviet writer and political activist who lived from 1868 to 1936. Born in Nizhny Novgorod, he endured a difficult childhood that inspired much of his early literary work. Gorky rose to fame with short stories describing the lives of marginalized social groups, eventually achieving worldwide acclaim for his powerful prose and drama, including the famous play The Lower Depths and the novel Mother. A prominent figure in the Russian revolutionary movement, he maintained a complex relationship with the Bolshevik party and spent several years in self-imposed exile in Italy. Upon his return to the Soviet Union in the 1930s at the invitation of Joseph Stalin, Gorky was celebrated as a founder of Socialist Realism, the official Soviet literary doctrine. He remained an influential literary administrator and public intellectual until his death in Moscow in 1936.
pel: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known universally as Pelé, was a Brazilian professional footballer widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. Born on October 23, 1940, in Três Corações, Brazil, he began his senior club career with Santos FC at age fifteen and made his international debut for Brazil at sixteen. Pelé is the only player to have won three FIFA World Cup tournaments, lifting the trophy in 1958, 1962, and 1970. During his club career with Santos, he won numerous national and international titles, including two Copa Libertadores trophies, before ending his playing days with the New York Cosmos in 1977. Over his career, he scored more than one thousand goals across official and friendly matches. Following his retirement, Pelé served as a global ambassador for football and as Brazil's Extraordinary Minister for Sport. He died on December 29, 2022, in São Paulo.
roald-amundsen: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was a Norwegian explorer who lived from 1872 to 1928 and became one of the key figures of polar exploration. Internationally known for his remarkable navigational skills and meticulous planning, he led the first expedition to successfully reach the South Pole, arriving on December 14, 1911. Before his Antarctic triumph, Amundsen achieved another historical milestone between 1903 and 1906 by leading the first ship navigation through the Northwest Passage. In 1926, he participated in the airship Norge expedition, which accomplished the first verified air crossing of the Arctic and the first undisputed arrival at the North Pole. Consequently, Amundsen is recognized as the first person to reach both the North and South Poles. He disappeared in June 1928 while participating in a search and rescue mission for a crashed airship in the Arctic Ocean.
rafael-correa: Rafael Vicente Correa Delgado is an Ecuadorian politician and economist who served as the President of Ecuador from 2007 to 2017. Internationally known for leading the left-wing Citizens' Revolution movement, he implemented significant political, economic, and social reforms, including a new constitution in 2008 and increased public spending that reduced poverty and improved national infrastructure. Educated in Ecuador, Belgium, and the United States, Correa served briefly as Minister of Economy and Finance before winning the presidency in 2006. Following the end of his third consecutive presidential term, he relocated to Belgium, his wife's home country. In 2020, an Ecuadorian court convicted him in absentia of corruption and sentenced him to eight years in prison. Maintaining his innocence and claiming political persecution, Correa was granted political asylum by Belgium in 2022, though Ecuadorian judicial authorities continue to seek his extradition, classifying him as a fugitive from justice, or prófugo de la justicia.
freddie-mercury: Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara on September 5, 1946, was an internationally known British singer, songwriter, and musician who achieved global fame as the frontman of the rock band Queen. Born in Zanzibar to Parsi-Indian parents, he spent much of his childhood in India before immigrating to England in 1964.
