In 1970, he co-founded Queen alongside guitarist Brian May and drummer Roger Taylor, later joined by bassist John Deacon. Known for his theatrical stage presence and a versatile four-octave vocal range, Mercury composed numerous enduring hits for the group, including Bohemian Rhapsody, Killer Queen, Somebody to Love, Don't Stop Me Now, and We Are the Champions. He also pursued solo projects, notably recording the 1988 album Barcelona with Spanish soprano Montserrat Caballé. Following a brilliant career that redefined rock performance, Mercury died on November 24, 1991, at age forty-five due to complications from AIDS.
john-maynard-keynes: John Maynard Keynes, born in 1883 and died in 1946, was a British economist whose ideas fundamentally altered the theory and practice of modern macroeconomics and national economic policies. Educated at Eton College and King's College, Cambridge, Keynes served in the British Treasury during the First World War. He gained international renown with his 1919 book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which criticized the heavy reparations imposed on Germany after the war. His landmark 1936 work, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, challenged classical economic doctrine by advocating for active government intervention, public spending, and fiscal policy to manage aggregate demand and mitigate economic recessions. Near the end of his life, Keynes played a decisive role in shaping the post-war global financial architecture at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference, contributing to the establishment of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Keynesian economics remains central to modern macroeconomic theory.
guillermo-lasso: Guillermo Alberto Santiago Lasso Mendoza is an Ecuadorian politician and businessman who served as the 55th President of Ecuador from May 2021 to November 2023. Born in Guayaquil on November 16, 1955, Lasso pursued a career in the financial sector, eventually becoming the executive president of Banco de Guayaquil. He entered public service in the late 1990s, serving as Governor of Guayas and briefly as Minister of Economy. In 2012, he founded the center-right Creating Opportunities party. After unsuccessful presidential bids in 2013 and 2017, Lasso won the 2021 general election. His presidency focused on economic liberalization and a swift COVID-19 vaccination campaign, but encountered significant obstacles due to rising gang violence and political deadlock. In May 2023, amid impeachment proceedings, Lasso invoked the constitutional mechanism known as muerte cruzada, dissolving the National Assembly and calling early elections. He opted not to run and stepped down in November 2023.
kofi-annan: Kofi Atta Annan was a Ghanaian diplomat who served as the seventh Secretary-General of the United Nations from January 1997 to December 2006. Born on April 8, 1938, in Kumasi, Ghana, Annan joined the United Nations system in 1962 as an officer with the World Health Organization. He advanced through the organizational ranks, eventually serving as the Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations during the mid-1990s. As Secretary-General, he prioritized reforming UN bureaucracy, advocating for human rights, and promoting global development initiatives. He launched the Millennium Development Goals in 2000 and helped create the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. In 2001, Annan and the United Nations were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their efforts toward a better organized and more peaceful world. Following his UN tenure, he established the Kofi Annan Foundation and mediated various international conflicts. He died in Switzerland on August 18, 2018.
lyndon-b-johnson: Lyndon Baines Johnson (1908–1973) was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. Internationally known for his extensive domestic legislation and his leadership during the Vietnam War, Johnson initially assumed the presidency following the assassination of John F. Kennedy. He subsequently won a full term in a landslide victory in the 1964 presidential election. Before reaching the White House, the Texas Democrat served in the U.S. House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate, and as vice president. Johnson’s ambitious domestic platform, known as the Great Society, led to the passage of landmark civil rights and healthcare legislation, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, Medicare, and Medicaid. However, his presidency was increasingly dominated by the escalation of United States military involvement in the Vietnam War. Widespread public opposition to the conflict ultimately prompted Johnson to decline seeking reelection in 1968.
huang-xianfan: Huang Xianfan was a prominent twentieth-century Chinese historian, ethnologist, and educator. Born in Fusui, Guangxi, in 1899, he received his education at Beijing Normal University and Tokyo Imperial University. Over a distinguished career spanning several decades, Huang taught at numerous prestigious institutions, including Sun Yat-sen University, Guangxi University, and Guangxi Normal University. He made foundational contributions to the study of Chinese history and minority nationalities. Huang is widely considered the father of Zhuangology, the academic field dedicated to the history, language, and culture of the Zhuang ethnic group, China's largest minority population. His scholarly output included comprehensive texts on Chinese history and pioneering field studies in Guangxi. Despite facing political persecution as a labeled rightist during the late 1950s, he remained dedicated to education and research until his death in 1982. Today, Huang Xianfan is recognized as one of the most influential figures in modern Chinese ethnic studies.
francisco-goya: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes was a Spanish painter and printmaker born in Fuendetodos, Spain, on March 30, 1746. He is widely considered one of the most significant Spanish artists of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, often described as both the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. Goya achieved national prominence as a court painter to the Spanish Crown, serving under King Charles III and King Charles IV. His early career featured colorful tapestry cartoons and formal portraits of the nobility. However, a severe illness in 1792 left him permanently deaf, leading to a dramatic shift in his artistic style toward darker, more psychological, and politically critical subject matter. His notable works include print series such as Los Caprichos and masterful paintings like The Third of May 1808. Goya later created his haunting Black Paintings before moving to France, where he died on April 16, 1828.
rafael-orozco-maestre: Rafael José Orozco Maestre was a prominent Colombian singer and one of the most influential figures in vallenato music. Born on March 24, 1954, in Becerril, Cesar, Colombia, he developed an interest in singing during his youth. In 1976, Orozco Maestre co-founded the acclaimed musical group El Binomio de Oro alongside accordionist Israel Romero. As the group's lead vocalist, he introduced a romantic interpretation to traditional vallenato, which modernized the genre and expanded its commercial audience. Under his vocal leadership, El Binomio de Oro achieved international success, earning multiple gold and platinum records while touring extensively across Latin America, the Caribbean, and the United States. On June 11, 1992, Orozco Maestre was fatally shot outside his home in Barranquilla, Colombia. Despite his untimely death, his recordings and charismatic stage persona left an enduring mark on Colombian popular culture and Latin American music history.
lech-wa-sa: Lech Wałęsa, born on September 29, 1943, is a Polish statesman, trade union organizer, and human rights activist who served as the President of Poland from 1990 to 1995. Originally employed as an electrician at the Gdańsk Shipyard, Wałęsa became an ardent labor activist during the late 1960s and 1970s. In 1980, he led a historic strike that resulted in the Gdańsk Agreement, which allowed workers to form independent trade unions. He co-founded and headed Solidarity, the first independent labor union in the Soviet bloc. Despite facing government persecution and internment under martial law, Wałęsa maintained nonviolent resistance, earning him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. He subsequently led negotiations with the communist government during the Round Table Talks of 1989. These discussions paved the way for semi-free elections and Poland's transition to a democratic state, where Wałęsa was elected as the country's first post-communist president.
michael-faraday: Michael Faraday was an eminent British scientist born on September 22, 1791, in Newington Butts, England, and died on August 25, 1867. Raised in a working-class family with little formal education, Faraday educated himself during an apprenticeship with a London bookbinder. In 1813, he became a laboratory assistant to chemist Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution, where he spent most of his career. Faraday made fundamental contributions to physics and chemistry. His primary discoveries include electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism, and the laws of electrolysis. He invented early devices for electromagnetic rotation, creating the foundation for electric motor and generator technology. In chemistry, Faraday discovered benzene, invented an early form of the Bunsen burner, and popularized terms such as anode, cathode, and ion. He served as the first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry at the Royal Institution, establishing its annual Christmas Lectures. Faraday is remembered as one of history's greatest experimental scientists.
diego-maradona: Diego Armando Maradona was an Argentine professional football player and manager who is widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. Born on October 30, 1960, in Lanús, Argentina, he began his senior career at Argentinos Juniors before transferring to Boca Juniors. Maradona later played for European clubs including Barcelona and Napoli, where he achieved historic success, leading Napoli to two Serie A titles and a UEFA Cup. Internationally, he earned 91 caps for Argentina and scored 34 goals. He captained his country to victory in the 1986 FIFA World Cup, a tournament highlighted by his memorable performances against England. Following his retirement from playing, Maradona transitioned into management, coaching several clubs and serving as head coach of the Argentine national team from 2008 to 2010. He died on November 25, 2020, leaving a lasting legacy in global football.
eminem: Marshall Bruce Mathers III, known professionally as Eminem, is an American rapper, record producer, and actor born on October 17, 1972. He is credited with popularizing hip hop to a broader audience and is regarded as one of the most successful hip hop artists in history. Mathers achieved mainstream fame in 1999 with his album The Slim Shady LP, winning a Grammy Award for Best Rap Album. His subsequent projects, The Marshall Mathers LP and The Eminem Show, achieved massive commercial success worldwide. In 2002, Eminem starred in the drama film 8 Mile, winning the Academy Award for Best Original Song for Lose Yourself, making him the first hip hop artist to receive the honor. As an executive, he established Shady Records. Mathers has sold over two hundred million records globally and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
sim-n-bol-var: Simón Bolívar, whose full name was Simón José Antonio de la Santísima Trinidad Bolívar y Palacios Ponte-Andrade y Blanco, was an internationally known Venezuelan statesman and military officer (1783–1830). Born in Caracas to a wealthy aristocratic family, he played a central role in the South American wars of independence against Spanish colonial rule. Influenced by Enlightenment ideas, Bolívar led military campaigns that liberated present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, which was named in his honor. In 1819, he established Gran Colombia, a republic encompassing much of northern South America, and served as its president until 1830. Often referred to as El Libertador, or The Liberator, his political vision aimed to create a unified Hispanic America, though political factionalism ultimately led to the dissolution of Gran Colombia before his death in Santa Marta, Colombia. Bolívar remains one of the most prominent geopolitical figures in Latin American history.
alexandre-dumas: Alexandre Dumas, born Dumas Davy de la Pailleterie, was a celebrated French writer and dramatist born on July 24, 1802, in Villers-Cotterêts, France. He was the son of Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, a French general born to a nobleman and an enslaved Afro-Caribbean woman. Dumas began his literary career writing plays, achieving early success with popular romantic dramas. He later transitioned to authoring serialized historical adventure novels, gaining immense international acclaim. His most famous works, including The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, were published in the mid-1840s. Prolific and versatile, he authored hundreds of plays, novels, and travel journals, often working alongside collaborators such as Auguste Maquet. Characterized by rapid pacing and vivid storytelling, his books were translated into numerous languages and adapted into countless stage productions and films. Dumas died on December 5, 1870, in Puys, France. He remains one of France's most widely read authors.
j-k-rowling: Joanne Rowling, internationally known by her pen name J. K. Rowling, is a British author and philanthropist born on July 31, 1965, in Yate, Gloucestershire, England. She achieved global fame as the creator of the Harry Potter fantasy series, which has sold over 600 million copies worldwide and been translated into dozens of languages. The seven-book series inspired a hugely successful film franchise, spin-offs, and an expansive media brand. Rowling has also written fiction for adults, including The Casual Vacancy and a crime novel series featuring detective Cormoran Strike published under the pseudonym Robert Galbraith. Beyond her literary career, Rowling is a prominent philanthropist. She established the Volant Charitable Trust to support women, children, and social inequality initiatives, and founded Lumos, an international charity working to end the institutionalization of children. Her contributions to literature and charity have earned her numerous awards and international recognition throughout her career.
justin-bieber: Justin Drew Bieber is an internationally known Canadian singer-songwriter born on March 1, 1994, in London, Ontario. Discovered in 2007 by talent manager Scooter Braun after posting cover songs on YouTube, Bieber signed with RBMG Records in 2008. He achieved rapid global fame following the release of his debut extended play, My World, in 2009, and his first full-length studio album, My World 2.0, in 2010, which featured the hit single Baby. As his career progressed, Bieber transitioned toward a mix of pop, R&B, and electronic music. Subsequent successful albums include Purpose in 2015, Changes in 2020, and Justice in 2021, yielding chart-topping tracks such as Sorry, Love Yourself, and Peaches. Throughout his career, Bieber has earned two Grammy Awards, multiple American Music Awards, and numerous Billboard Music Awards, establishing himself as one of the best-selling music artists of all time.
henri-matisse: Henri-Émile-Benoît Matisse was a prominent French artist who lived from 1869 to 1954. Internationally known for his expressive use of color and fluid draughtsmanship, he played a central role in the development of modern art during the early twentieth century. Born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis, Matisse initially studied law before turning to painting in 1889. He emerged as a leader of the short-lived Fauvist movement in the early 1900s, producing works characterized by vivid, non-naturalistic colors and bold brushwork. Throughout his long career, Matisse mastered multiple mediums, including sculpture, printmaking, and drawing. In his later years, facing health issues that hindered his ability to paint, he developed an innovative technique of creating large-scale paper cut-outs. Along with Pablo Picasso, Matisse is widely regarded as one of the defining figures in twentieth-century visual arts. He died in Nice, France, at age eighty-four.
anna-netrebko: Anna Yuryevna Netrebko is a Russian and Austrian operatic soprano born on September 18, 1971, in Krasnodar, Soviet Union. She studied vocal performance at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory and was discovered by conductor Valery Gergiev at the Mariinsky Theatre. Netrebko achieved international fame in 2002 after performing as Donna Anna in Mozart's Don Giovanni at the Salzburg Festival. Renowned for her vocal versatility and stage presence, she became a leading performer at major opera houses worldwide, including the Metropolitan Opera, the Royal Opera House, and the Vienna State Opera. Her repertoire spans bel canto, lyric, and dramatic soprano roles in works by Verdi, Puccini, Mozart, and Tchaikovsky. She acquired Austrian citizenship in 2006. In 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Netrebko faced scrutiny regarding her political ties, leading to canceled engagements at some Western venues. She later condemned the war and resumed performing internationally.
simone-de-beauvoir: Simone Lucie Ernestine Bertrand de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was an internationally known French philosopher, social theorist, novelist, and political activist. Born in Paris, she studied philosophy at the Sorbonne, where she formed a lifelong intellectual and personal partnership with Jean-Paul Sartre. De Beauvoir made foundational contributions to existentialist thought and feminist theory. Her groundbreaking 1949 treatise, The Second Sex, offered a comprehensive analysis of women's historic subjugation and the social construction of gender, significantly influencing second-wave feminism. In addition to her theoretical treatises, such as The Ethics of Ambiguity, she wrote acclaimed literary works, including the novel The Mandarins, which was awarded the Prix Goncourt in 1954. Throughout her life, de Beauvoir remained committed to political activism, advocating for women's rights, reproductive freedom, and anti-colonial causes. Her extensive memoirs, novels, and philosophical writings established her enduring legacy as one of the twentieth century's most influential intellectuals.
peter-the-great: Pyotr Alekseyevich Romanov, internationally known as Peter the Great, was a monarch who ruled Russia as Tsar from 1682 and as its first Emperor from 1721 until his death in 1725. Born in Moscow in 1672, he initiated extensive political, cultural, and military reforms designed to modernize Russia according to Western European models. His victory in the Great Northern War against Sweden expanded Russian territory along the Baltic Sea, establishing the nation as a major European power. In 1703, Peter founded the city of Saint Petersburg, which became the imperial capital in 1712. He reorganized the military, created the Imperial Russian Navy, restructured government administration, and imposed cultural changes, including compulsory secular education for nobility. While his autocracy and rapid Westernization faced internal resistance and cost many lives, Peter transformed Russia into a formidable empire, leaving a profound and enduring legacy on Eastern European history.
michael-schumacher: Michael Schumacher is a German former racing driver who competed in Formula One from 1991 to 2006 and from 2010 to 2012. Born on January 3, 1969, in Hürth, West Germany, he is widely regarded as one of the greatest drivers in motorsport history. Schumacher won a joint-record seven Formula One World Drivers' Championship titles, securing his first two championships with Benetton in 1994 and 1995. He then joined Ferrari, where he won five consecutive titles from 2000 to 2004, leading an unprecedented era of success for the team. At the time of his final retirement, he held the records for the most race victories, pole positions, and podium finishes in Formula One. After retiring for a second time, Schumacher suffered a severe brain injury in a skiing accident in December 2013. He has since been receiving private medical care.
honor-de-balzac: Honoré de Balzac was a French novelist and playwright born on May 20, 1799, in Tours, France. He is widely regarded as one of the founding figures of literary realism in European literature. His magnum opus, a vast collection of interlinked novels and short stories titled La Comédie humaine, offers a comprehensive panoramic view of French society following the fall of Napoleon Bonaparte in 1815. Through meticulous observation and complex characterization, Balzac depicted individuals from all social strata, examining themes of ambition, wealth, passion, and social mobility. Famous works within this sequence include Le Père Goriot and Eugénie Grandet. Renowned for his obsessive work ethic and heavy coffee consumption, Balzac wrote relentlessly to manage substantial personal debts. Shortly before his death, he married the Polish countess Ewelina Hańska. Balzac died in Paris on August 18, 1850, leaving a profound legacy that influenced generations of writers worldwide.
gerald-ford: Gerald Rudolph Ford Jr., born Leslie Lynch King Jr. on July 14, 1913, was an American politician who served as the 38th president of the United States from 1974 to 1977. Internationally known for his political leadership during a domestic crisis, Ford remains the only person to hold both the vice presidency and presidency without being elected to either office. Before entering the executive branch, he served in the United States House of Representatives for 24 years representing Michigan, eventually becoming House Minority Leader. Ford became vice president in 1973 following Spiro Agnew's resignation and assumed the presidency after Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 amid the Watergate scandal. His presidential term featured the controversial pardon of Nixon, economic challenges like stagflation, and foreign policy developments such as the Helsinki Accords. Ford lost the 1976 election to Jimmy Carter and died on December 26, 2006.
xi-jinping: Xi Jinping, born on June 15, 1953, in Beijing, is a Chinese politician who has served as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and Chairman of the Central Military Commission since 2012. He has also been the President of the People's Republic of China since 2013. The son of communist veteran Xi Zhongxun, he worked in rural Shaanxi during the Cultural Revolution before earning a degree in chemical engineering from Tsinghua University. Xi rose through provincial administrative roles in Fujian, Zhejiang, and Shanghai, entering the Politburo Standing Committee in 2007 and serving as Vice President from 2008 to 2013. As China's paramount leader, Xi initiated a sweeping anti-corruption campaign, promoted the Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure project, and oversaw a more assertive foreign policy. In 2018, term limits for the presidency were removed, and in 2022, he secured an unprecedented third term as party leader.
frank-lloyd-wright: Frank Lloyd Wright, born Frank Lincoln Wright on June 8, 1867, was an internationally known American architect, interior designer, writer, and educator. Over a creative career spanning seven decades, he designed more than 1,000 structures, of which over 500 were fully realized. Wright pioneered the Prairie School movement, an architectural style characterized by low roofs, open floor plans, and prominent horizontal lines that harmonized with the Midwestern landscape. He developed the philosophy of organic architecture, which aimed to design structures in harmony with humanity and their surrounding environment. Among his most famous designs are Fallingwater in rural Pennsylvania, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York City, and the Robie House in Chicago. He also established the Taliesin fellowship communities in Wisconsin and Arizona to educate future generations of architects. Wright died on April 9, 1959, in Phoenix, Arizona, leaving a lasting legacy in modern architecture.
andy-warhol: Andy Warhol, born Andrew Warhola Jr. on August 6, 1928, was an American artist, film director, and producer who became a leading figure in the Pop Art movement. Raised in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, he initially achieved success as a commercial illustrator in New York City during the 1950s. By the 1960s, Warhol gained international fame for his innovative artworks exploring consumer culture, celebrity, and mass media. He employed silkscreen printing to create iconic images of everyday objects, such as Campbell's Soup Cans, and famous personalities, including Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley. Warhol also established a studio known as The Factory, which served as a creative hub for artists, musicians, and intellectuals. In addition to visual art, he directed experimental films, produced music for the rock band The Velvet Underground, and founded Interview magazine. Warhol died in New York City on February 22, 1987, leaving a lasting legacy in contemporary art.
dmitry-medvedev: Dmitry Anatolyevich Medvedev is a Russian politician who has served as the Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of Russia since 2020. Born on September 14, 1965, in Leningrad, he studied law at Leningrad State University, where he later taught. Medvedev began his public service career in Saint Petersburg local government alongside Vladimir Putin before moving to Moscow to manage Putin's 2000 presidential campaign. He subsequently held key leadership roles, including chairman of Gazprom and First Deputy Prime Minister. Medvedev served as President of Russia from 2008 to 2012. His tenure focused on economic modernization, technological innovation, and international agreements, including the New START treaty. Following his presidency, he was appointed Prime Minister of Russia, a role he held from 2012 to 2020. Upon resigning from the premiership in January 2020, he assumed his post as Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of Russia.
henrik-ibsen: Henrik Johan Ibsen was an internationally known Norwegian playwright and theatre director who lived from 1828 to 1906. Often referred to as the father of realism, he is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in modern Western theatre. Born in Skien, Norway, Ibsen began his career working as an apothecary assistant before turning to literature and drama. He gained practical experience as a director and resident playwright at theatres in Bergen and Kristiania. In 1864, Ibsen left Norway for a long period of self-imposed exile in Italy and Germany, during which he wrote his most famous works. His verse dramas Brand and Peer Gynt gained critical acclaim, but his realistic prose plays, such as A Doll's House, Ghosts, and Hedda Gabler, brought him international fame. These works critically examined contemporary middle-class morality and social issues. He returned to Norway in 1891 and died in Kristiania in 1906.
steven-spielberg: Steven Allan Spielberg is an American filmmaker born on December 18, 1946, in Cincinnati, Ohio. Considered one of the most commercially successful and influential directors in cinema history, he emerged as a leading figure of the New Hollywood era during the 1970s. Spielberg gained widespread recognition with the blockbuster Jaws in 1975, which fundamentally changed the film industry's approach to summer releases. He subsequently directed major critical and commercial hits, including Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Raiders of the Lost Ark, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, and Jurassic Park. Expanding into historical drama, he directed Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan, winning Academy Awards for Best Director for both films. Beyond directing, Spielberg co-founded the production companies Amblin Entertainment and DreamWorks SKG, contributing significantly to modern television and film production. His work spans multiple genres, earning him critical acclaim, numerous accolades, and a profound impact on global popular culture.
mile-zola: Émile Édouard Charles Antoine Zola was an internationally known French novelist, journalist, playwright, and poet who lived from 1840 to 1902. As a leading figure in the literary school of naturalism, Zola transformed late nineteenth century literature through his rigorous, scientific approach to depicting social reality. He is best remembered for his monumental twenty volume novel cycle, Les Rougon-Macquart, which painstakingly tracked the influence of heredity and environment on a single family under the Second French Empire. Notable works within this series include Germinal, L'Assommoir, and Nana. Beyond his creative prose and theatrical works, Zola was a prominent journalist whose political activism dramatically impacted French history. In 1898, he published his famous open letter J'Accuse, defending the wrongly accused Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus, an act that galvanised the Dreyfus Affair and solidified Zola's status as a major public intellectual. He died in Paris in 1902.
james-madison: James Madison Jr. was an American statesman, diplomat, and Founding Father who served as the fourth president of the United States from 1809 to 1817. Born in Port Conway, Virginia, in 1751, he played a pivotal role in drafting and promoting the United States Constitution and the Bill of Rights, earning him the informal title Father of the Constitution. Madison co-authored The Federalist Papers alongside Alexander Hamilton and John Jay to encourage the ratification of the Constitution. Before his presidency, he served as a member of the United States House of Representatives and as Secretary of State under Thomas Jefferson. During his presidency, Madison led the nation through the War of 1812 against Great Britain, which affirmed American sovereignty. After completing his second term, he retired to Montpelier, his estate in Virginia, where he died in 1836.
louis-armstrong: Louis Daniel Armstrong was an American jazz trumpeter, cornetist, and singer who became one of the most influential figures in twentieth-century music. Born in New Orleans on August 4, 1901, Armstrong developed his musical skills in local brass bands and riverboats before moving to Chicago in 1922 to join King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. Through his groundbreaking recordings with his Hot Five and Hot Seven ensembles in the late 1920s, he shifted the focus of jazz from collective improvisation to individual solo virtuosity. Renowned for his inventive rhythmic phrasing, brilliant high-register trumpet playing, and gravelly singing voice, Armstrong popularised scat singing and expanded the artistic boundaries of popular music. Over a career spanning five decades, he achieved global fame, toured internationally as a cultural ambassador, and recorded iconic hits such as Hello, Dolly! and What a Wonderful World. Armstrong died in New York City on July 6, 1971.
beyonc: Beyoncé Giselle Knowles-Carter, born September 4, 1981, is an American singer, songwriter, record producer, and dancer. Raised in Houston, Texas, she performed in various singing and dancing competitions as a child before gaining fame in the late 1990s as the lead singer of Destiny's Child, one of the best-selling girl groups of all time. Following the group's hiatus, she released her debut solo album, Dangerously in Love, in 2003, which earned five Grammy Awards and featured two Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles. Over the following decades, she established a successful solo career with critically acclaimed albums including B'Day, I Am... Sasha Fierce, Lemonade, and Renaissance. Recognized for her vocal abilities, stage presence, and visual albums, she has achieved global commercial success. As one of the world's best-selling music artists, she holds the record for the most Grammy Awards won by any individual.
ernest-rutherford: Ernest Rutherford, 1st Baron Rutherford of Nelson, was a New Zealand-born British physicist widely regarded as the father of nuclear physics. Born on August 30, 1871, in Brightwater, New Zealand, he studied at Canterbury College before earning a scholarship to Trinity College, Cambridge. Rutherford discovered radioactive half-life, proved that radioactivity involves the nuclear transmutation of chemical elements, and identified and named alpha and beta radiation. In 1908, he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Through his landmark gold foil experiment, he discovered the atomic nucleus, establishing the planetary model of the atom. In 1919, he achieved the world's first artificial nuclear reaction by splitting nitrogen nuclei. He later served as director of the Cavendish Laboratory and president of the Royal Society. Rutherford died in Cambridge on October 19, 1937, and was interred in Westminster Abbey near Sir Isaac Newton.
octave-mirbeau: Octave Henri Marie Mirbeau was an influential French novelist, playwright, art critic, and journalist who lived from 1848 to 1917. Born in Normandy, Mirbeau established himself as a prominent and fiercely independent literary figure during the French Third Republic. Known for his sharp wit and opposition to bourgeois hypocrisy, he wrote numerous articles, essays, and novels that challenged social norms. His most famous literary works include the decadent novel The Torture Garden, published in 1899, and the satirical book The Diary of a Chambermaid, released in 1900. As a playwright, he achieved major success with his 1903 comedy Business is Business. Beyond literature, Mirbeau was an early champion of Impressionist art, passionately defending painters such as Claude Monet, Auguste Rodin, Vincent van Gogh, and Paul Cézanne. Through his journalism and artistic advocacy, Mirbeau left a lasting impact on European culture.
angelina-jolie: Angelina Jolie Voight was born on June 4, 1975, in Los Angeles, California. She is an internationally known American actress, filmmaker, and humanitarian. Jolie established herself as a prominent Hollywood star after winning an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her performance in Girl, Interrupted in 1999. She achieved global fame portraying the video game heroine Lara Croft in Lara Croft: Tomb Raider in 2001, which established her as a leading action star. Her later major film credits include Mr. and Mrs. Smith, Wanted, Salt, and the Maleficent series. As a director, screenwriter, and producer, she has helmed several projects, including the acclaimed dramas Unbroken and First They Killed My Father. Beyond her film career, Jolie is recognized for her dedicated humanitarian work. She served as a Special Envoy for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees for over a decade, advocating for refugees and displaced persons globally.
saddam-hussein: Saddam Hussein Abd al-Majid al-Tikriti was an Iraqi politician and revolutionary who served as the president of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. Born in 1937, he rose to prominence through the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party. After helping lead the 1968 coup, he served as vice president before formally assuming the presidency. His authoritarian government maintained strict political control and suppressed internal dissent, while using oil revenues to modernize Iraq's economy, infrastructure, and armed forces. His rule was characterized by severe human rights abuses, including violent campaigns targeting Kurdish and Shia populations. Internationally, his aggressive foreign policy led to the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 to 1988 and the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which prompted the 1991 Gulf War. In 2003, a United States-led coalition invaded Iraq, removing Hussein from power. Captured later that year, he was tried by an Iraqi special tribunal for crimes against humanity and executed in December 2006.
enrico-fermi: Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist who made fundamental contributions to quantum mechanics, nuclear physics, and statistical mechanics. Born in Rome, Italy, in 1901, Fermi demonstrated extraordinary mathematical and scientific aptitude from a young age. He earned his doctorate from the University of Pisa in 1922 and later became a professor of theoretical physics at the University of Rome. In 1938, Fermi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on induced radioactivity by neutron bombardment. That same year, he fled fascist Italy with his family and emigrated to the United States. In 1942, at the University of Chicago, Fermi led the team that constructed Chicago Pile-1, achieving the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. He subsequently served as a key leader in the Manhattan Project. Following the war, Fermi resumed his academic career and conducted pioneering research on subatomic particles until his death in 1954.
antoine-de-saint-exup-ry: Antoine Marie Jean-Baptiste Roger de Saint-Exupéry was a French writer and aviator, born in Lyon on June 29, 1900. Internationally known for his literary masterpieces and pioneering aviation career, he successfully combined high-altitude adventure with profound philosophical reflection. Saint-Exupéry began flying during his military service in 1921 and later became an airmail pilot, pioneering postal routes across Europe, North Africa, and South America. His dangerous experiences in the cockpit deeply influenced his major literary works, including Southern Mail, Night Flight, and Wind, Sand and Stars. He achieved enduring international fame with his 1943 masterpiece, The Little Prince, a poetic fable concerning love, friendship, and human nature that remains one of the most translated books worldwide. Following the outbreak of World War II, he served as a reconnaissance pilot. On July 31, 1944, Saint-Exupéry disappeared during a wartime flight over the Mediterranean Sea, leaving behind a profound literary legacy.
pablo-neruda: Pablo Neruda, born Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto, was a prominent Chilean poet, diplomat, and politician. Born on July 12, 1904, in Parral, Chile, he adopted his pen name in his youth, which later became his legal name. Neruda gained international fame at age nineteen with his collection Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair. Over his career, he wrote in various styles, including surrealist poems, historical epics like Canto General, and overtly political works. Alongside his literary achievements, Neruda served as a diplomat in several countries and was elected as a senator for the Chilean Communist Party in 1945. Forced into exile due to his political activities in the late 1940s, he later returned to Chile and served as ambassador to France under President Salvador Allende. Neruda was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971. He died on September 23, 1973, shortly after the Chilean military coup.
heinrich-heine: Christian Johann Heinrich Heine, born Harry Heine, was an internationally acclaimed German poet, writer, and literary critic who lived from 1797 to 1856. Born in Düsseldorf to a Jewish family, he studied law and converted to Lutheranism in 1825 to improve his career prospects. Heine achieved widespread fame with his 1827 poetry collection, Buch der Lieder, which became one of the most popular works in German literature. His lyric poems were frequently set to music by prominent Romantic composers such as Franz Schubert and Robert Schumann. Faced with strict censorship and political persecution in Germany due to his radical, satirical views, Heine moved to Paris in 1831, where he spent the remainder of his life. There, he authored significant essays, cultural critiques, and satirical masterpieces including Deutschland. Ein Wintermärchen. Despite suffering from a severe neurological illness that left him bedridden during his final years, Heine continued writing until his death in Paris in 1856.
akira-kurosawa: Akira Kurosawa was an internationally known Japanese filmmaker whose career spanned over five decades, from 1943 to 1993. Born in Tokyo on March 23, 1910, he originally studied Western-style painting before entering the film industry as an assistant director in 1936. He made his directorial debut with Sanshiro Sugata in 1943. Kurosawa achieved global prominence with Rashomon in 1950, a film that won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival and opened Western markets to Japanese cinema. Over his career, he directed thirty feature films, including critically acclaimed works such as Seven Samurai, Yojimbo, Kagemusha, and Ran. Renowned for his dynamic visual framing, precise editing, and masterful storytelling, his work deeply influenced generations of international directors. He frequently collaborated with actor Toshiro Mifune. Kurosawa received the Academy Honorary Award in 1990 and died in Tokyo on September 6, 1998.
ludwig-wittgenstein: Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein was an internationally known Austrian philosopher and logician who lived from 1889 to 1951. Born in Vienna into a prominent industrialist family, he originally studied aeronautical engineering before moving to Cambridge University to study logic under Bertrand Russell. Wittgenstein made foundational contributions to modern logic, the philosophy of mathematics, the philosophy of mind, and the philosophy of language. During his lifetime, he published only one major philosophical book, the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus in 1921, which sought to define the relationship between language and reality. After working for years as a primary school teacher, he returned to Cambridge in 1929 and eventually became a professor of philosophy. His second major work, Philosophical Investigations, was published posthumously in 1953. It introduced the concept of language games and presented a radical revision of his earlier ideas. Today, Wittgenstein is recognized as one of the most significant philosophers of the twentieth century.
max-weber: Maximilian Carl Emil Weber was an internationally known German sociologist, philosopher, and political economist whose ideas profoundly influenced modern social theory and research. Born on April 21, 1864, in Erfurt, Prussia, Weber pursued extensive studies in law, history, and economics, eventually holding academic positions at the universities of Freiburg, Heidelberg, and Munich. Alongside Karl Marx and Émile Durkheim, he is widely regarded as a principal architect of modern social science. Weber is best known for his landmark thesis in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, which proposed a connection between ascetic Protestantism and the rise of industrial capitalism. His scholarship also explored bureaucracy, rationalization, disenchantment, and authority categorized into traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal forms. In addition, he made key contributions to political theory and economic history before his death on June 14, 1920.
victoria: Alexandrina Victoria, born on May 24, 1819, served as Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from June 20, 1837, until her death on January 22, 1901. Inheriting the throne at age eighteen following the death of her uncle King William IV, her reign spanned sixty-three years and seven months, a historical period known as the Victorian era. In 1840, she married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, with whom she had nine children. Their children married into royal families across the continent, earning Victoria the nickname the grandmother of Europe. She additionally assumed the title of Empress of India in 1876. Her reign was characterized by vast industrial, cultural, scientific, and political shifts within Great Britain, alongside a major expansion of the British Empire worldwide. Victoria maintained a strictly constitutional role, shaping the modern British monarchy before her death at eighty-one.
aung-san-suu-kyi: Aung San Suu Kyi, whose full name is Aung San Suu Kyi, is a Burmese politician, author, and diplomat born on June 19, 1945. She is internationally known as the former State Counsellor of Myanmar and Leader of the National League for Democracy. The daughter of General Aung San, a key figure in Burma's independence, she became a prominent opposition figure during the 1988 pro-democracy movement. Between 1989 and 2010, she spent nearly fifteen years under house arrest, during which she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 for her nonviolent campaign. After her release, she led her party to a landslide victory in the 2015 general election, assuming power as State Counsellor in 2016. Her leadership subsequently faced intense international criticism regarding the military's campaign against the Rohingya population. In February 2021, she was ousted by the military, detained, and later convicted in closed legal proceedings.
nikita-khrushchev: Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev was a prominent Soviet politician who led the Soviet Union as First Secretary of the Communist Party from 1953 to 1964 and Premier from 1958 to 1964. Born in 1894 in Kalinovka, he joined the Bolsheviks in 1918 and advanced through the party hierarchy during Joseph Stalin's rule. After Stalin died in 1953, Khrushchev won the political power struggle. In 1956, he delivered the Secret Speech, which denounced Stalinist repression and launched an era of reform known as de-Stalinization. His leadership coincided with key Cold War milestones, including the launch of Sputnik, the construction of the Berlin Wall, and the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which brought superpowers to the brink of war. Domestically, Khrushchev promoted agricultural initiatives and economic restructuring, though results were mixed. Colleagues ousted him from power in 1964, citing erratic behavior and policy failures. He spent his final years in retirement before dying in Moscow in 1971.
shinz-abe: Shinzo Abe was a Japanese politician who served as the prime minister of Japan and president of the Liberal Democratic Party from 2006 to 2007 and again from 2012 to 2020. Born into a prominent political family in Tokyo on September 21, 1954, he became Japan's youngest post-war prime minister during his first term and eventually the longest-serving prime minister in the country's history. Abe was internationally recognized for his signature economic policy platform, known as Abenomics, which combined aggressive monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms to revive Japan's stagnant economy. In foreign policy, he advocated for a stronger defense posture, attempted to revise the pacifist Article 9 of Japan's constitution, and promoted the concept of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific alongside the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue. Health issues caused by ulcerative colitis led to his resignations in both 2007 and 2020. On July 8, 2022, Abe was assassinated while delivering a political campaign speech in Nara.
silvio-berlusconi: Silvio Berlusconi was an Italian media tycoon and politician who served as the Prime Minister of Italy in four governments across three distinct periods between 1994 and 2011. Born in Milan, he built a vast financial empire through his holding company, Fininvest, which expanded into commercial television, publishing, insurance, and the ownership of A.C. Milan football club. Entering politics in 1993, he founded the center-right party Forza Italia and quickly rose to power. Berlusconi became the longest-serving prime minister of post-World War II Italy, dominating the country's political and cultural landscape for nearly three decades. His tenure was characterized by significant economic influence and political polarization, alongside numerous legal battles and personal scandals. Despite convictions for tax fraud that temporarily led to his ban from public office, he remained an influential figure in Italian politics until his death in June 2023 at the age of 86.
h-g-wells: Herbert George Wells, known professionally as H. G. Wells, was an internationally acclaimed English writer born on September 21, 1866, in Bromley, Kent, who died on August 13, 1946, in London. Prolific across many genres, Wells wrote dozens of novels, short stories, social commentary, history, and biography. He achieved worldwide fame primarily as a pioneer of science fiction. His landmark early works, including The Time Machine, The Island of Doctor Moreau, The Invisible Man, and The War of the Worlds, popularized major concepts such as time travel, biological modification, invisibility, and alien invasion. Beyond fiction, Wells was a prominent public intellectual, outspoken socialist, and proponent of global governance. He wrote influential non-fiction, such as The Outline of History, which achieved widespread popular success. Today, Wells is remembered as a foundational figure in modern speculative fiction and a key social thinker.
anatole-france: François-Anatole Thibault, internationally known by his pen name Anatole France, was a prominent French poet, journalist, and novelist. Born in Paris in 1844, he spent his youth surrounded by books in his father's bookstore, which shaped his lifelong passion for literature. France achieved early commercial and critical success with his 1881 novel The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard. Throughout his career, he became celebrated for his ironic wit, elegant prose, and skeptical humanism, writing influential works such as Thais, Penguin Island, and The Gods Are Athirst. He was elected to the Academie francaise in 1896 and actively supported Alfred Dreyfus during the Dreyfus affair. In 1921, France was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in recognition of his literary achievements and nobility of style. He died in 1924 near Tours, leaving a lasting legacy as one of the defining figures of French literature.
katsushika-hokusai: Katsushika Hokusai, born Tokitaro in Edo, was an internationally known Japanese artist, painter, and printmaker who lived from 1760 to 1849. He became a leading master of the ukiyo-e genre, producing woodblock prints and paintings that captured landscapes, flora, fauna, and scenes of daily life. Throughout his lengthy career spanning over seven decades, he used dozens of art names to mark different phases of his creative evolution. His most famous achievement is the woodblock print series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, created in the early 1830s, which includes the iconic print The Great Wave off Kanagawa. This masterpiece significantly influenced Western art, especially Impressionism and Post-Impressionism in late nineteenth-century Europe. Hokusai also created the Hokusai Manga, a fifteen-volume collection of sketches that documented Japanese culture and folklore. His innovative compositions, dynamic lines, and use of Prussian blue transformed Japanese landscape art until his death at age eighty-eight.
robin-williams: Robin McLaurin Williams was an internationally known American actor and comedian who lived from July 21, 1951, to August 11, 2014. Born in Chicago, Illinois, Williams studied acting at the Juilliard School before rising to fame in the late 1970s playing the alien Mork on the television sitcom Mork and Mindy. Renowned for his improvisational skills and vocal versatility, he transitioned into a highly successful film career featuring both comedic and dramatic roles. His prominent films include Good Morning, Vietnam, Dead Poets Society, Aladdin, and Mrs. Doubtfire. In 1998, Williams received the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance as Dr. Sean Maguire in Good Will Hunting. Over his career, he also won six Golden Globe Awards, two Primetime Emmy Awards, and five Grammy Awards. Williams died by suicide at his home in Paradise Cay, California, at the age of 63.
selena-gomez: Selena Marie Gomez is an internationally known American singer, actress, and producer born on July 22, 1992, in Grand Prairie, Texas. She began her acting career as a child on the children's television series Barney & Friends before gaining widespread fame for her starring role as Alex Russo on the Disney Channel series Wizards of Waverly Place from 2007 to 2012. Transitioning into a successful music career, Gomez initially fronted the pop band Selena Gomez & the Scene before establishing herself as a solo artist. Her solo studio albums, including Stars Dance, Revival, and Rare, reached the top of the Billboard 200 chart. Alongside her music career, she has acted in films such as Spring Breakers and critically acclaimed television series like Only Murders in the Building, for which she also serves as an executive producer. Gomez is additionally recognized for her philanthropic work and her cosmetics brand, Rare Beauty.
thomas-mann: Paul Thomas Mann was a German novelist, short story writer, and social critic born in Lübeck on June 6, 1875. He became one of the most prominent literary figures of the twentieth century. Mann achieved early fame with his 1901 epic novel Buddenbrooks, which chronicled the decline of a wealthy merchant family. His subsequent major works, including Death in Venice and The Magic Mountain, explored complex psychological, philosophical, and societal themes. In 1929, Mann was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, primarily in recognition of Buddenbrooks. Following the rise of Adolf Hitler in 1933, Mann went into exile, eventually settling in the United States, where he became a vocal opponent of National Socialism through writings and radio broadcasts. He later published Doctor Faustus before returning to Europe. Mann died in Zurich, Switzerland, on August 12, 1955.
mark-zuckerberg: Mark Elliot Zuckerberg is an American Internet entrepreneur, media magnate, and philanthropist best known for co-founding the social media platform Facebook. Born on May 14, 1984, in White Plains, New York, he attended Harvard University, where he launched Facebook from his dorm room in February 2004 alongside his college roommates. The platform quickly expanded globally, transforming online communication and digital social networking. Zuckerberg has served as the chief executive officer and controlling shareholder of the company throughout its growth. In October 2021, Facebook Inc. rebranded as Meta Platforms to emphasize its shift toward developing the metaverse, while continuing to operate major applications such as Instagram, WhatsApp, and Facebook. Beyond his business operations, Zuckerberg co-founded the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative in 2015 with his wife, Priscilla Chan, directing substantial philanthropic resources toward biomedical research and education. He remains an influential global business leader.
andrew-jackson: Andrew Jackson was an American lawyer, general, and statesman who served as the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837. Born on March 15, 1767, in the Waxhaws region between North and South Carolina, Jackson rose to national prominence as a major general in the United States Army during the War of 1812, notably defeating British forces at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815. His political career culminated in his election to the presidency as the candidate of the newly formed Democratic Party. During his administration, Jackson expanded executive power, championed the rights of white male citizens, and opposed the Second Bank of the United States. His presidency was also marked by the Nullification Crisis and the passage of the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which led to the forced relocation of tens of thousands of Native Americans. Jackson died on June 8, 1845, in Nashville, Tennessee.
william-blake: William Blake was an English poet, painter, and printmaker who lived from 1757 to 1827. Born in London, he demonstrated early artistic talent and briefly attended the Royal Academy of Arts. Although largely unappreciated during his lifetime, Blake is today internationally known for his visionary poetry and visual art, which made significant contributions to the Romantic movement. He invented illuminated printing, a relief etching method that combined his written text and hand-colored illustrations on single plates. His famous works include Songs of Innocence and of Experience, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and Jerusalem. Blake created a complex personal mythology incorporating spiritual and philosophical themes that critiqued the social and religious norms of his era. Today, the full name William Blake represents one of the most original figures in Western culture, whose legacy continues to exert a powerful influence on literature and the visual arts worldwide.
hermann-hesse: Hermann Karl Hesse was an internationally known German-Swiss poet, novelist, and painter who lived from 1877 to 1962. Born in Calw, Germany, he later became a Swiss citizen in 1923. Hesse gained widespread acclaim for his psychological and philosophical writings, which often explored an individual's struggle for authenticity, self-knowledge, and spiritual enlightenment. His celebrated works include Demian, Steppenwolf, Siddhartha, and The Glass Bead Game. These novels drew heavily on his interest in Eastern philosophy, Jungian psychoanalysis, and personal spiritual quests. In 1946, Hesse was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for his inspired writings, which exemplified classical humanitarian ideals and high artistic style. Beyond his literary achievements, he was an accomplished watercolor painter who produced thousands of artworks during his lifetime. Hesse spent his later years in Montagnola, Switzerland, where he died in 1962. Today, his works remain widely translated and read across the globe, maintaining his enduring literary legacy.
helen-keller: Helen Adams Keller, who lived from 1880 to 1968, was an internationally renowned American deafblind author, political activist, lecturer, and scholar. Born in Tuscumbia, Alabama, Keller lost her sight and hearing at nineteen months old following an illness. In 1887, she began her education under Anne Sullivan, who taught her to communicate using touch. Keller made extraordinary academic progress, ultimately becoming the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree when she graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904. She published twelve books, including her famous autobiography, The Story of My Life, and lectured worldwide on disability rights. Beyond her advocacy for the blind and deaf, Keller was a committed socialist, co-founding the American Civil Liberties Union and campaigning for women's suffrage, labor rights, and antimilitarism. She spent her life traveling extensively to promote social reform and raise funds for the American Foundation for the Blind.
john-quincy-adams: John Quincy Adams was an American statesman, diplomat, lawyer, and diarist. Born in Braintree, Massachusetts, in 1767, he was the son of John Adams, the second United States president. Before assuming national executive office, Adams built an extensive diplomatic career, serving as minister to several European nations and helping negotiate the Treaty of Ghent, which officially ended the War of 1812. As Secretary of State under James Monroe, he was the primary author of the Monroe Doctrine. Internationally known, he is best known for serving as President of the United States from 1825 to 1829. After leaving the presidency, Adams was elected to the United States House of Representatives in 1830, becoming the first former president to serve in Congress. He served in the House for seventeen years, where he emerged as a prominent opponent of slavery until his death in 1848.
boris-yeltsin: Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as the first President of the Russian Federation from 1991 to 1999. Born on February 1, 1931, in Butka, Soviet Union, Yeltsin worked in construction before rising through the Communist Party ranks to become the party chief in Sverdlovsk and later Moscow. In the late 1980s, he emerged as a prominent democratic reformer opposing the party establishment. Elected President of the Russian SFSR in June 1991, Yeltsin gained widespread acclaim for standing against the August 1991 hardline coup attempt. Later that year, he played a central role in the dissolution of the Soviet Union. As president of independent Russia, he implemented radical market economic reforms, known as shock therapy, and navigated political crises, including the 1993 constitutional showdown and the First Chechen War. Yeltsin resigned on December 31, 1999, naming Vladimir Putin as his acting successor. He died on April 23, 2007.
naguib-mahfouz: Naguib Mahfouz Abdelaziz Ibrahim Ahmed Al-Basha was a celebrated Egyptian writer who became one of the first contemporary figures in Arabic literature to explore themes of existentialism and modern social realism. Born on December 11, 1911, in Cairo, Mahfouz spent most of his life working as a civil servant while writing extensively. Over a career spanning seven decades, he published dozens of novels, hundreds of short stories, and numerous plays and movie scripts. His famous Cairo Trilogy vividly depicted Egyptian society across three generations during the early twentieth century. His controversial 1959 novel, Children of Gebelawi, drew significant critical acclaim alongside opposition from religious conservatives. In 1988, Mahfouz was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first Arabic-language writer to receive the honor. Despite surviving an assassination attempt by religious extremists in 1994 that impaired his right hand, he continued to write until his death in Cairo on August 30, 2006.
woody-allen: Allan Stewart Konigsberg, later legally changed to Heywood Allen and known professionally as Woody Allen, is an American filmmaker, actor, and comedian born on November 30, 1935, in Brooklyn, New York City. Allen began his career in the 1950s writing material for television and performing as a stand-up comedian. He gained widespread recognition in the 1970s for directing and starring in a series of influential comedy films. Known for his distinctive tragicomic style, intellectual humor, and neurotic screen persona, Allen frequently sets his narratives in New York City. His extensive filmography includes acclaimed works such as Annie Hall, Manhattan, Hannah and Her Sisters, and Midnight in Paris. Over a career spanning more than six decades, he has received four Academy Awards, including one for Best Director and three for Best Original Screenplay. Allen remains one of the most prolific figures in modern American cinema.
roger-federer: Roger Federer is a retired Swiss professional tennis player, born on August 8, 1981, in Basel, Switzerland. Widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players in history, he dominated the sport during the 2000s and 2010s. Federer turned professional in 1998 and captured his first Grand Slam singles title at Wimbledon in 2003. Over his illustrious career, he secured 20 Grand Slam men's singles titles, including a record eight Wimbledon championships, six Australian Opens, five US Opens, and one French Open. He held the Association of Tennis Professionals world number one ranking for 310 weeks, including a record 237 consecutive weeks from 2004 to 2008. Federer also won 103 ATP singles titles, an Olympic gold medal in doubles in 2008, and a silver medal in singles in 2012. Renowned for his effortless playing style, exceptional footwork, and sportsmanship, he officially retired from professional tennis in September 2022.
virginia-woolf: Adeline Virginia Woolf, born Stephen on January 25, 1882, in London, was an English writer regarded as one of the most important modernist authors of the twentieth century. Raised in an intellectual household, she began writing professionally in 1900. She became a central figure in the Bloomsbury Group, an influential circle of English writers, intellectuals, and artists. In 1912, she married Leonard Woolf, and together they founded the Hogarth Press in 1917, publishing her works alongside those of other prominent writers. Woolf pioneered the stream of consciousness narrative technique, exploring internal monologue and psychological time in celebrated novels such as Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse, and Orlando. Her non-fiction essay A Room of One's Own remains a foundational text in feminist literary criticism, examining the social and financial obstacles faced by female writers. Throughout her life, Woolf suffered from severe mental illness. She died by suicide on March 28, 1941, near her home in Sussex.
marlon-brando: Marlon Brando Jr. was an American actor widely regarded as one of the most influential performers in twentieth century cinema. Born on April 3, 1924, in Omaha, Nebraska, he studied acting under Stella Adler, becoming a key proponent of Method acting. Brando achieved critical acclaim on stage and screen as Stanley Kowalski in A Streetcar Named Desire. He won his first Academy Award for Best Actor for his portrayal of Terry Malloy in On the Waterfront in 1954. After a period of commercial decline in the 1960s, Brando delivered an iconic performance as Vito Corleone in The Godfather in 1972, winning his second Academy Award. He later starred in Last Tango in Paris and Apocalypse Now. Beyond his film career, Brando was a vocal activist who supported the Civil Rights Movement and Native American rights. He died on July 1, 2004, in Los Angeles, California.
jackie-chan: Jackie Chan, born Chan Kong-sang on April 7, 1954, in Hong Kong, is an internationally renowned actor, martial artist, filmmaker, and stuntman. Chan began his training at a young age at the China Drama Academy, a Peking Opera school, where he developed expertise in martial arts, acrobatics, and singing. He entered the film industry as a stuntman in the 1970s before achieving stardom by pioneering a unique genre of comedic martial arts cinema. Known for performing his own dangerous stunts, Chan gained global acclaim with Hong Kong classics such as Drunken Master and the Police Story series. His transition to Hollywood produced box-office hits like Rumble in the Bronx, the Rush Hour franchise, and Shanghai Noon. Over a career spanning six decades, Chan has starred in over 150 films and received an Academy Honorary Award in 2016 for his achievements in cinema.
isaac-asimov: Isaac Asimov was an American writer and biochemist who became one of the most prolific authors in the English language. Born Isaak Yudovich Ozimov in Petrovichi, Russia, around January 2, 1920, he emigrated with his family to the United States in 1923 and grew up in Brooklyn, New York. He earned a doctorate in chemistry from Columbia University in 1948 and later joined the faculty at Boston University School of Medicine, where he served as a professor of biochemistry. Asimov wrote or edited more than 500 books, spanning science fiction, popular science, history, and literary criticism. He is best remembered for his foundational science fiction works, including the Foundation series and his Robot stories, which introduced the Three Laws of Robotics. Alongside Arthur C. Clarke and Robert A. Heinlein, he was considered one of the premier science fiction writers of his era. Asimov died in New York City on April 6, 1992.
gustave-flaubert: Gustave Flaubert was a renowned nineteenth-century French novelist who became internationally known for his meticulous stylistic precision and foundational contributions to literary realism. Born in Rouen on December 12, 1821, he abandoned early legal studies to dedicate his life entirely to writing, residing primarily at his family estate in Croisset. His debut novel, Madame Bovary, published in 1857, earned immediate literary acclaim and scandal, leading to an unsuccessful prosecution for immorality. The masterpiece established his reputation through its objective depiction of provincial bourgeois life and the tragic pursuit of romantic ideals. Flaubert subsequently authored the historical novel Salammbo in 1862, the sweeping social critique Sentimental Education in 1869, and the short-story collection Three Tales in 1877. Famous for his relentless search for the exact word, or le mot juste, Flaubert spent years perfecting each manuscript. He died in Croisset on May 8, 1880, leaving a profound influence on modern fiction.
kim-il-sung: Kim Il-sung, born Kim Song-ju on April 15, 1912, was a North Korean politician who served as the Supreme Leader of North Korea from its founding in 1948 until his death in 1994. Before taking power, he led anti-Japanese guerrilla units in Manchuria during the 1930s and later served in the Soviet Red Army. Following World War II and the division of Korea, Soviet authorities selected him to lead the newly established state. Kim authorized the invasion of South Korea in 1950, initiating the Korean War, which ended in an armistice in 1953. As leader, he held the posts of Premier and later President, consolidating political power under the Workers' Party of Korea. He developed Juche, an ideology emphasizing state self-reliance, and fostered a pervasive cult of personality. Kim died on July 8, 1994, and was succeeded by his son, Kim Jong-il. He was later declared the Eternal President of North Korea.
franz-schubert: Franz Peter Schubert (1797–1828) was an Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Born in Himmelpfortgrund, near Vienna, Schubert demonstrated early musical talent as a singer, violinist, and pianist. He studied under Antonio Salieri before focusing entirely on composition. Despite a short lifetime, he produced a vast body of work, including over six hundred Lieder, which redefined the German art song genre through compositions such as Erlkönig. In addition to vocal music, Schubert composed major orchestral works, notably his Eighth Symphony, known as the Unfinished Symphony, and the Ninth Symphony. His output also encompasses chamber music, including the Trout Quintet, alongside numerous piano sonatas, sacred works, and stage music. Schubert spent most of his life in Vienna, where he enjoyed a close circle of supporters but limited public acclaim during his lifetime. Today, he is internationally recognized as a foundational figure in Western classical music.
herbert-hoover: Herbert Clark Hoover lived from 1874 to 1964 and served as the thirty-first president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. Born in West Branch, Iowa, he achieved international renown as a successful mining engineer before turning to public service. During World War I, Hoover gained global acclaim for directing massive international relief efforts through the Commission for Relief in Belgium and as head of the United States Food Administration, delivering crucial food aid across war-torn Europe. He subsequently served as United States Secretary of Commerce under Presidents Warren G. Harding and Calvin Coolidge. Elected president in 1928, Hoover's administration was severely defined by the Wall Street Crash of 1929 and the onset of the Great Depression. His policy responses failed to abate the economic crisis, resulting in his electoral defeat in 1932. In his post-presidency, Hoover led administrative reorganization commissions and advised on international relief.
kamala-harris: Kamala Devi Harris is an American politician and attorney who served as the 49th Vice President of the United States from 2021 to 2025. Born on October 20, 1964, in Oakland, California, she graduated from Howard University and the University of California, Hastings College of the Law. Harris began her legal career in Alameda County before being elected District Attorney of San Francisco in 2003. She subsequently served as the Attorney General of California from 2011 to 2017. In 2016, Harris was elected to the United States Senate representing California, becoming a prominent member of the Democratic Party. As Vice President alongside President Joe Biden, she became the highest-ranking female official in United States history, as well as the first African American and South Asian American Vice President. In 2024, Harris became the Democratic nominee for President of the United States following President Biden's decision to end his reelection campaign.
jonathan-swift: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish satirist, essayist, political pamphleteer, poet, and Anglican cleric who lived from 1667 to 1745. Born in Dublin, Ireland, he received his education at Trinity College, Dublin, before moving to England to work as a secretary to Sir William Temple. Swift later took holy orders and eventually became the Dean of Saint Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, a position he held for several decades. He gained international renown for his prose satire, authoring famous works such as the prose masterpiece Gulliver's Travels, published in 1726. His other prominent compositions include the biting satirical essay A Modest Proposal and A Tale of a Tub. Using various pseudonyms, including Lemuel Gulliver and Isaac Bickerstaff, Swift frequently addressed contemporary political, social, and religious matters in Great Britain and Ireland. He died in Dublin in 1745, leaving an enduring legacy as one of the English language's premier prose satirists.
jacques-chirac: Jacques René Chirac was a French politician who served as the President of France from 1995 to 2007. Born in Paris on November 29, 1932, Chirac enjoyed a long and influential career in French politics spanning several decades. Before his presidency, he served two terms as Prime Minister of France, from 1974 to 1976 and again from 1986 to 1988, and was the Mayor of Paris from 1977 to 1995. As president, Chirac ended conscription, reduced the presidential term from seven to five years, and guided France through the adoption of the euro currency. Internationally, he was particularly renowned for his firm opposition to the 2003 United States-led invasion of Iraq. Chirac was also the first French president to formally acknowledge the French state's role in the wartime deportation of Jewish citizens. He left office in 2007 and passed away on September 26, 2019, in Paris.
ingmar-bergman: Ernst Ingmar Bergman was a Swedish director, screenwriter, and producer recognized as one of the most influential figures in modern cinema. Born in Uppsala, Sweden, on July 14, 1918, he began his career in the theater before transitioning to film in the 1940s. Over a career spanning more than six decades, Bergman directed over sixty films and wrote numerous scripts, earning international acclaim for his profound exploration of existential themes, psychological tension, mortality, and faith. His landmark works, including The Seventh Seal and Wild Strawberries, both released in 1957, helped define international art-house cinema. Later masterworks such as Persona, Cries and Whispers, and Fanny and Alexander further established his reputation for complex character studies and innovative cinematic techniques. He frequently collaborated with a dedicated ensemble of actors and cinematographer Sven Nykvist. Bergman died on the island of Faro on July 30, 2007, leaving a lasting legacy in world cinema.
diego-vel-zquez: Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a prominent Spanish painter who lived from 1599 to 1660. Born in Seville, he became one of the most celebrated artists of the Spanish Golden Age and the Baroque period. Velázquez gained widespread recognition as the principal court painter for King Philip IV of Spain, a position he held for nearly four decades. His works included numerous portraits of the royal family, Spanish nobles, and common people, alongside historical and mythological scenes. Known for his masterful use of light, subtle color palettes, and realistic individualization, his masterpiece is widely considered to be Las Meninas, painted in 1656. Other notable works include The Surrender of Breda and a renowned portrait of Pope Innocent X. Velázquez died in Madrid in August 1660. His innovative technique and individualistic style profoundly influenced subsequent generations of European painters, particularly nineteenth century realists and impressionists.
richard-feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman was an internationally known American theoretical physicist who lived from May 11, 1918, to February 15, 1988. He made groundbreaking contributions to quantum mechanics, particularly through his path integral formulation and the development of quantum electrodynamics. To visually represent the behavior of subatomic particles, he invented intuitive graphical representations known as Feynman diagrams. During World War II, Feynman assisted in the development of the atomic bomb as part of the Manhattan Project. In 1965, he was jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics alongside Julian Schwinger and Shin'ichiro Tomonaga for his fundamental work in quantum electrodynamics. Later in his life, he served on the Rogers Commission, which investigated the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger disaster, where he demonstrated the failure of the shuttle's O-rings under cold temperatures. Feynman was also a famed educator and popularizer of science, authoring the influential textbook series The Feynman Lectures on Physics.
charles-iii-of-the-united-kingdom: Charles III, born Charles Philip Arthur George on November 14, 1948, is King of the United Kingdom and fourteen other Commonwealth realms. He acceded to the throne on September 8, 2022, following the death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II. As the eldest child of Elizabeth and Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, Charles was the longest serving heir apparent in British history, holding the title of Prince of Wales from 1958 until his accession. Educated at Cambridge University, he served in the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force. In 1976, he established The Prince's Trust and became a prominent advocate for environmental conservation, sustainable agriculture, and urban planning. Charles married Lady Diana Spencer in 1981, with whom he had two sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, before their divorce in 1996. He married Camilla Parker Bowles in 2005. His coronation took place at Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023.
igor-stravinsky: Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky was an internationally known Russian, French, and American composer born in Oranienbaum, Russia, in 1882. He died in New York City in 1971. Stravinsky achieved international fame early in his career through his collaboration with impresario Sergei Diaghilev and the Ballets Russes in Paris. His groundbreaking ballet scores, including The Firebird, Petrushka, and The Rite of Spring, revolutionized twentieth-century classical music through their complex rhythms and bold orchestration. Over his long career, his stylistic evolution spanned three distinct phases: an early Russian period, a middle Neoclassical period characterized by a revival of traditional forms, and a final Serial period utilizing twelve-tone techniques. He acquired French citizenship in 1934 and later became an American citizen in 1945 after moving to the United States. Today, Stravinsky is widely recognized as one of the most influential composers of the modern era, whose diverse catalog shaped global musical history.
aleksandr-solzhenitsyn: Aleksandr Isayevich Solzhenitsyn was a Russian writer, publicist, poet, and politician who lived from 1918 to 2008. Born in Kislovodsk, he served in the Red Army during World War II. In 1945, he was arrested for criticizing Joseph Stalin in private correspondence and served eight years in labor camps, followed by internal exile. These experiences deeply influenced his literary creations, which exposed Soviet political repression. His 1962 novella, One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, brought him international fame. Solzhenitsyn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970.
