Fourier is best known for initiating the investigation of Fourier series, which allowed complex periodic functions to be represented as sums of simpler trigonometric functions. His seminal work on heat flow, published in his 1822 treatise The Analytical Theory of Heat, revolutionized mathematical physics and laid the groundwork for modern signal processing and harmonic analysis. Additionally, Fourier is recognized for first describing what is now known as the greenhouse effect, calculating that Earth's atmosphere traps thermal radiation. He died in Paris in 1830, leaving a lasting mathematical legacy.
john-mccain: John Sidney McCain III was an American politician and military officer who served as a United States senator from Arizona from 1987 until his death in 2018. Born on August 29, 1936, into a military family, McCain graduated from the United States Naval Academy and became a naval aviator. During the Vietnam War, his plane was shot down in 1967, leading to over five years of imprisonment as a prisoner of war, during which he was tortured. After retiring from the Navy, McCain entered politics, serving in the United States House of Representatives from 1983 to 1987 before entering the Senate. Known for his independent political stance and maverick reputation, he was the Republican nominee for president in 2008, losing to Barack Obama. McCain remained a prominent national figure and an influential voice on foreign policy until his death from brain cancer on August 25, 2018.
doris-lessing: Doris May Lessing, born Doris May Tayler, was an internationally acclaimed British novelist, poet, playwright, librettist, biographer, and short story writer. She was born on October 22, 1919, in Kermanshah, Persia, and grew up in Southern Rhodesia. In 1949, she moved to London, publishing her debut novel, The Grass Is Singing, in 1950. Her literary career spanned more than six decades, exploring themes of politics, human psychology, and social conflict. Lessing achieved major acclaim with her landmark 1962 novel, The Golden Notebook, a pivotal work in twentieth century fiction. Her versatile output encompassed speculative fiction, such as the Canopus in Argos series, alongside plays, opera librettos, poetry, and memoirs. In 2007, she received the Nobel Prize in Literature, recognized for her epic story of the female experience. She died on November 17, 2013, in London, leaving behind a lasting literary legacy.
miley-cyrus: Miley Ray Cyrus, born Destiny Hope Cyrus on November 23, 1992, is an American singer, actress, and television personality. The daughter of country music singer Billy Ray Cyrus, she achieved international fame as a teen idol while starring in the Disney Channel television series Hannah Montana from 2006 to 2011. Following her television success, Cyrus established a prominent music career known for her versatile artistic reinventions across pop, rock, country, and hip-hop. Her successful discography includes major albums such as Bangerz, Plastic Hearts, and Endless Summer Vacation, featuring hit singles like Wrecking Ball and Flowers, the latter earning her two Grammy Awards in 2024. In addition to her recording career, Cyrus has starred in feature films including The Last Song and served as a coach on the singing competition television show The Voice. She is widely recognized for her distinctive raspy vocal style and lasting cultural influence.
alexander-fleming: Sir Alexander Fleming was a Scottish biologist, pharmacologist, botanist, and Nobel laureate whose scientific discoveries transformed twentieth-century medicine. Born on August 6, 1881, in Darvel, Scotland, Fleming received his medical education at St Mary's Hospital Medical School in London, where he spent most of his research career. In 1923, he identified lysozyme, a naturally occurring antibacterial enzyme found in human tissues and secretions. His breakthrough discovery came in 1928, when he observed that a mold, later identified as Penicillium rubens, inhibited the growth of staphylococci bacteria. Fleming named the active substance penicillin and published his research in 1929. Although he struggled to isolate the compound in large quantities, scientists Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain later developed it into a mass-produced drug. For this vital achievement, Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Florey and Chain. Knighted in 1944, Fleming died in London on March 11, 1955.
chester-a-arthur: Chester Alan Arthur was an American politician and attorney who served as the twenty-first president of the United States from 1881 to 1885. Born in Vermont in 1829, Arthur practiced law in New York City and held political appointments, including Collector of the Port of New York. He was elected vice president in 1880 on the Republican ticket alongside James A. Garfield. Following Garfield's assassination in September 1881, Arthur succeeded to the presidency. As president, he championed civil service reform, culminating in the signing of the landmark Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883. Arthur also presided over the modernization of the United States Navy and enacted tariff reforms. He signed the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 after negotiating a reduction in its duration. Suffering from poor health, Arthur did not actively seek renomination and left office in 1885, dying in 1886.
wole-soyinka: Akinwande Oluwole Babatunde Soyinka is a Nigerian playwright, poet, novelist, and essayist born on July 13, 1934, in Abeokuta, Nigeria. He pursued higher education at University College Ibadan and the University of Leeds in England, where he developed a passion for theater. Soyinka wrote extensively in English, blending traditional Yoruba folklore and mythology with Western dramatic techniques. His notable literary works include the plays The Lion and the Jewel, A Dance of the Forests, and Death and the King's Horseman, as well as the novel The Interpreters. In 1986, Soyinka became the first Black African to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Throughout his life, he has been an outspoken political activist, frequently criticizing authoritarian regimes in Nigeria, which led to his imprisonment during the Nigerian Civil War and periods of political exile. He remains an influential voice in global literature and human rights.
yoshihide-suga: Yoshihide Suga is a Japanese politician who served as the Prime Minister of Japan and President of the Liberal Democratic Party from September 2020 to October 2021. Born on December 6, 1948, in Akita Prefecture, he began his political career as a municipal council member in Yokohama before being elected to the House of Representatives in 1996. Suga gained national prominence as the longest-serving Chief Cabinet Secretary in Japanese history, holding the post from 2012 to 2020 under Prime Minister Shinzo Abe. Upon Abe's resignation due to health issues, Suga was chosen to lead the government. As Prime Minister, Suga oversaw Japan's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, spearheaded the national vaccination drive, and hosted the rescheduled 2020 Tokyo Summer Olympics in 2021. He also pledged that Japan would achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. Suga decided not to seek re-election as party leader in late 2021, ending his premiership, and was succeeded by Fumio Kishida.
eddie-murphy: Edward Regan Murphy is an American actor, comedian, singer, and writer born on April 3, 1961, in Brooklyn, New York. He rose to national prominence as a regular cast member on the sketch comedy show Saturday Night Live from 1980 to 1984, where his performances helped revitalize the program. Murphy transitioned to a highly successful film career, starring in hit comedy and action movies such as 48 Hrs., Trading Places, and the Beverly Hills Cop franchise during the 1980s. He later expanded his appeal through roles in family films, including The Nutty Professor and Dr. Dolittle, as well as providing the voice of Donkey in the animated Shrek series. In 2006, he received critical acclaim and an Academy Award nomination for his dramatic role in Dreamgirls. Recognized as one of the most influential stand-up comedians in history, Murphy was awarded the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 2015.
dan-brown: Daniel Gerhard Brown is an internationally known American novelist born on June 22, 1964, in Exeter, New Hampshire. He is best recognized for his thriller novels featuring the fictional Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon. Brown attended Amherst College, graduating in 1986, and briefly pursued a career in songwriting and musical performance before shifting his focus entirely to literature. His early works include Digital Fortress, Angels and Demons, and Deception Point. He achieved global literary prominence with his 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code, which explored themes of cryptography, secret societies, and art history. The book became a massive bestseller, sparking widespread public interest and leading to successful film adaptations. Brown continued the series with prominent sequels, including The Lost Symbol, Inferno, and Origin. His books have been translated into dozens of languages and have sold over two hundred million copies around the world.
abdullah-ii-of-jordan: Abdullah II bin Al-Hussein is the reigning King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, a position he has held since February 1999. Born in Amman on January 30, 1962, to King Hussein and Princess Muna al-Hussein, he is a member of the Hashemite dynasty, which claims direct descent from the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Abdullah received his education in Jordan, the United Kingdom, and the United States, later attending the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst. He served extensively in the Jordanian Armed Forces, eventually becoming the commander of the country's Special Forces. Upon his father's death, he ascended the throne and began implementing economic modernization reforms and administrative initiatives. Internationally known for his role as a regional mediator and advocate for Middle East peace, King Abdullah II maintains strong security and diplomatic ties with Western and Arab nations. Additionally, he serves as the official custodian of the Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem, emphasizing religious tolerance and interfaith dialogue.
robert-baden-powell-1st-baron-baden-powe: Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell, was a British Army officer, author, and the founder of the international Scout Movement. Born in London in 1857, he served in the military from 1876 to 1910, ultimately achieving the rank of lieutenant-general. He gained widespread recognition during the Second Boer War for his successful 217-day defense of Mafeking. Drawing on his military experiences, he authored Aids to Scouting, which inspired youth training. In 1907, he conducted an experimental youth camp on Brownsea Island, leading to his 1908 book Scouting for Boys. The book catalyzed the creation of the Scout Movement, which emphasized outdoor skills, character development, and self-reliance. Alongside his sister Agnes, he also assisted in founding the Girl Guides in 1910. Serving as Chief Scout, Baden-Powell spent his final years in Kenya, where he died in 1941.
edwin-hubble: Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who fundamentally changed the understanding of the cosmos. Born on November 20, 1889, in Marshfield, Missouri, Hubble earned degrees from the University of Chicago and Oxford University before pursuing astronomy at the Mount Wilson Observatory in California. In the 1920s, using the Hooker Telescope, he identified Cepheid variable stars in distant nebulae, proving that they were entire galaxies beyond the Milky Way. Shortly thereafter, Hubble observed that distant galaxies recede from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance, providing empirical evidence for an expanding universe. This relationship became known as Hubble's law. He also devised a classification system for galaxies, known as the Hubble sequence. Hubble died on September 28, 1953, in San Marino, California. His pioneering work in extragalactic astronomy profoundly shaped modern cosmology, leading NASA to name the Hubble Space Telescope in his honor.
lewis-hamilton: Sir Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton is a British racing driver competing in Formula One. Born on January 7, 1985, in Stevenage, England, he began karting at an early age and joined the McLaren young driver programme in 1998. Hamilton made his Formula One debut with McLaren in 2007, becoming the series' first Black driver. He won his first World Drivers' Championship title in 2008. In 2013, Hamilton moved to Mercedes, where he achieved major success, securing six additional world championships between 2014 and 2020. With seven world titles, he shares the record for the most drivers' championships with German driver Michael Schumacher. Hamilton also holds the all-time Formula One records for the most race victories, pole positions, and podium finishes. Additionally, he is known for his advocacy regarding environmentalism and diversity in motorsport. He was knighted in the 2021 New Year Honours.
dwayne-johnson: Dwayne Douglas Johnson, born May 2, 1972, is an American actor, producer, and former professional wrestler internationally known by his ring name The Rock. Before entering entertainment, Johnson played college football for the University of Miami, winning a national championship in 1991. He subsequently joined the World Wrestling Federation in 1996, where he became one of the most prominent and influential figures in professional wrestling history. Johnson transitioned into a mainstream acting career with his appearance in The Mummy Returns in 2001. He went on to star in numerous commercially successful films, including The Scorpion King, Moana, the Jumanji series, and several installments of the Fast & Furious franchise. Recognized as one of the highest-grossing film stars globally, he co-founded the production company Seven Bucks Productions and maintains various business ventures across sports, fitness, and consumer products.
paul-newman: Paul Leonard Newman was an American actor, film director, race car driver, and philanthropist, born on January 26, 1925, in Shaker Heights, Ohio. After studying at the Actors Studio, he made his Broadway debut in 1953 and soon established himself as a major Hollywood star. Renowned for his striking blue eyes and compelling performances, Newman starred in iconic films including The Hustler, Cool Hand Luke, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, The Sting, and The Verdict. He earned ten Academy Award nominations, winning Best Actor for The Color of Money in 1986, as well as an Honorary Oscar and the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award. Outside of entertainment, Newman was an accomplished sports car racer, winning multiple driver championships. In 1982, he co-founded Newman's Own, a food company donating all post-tax profits to charitable causes. Newman died on September 26, 2008, in Westport, Connecticut.
henry-dunant: Jean-Henri Dunant, born on May 8, 1828, in Geneva, Switzerland, was a Swiss businessman, social activist, and humanitarian. While traveling on business in 1859, Dunant witnessed the horrific aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in present-day Italy. Appalled by the severe lack of care for wounded soldiers, he organized local civilians to provide medical assistance regardless of military affiliation. Returning to Geneva, he recorded his experiences in the 1862 book A Memory of Solferino, in which he proposed creating a neutral international organization to assist wartime casualties. This initiative led directly to the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross in 1863 and inspired the adoption of the first Geneva Convention in 1864. Despite suffering personal bankruptcy and spending years in obscurity, Dunant eventually received global recognition for his work. In 1901, he received the inaugural Nobel Peace Prize jointly with Frédéric Passy. Dunant died on October 30, 1910.
hayao-miyazaki: Hayao Miyazaki, born January 5, 1941, in Tokyo, Japan, is an internationally known Japanese animator, film director, screenwriter, and mangaka. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential figures in the history of animated cinema. Miyazaki began his professional career in 1963 at Toei Animation, contributing to numerous television series and feature films. In 1985, he co-founded Studio Ghibli alongside fellow filmmaker Isao Takahata and producer Toshio Suzuki. Through Studio Ghibli, Miyazaki wrote and directed critically acclaimed animated classics, including Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Howl's Moving Castle. His 2001 masterpiece, Spirited Away, achieved international commercial success and won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. He earned a second Academy Award for his 2023 film, The Boy and the Heron. Miyazaki's distinct storytelling frequently addresses themes of environmentalism, pacifism, aviation, and complex human relationships.
wolfgang-pauli: Wolfgang Ernst Pauli was an Austrian-born theoretical physicist who made fundamental contributions to quantum mechanics. Born in Vienna on April 25, 1900, he completed his doctorate under Arnold Sommerfeld at the University of Munich in 1921. Pauli is best known for formulating the Pauli exclusion principle in 1925, which asserts that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously. This breakthrough was essential to understanding electron configurations, chemical properties, and atomic structure, earning him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945 after being nominated by Albert Einstein. In 1930, Pauli also theoretically predicted the existence of the neutrino to explain the conservation of energy in beta decay. He spent much of his academic career as a professor of theoretical physics at ETH Zurich and became a Swiss citizen in 1949. Pauli passed away in Zurich on December 15, 1958.
roald-dahl: Roald Dahl was a British novelist, short-story writer, poet, screenwriter, and fighter pilot, born on September 13, 1916, in Llandaff, Cardiff, Wales, to Norwegian parents. During the Second World War, he served as a fighter pilot in the Royal Air Force and later worked as an intelligence officer. Dahl began his literary career writing about his wartime experiences before transitioning to macabre short stories for adults and darkly comedic literature for children. He gained international fame for his children's books, which include James and the Giant Peach, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda, The BFG, and The Witches. His works frequently featured unsentimental humor and unexpected plot twists, endearing him to generations of readers worldwide. Dahl also wrote screenplays, including the James Bond film You Only Live Twice. He died on November 23, 1990, leaving a legacy as one of the world's best-selling authors.
gao-xingjian: Gao Xingjian is a Chinese-born French novelist, playwright, critic, and painter, born on January 4, 1940, in Ganzhou, Jiangxi province, China. He studied French literature at the Beijing Foreign Studies University, graduating in 1962. Gao began his career as a translator and writer, becoming a prominent figure in the post-Cultural Revolution avant-garde theater scene in Beijing. His experimental plays, such as Absolute Signal and Bus Stop, drew influence from European modernist theater, which ultimately led to state criticism and censorship. In 1987, Gao left China for Europe, eventually settling in Paris, France, where he was granted political asylum and became a French citizen in 1998. He gained international acclaim for his complex, semi-autobiographical novels, notably Soul Mountain and One Man's Bible. In 2000, Gao was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first Chinese-born writer to receive the honor. Today, he continues his artistic pursuits in France.
melania-trump: Melania Trump, born Melanija Knavs on April 26, 1970, is a Slovenian-American former fashion model who served as the First Lady of the United States from 2017 to 2021, and assumed the role again in 2025. Raised in Sevnica, Slovenia, she began modeling at an early age, working in Milan and Paris before moving to New York City in 1996. She married businessman Donald Trump in 2005 and became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2006, becoming the second foreign-born woman to serve as First Lady. During her first tenure as First Lady, she focused on child welfare initiatives, launching the Be Best awareness campaign in 2018 to address youth well-being, cyberbullying, and opioid abuse. She also oversaw various historical preservation projects within the White House complex. Following her husband's victory in the 2024 presidential election, she resumed her duties as First Lady of the United States in January 2025.
michael-phelps: Michael Fred Phelps II is an American former competitive swimmer born on June 30, 1985, in Baltimore, Maryland. Widely considered one of the greatest athletes in sports history, he is the most decorated Olympian of all time, having won a total of 28 Olympic medals. Phelps made his Olympic debut at the 2000 Sydney Games at age 15. Across five Olympic Games from 2000 to 2016, he accumulated 23 gold medals, three silver medals, and two bronze medals. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, he achieved a historic milestone by winning eight gold medals in a single Games, breaking Mark Spitz's 1972 record of seven. Throughout his career, Phelps set 39 world records in various individual and relay events, primarily specializing in the butterfly, individual medley, and freestyle disciplines. After temporarily retiring in 2012, he returned for the 2016 Rio Olympics before permanently retiring from competitive swimming.
julia-gillard: Julia Eileen Gillard is an Australian former politician who served as the Prime Minister of Australia from 2010 to 2013, becoming the first woman to hold the position. Born in Barry, Wales, in 1961, her family migrated to Adelaide, Australia, in 1966. Before entering public office, Gillard practiced law, specializing in industrial matters. She was elected to the Australian House of Representatives for the Labor Party in 1998. Following Labor's 2007 election victory, she became Deputy Prime Minister under Kevin Rudd. In June 2010, Gillard assumed the party leadership and was sworn in as Prime Minister. Her administration passed key legislative reforms, including the National Disability Insurance Scheme, national education initiatives, and a carbon pricing mechanism. Internationally known for her 2012 parliamentary address on misogyny, she retired from politics in 2013. Subsequently, Gillard chaired the Global Partnership for Education and mental health organization Beyond Blue.
john-forbes-nash: John Forbes Nash Jr. was an American mathematician and economist who made fundamental contributions to game theory, real algebraic geometry, and partial differential equations. Born on June 13, 1928, in Bluefield, West Virginia, he earned his doctorate from Princeton University in 1950. His doctoral dissertation introduced the concept of the Nash equilibrium, a fundamental framework in non-cooperative game theory that revolutionized modern economics. Nash served on the faculty at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and later returned to Princeton as a senior research mathematician. In 1994, he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences alongside Reinhard Selten and John Harsanyi. He also received the Abel Prize in 2015 for his work on nonlinear partial differential equations. Throughout his adult life, Nash managed severe paranoid schizophrenia, a struggle later portrayed in the biography and film A Beautiful Mind. He and his wife died in a car crash on May 23, 2015.
robert-downey-jr: Robert John Downey Jr. is an internationally known American actor who was born on April 4, 1965, in New York City. He made his acting debut as a child in his father's film Pound in 1970 and gained recognition in the 1980s as part of the Brat Pack. Downey achieved critical acclaim for his portrayal of Charlie Chaplin in the 1992 biographical film Chaplin, earning an Academy Award nomination. Following a period of personal and legal troubles related to substance abuse, he revitalized his career in the 2000s. Downey gained massive global popularity playing Tony Stark, also known as Iron Man, in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, beginning with Iron Man in 2008 and concluding with Avengers Endgame in 2019. He also starred as Sherlock Holmes in two feature films directed by Guy Ritchie. In 2024, Downey won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his role in Christopher Nolan's film Oppenheimer.
corazon-aquino: Maria Corazon Cojuangco Aquino was a Filipino politician who served as President of the Philippines from 1986 to 1992. Internationally known for her role in restoring democracy to the nation, she was the first female president of the Philippines and the first woman to hold the presidency in Asia. Aquino entered public life following the 1983 assassination of her husband, Benigno Aquino Jr., a prominent senator and leading political opponent of President Ferdinand Marcos. She united the political opposition against the regime and challenged Marcos in the snap presidential election of February 1986. Mass protests against election fraud culminated in the bloodless People Power Revolution, forcing Marcos into exile and installing Aquino as president. During her tenure, she oversaw the enactment of the 1987 Constitution, which limited executive power and restored a democratic bicameral legislature. She successfully defended her administration against multiple military coup attempts before peacefully completing her term in 1992.
bette-davis: Ruth Elizabeth Davis, internationally known as Bette Davis, was an American actress who lived from 1908 to 1989. Widely regarded as one of the greatest performers in Hollywood cinema history, she was noted for her willingness to play intense, unsympathetic characters across a wide range of film genres. After beginning her career on Broadway, Davis moved to Hollywood in 1930 and signed with Warner Bros. She achieved critical acclaim with films such as Of Human Bondage. Over her six-decade career, Davis earned ten Academy Award nominations for Best Actress and won twice, for her performances in Dangerous and Jezebel. Her other famous roles include All About Eve and What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? In addition to her acting success, she became the first female president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 1941. She continued acting in film, television, and theater until shortly before her death in 1989.
anne-bront: Anne Brontë was a British novelist and poet who lived from January 17, 1820, to May 28, 1849. She was the youngest member of the Brontë literary family, which included her sisters Charlotte and Emily. Writing under the pen name Acton Bell, she first published poetry alongside her sisters in 1846 before releasing her debut novel, Agnes Grey, in 1847. This work drew heavily on her personal experiences working as a governess. In 1848, she published her second novel, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, which gained widespread attention for its realistic depiction of alcoholism, marital breakdown, and the legal constraints placed on Victorian women. Throughout her brief career, Brontë adopted a realistic, unromanticized style that distinguished her work from that of her peers. She died of tuberculosis at the age of twenty-nine in Scarborough, Yorkshire, leaving behind an enduring contribution to English literature.
eva-per-n: María Eva Duarte de Perón, internationally known as Eva Perón or Evita, was an Argentine actress and politician who served as First Lady of Argentina from 1946 until her death in 1952. Born in Los Toldos in 1919, she moved to Buenos Aires in 1935 to pursue a career in stage, radio, and film acting. In 1944, she met Colonel Juan Domingo Perón, marrying him the following year. When Juan Perón was elected president in 1946, Eva became a prominent political figure. She advocated for labor rights, ran the Eva Perón Foundation to assist poor citizens, and successfully campaigned for women's suffrage, which was granted in 1947. She also established the Female Peronist Party in 1949. In 1951, she announced her candidacy for vice president but withdrew due to health issues and military opposition. Perón died of cancer in July 1952 at 33 years of age. She remains an iconic figure in Argentina.
julianne-moore: Julie Anne Smith, known professionally as Julianne Moore, is an internationally known British-American actress and author born on December 3, 1960. She began her acting career in television during the 1980s before transitioning to film in the 1990s. Moore gained critical acclaim for her versatile performances in both independent art-house films and major Hollywood productions. Her prominent film credits include Boogie Nights, The Big Lebowski, The End of the Affair, Far from Heaven, The Hours, and Children of Men. In 2015, she won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her portrayal of a professor with early-onset Alzheimer's disease in Still Alice. In addition to her Oscar, she has earned two Golden Globe Awards, a BAFTA Award, and two Emmy Awards. Outside of acting, Moore is an accomplished children's author, best known for creating the popular Freckleface Strawberry picture book series, which was later adapted into a musical.
daniel-craig: Daniel Wroughton Craig is an English actor who achieved international fame for portraying the secret agent James Bond. Born on March 2, 1968, in Chester, England, he trained at the National Youth Theatre and graduated from the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London in 1991. Craig began his career on stage and television, gaining critical recognition for the British television drama Our Friends in the North. His early film appearances included roles in Elizabeth, Lara Croft: Tomb Raider, Road to Perdition, and Layer Cake. In 2005, Craig was cast as the sixth actor to play James Bond, debuting in the critically acclaimed Casino Royale in 2006. He played the role across five films, ending with No Time to Die in 2021. Outside the franchise, Craig gained further acclaim as Detective Benoit Blanc in the mystery films Knives Out and Glass Onion. He was appointed Companion of the Order of Saint Michael and Saint George in 2022.
erich-fromm: Erich Pinchas Fromm was a renowned German sociologist, psychoanalyst, and humanistic philosopher who lived from 1900 to 1980. Born in Frankfurt am Main, he studied sociology and psychology at the University of Heidelberg before completing psychoanalytic training in Berlin. Associated early in his career with the Frankfurt School of critical theory, Fromm fled Nazi Germany in 1934 and emigrated to the United States. He synthesized Freudian psychoanalysis with social theory, developing a distinct framework known as humanistic psychoanalysis. His writings critically examined the psychological impacts of modern industrial capitalism, the nature of human freedom, and social alienation. Fromm authored several widely influential books, including Escape from Freedom in 1941 and The Art of Loving in 1956. Over his long career, he taught at major universities in the United States and Mexico before spending his final years in Switzerland, where he died in 1980.
paracelsus: Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, best known as Paracelsus, was a Swiss physician, philosopher, theologian, and alchemist born around 1493 in Egg, Switzerland. He revolutionized Renaissance medicine by rejecting the classical theories of Galen and Avicenna, emphasizing direct observation, empirical evidence, and practical experience instead. Paracelsus pioneered the medical use of chemicals and minerals, laying the foundations for modern pharmacology and iatrochemistry. He famously posited that all substances are toxic at high enough doses, establishing a core principle of modern toxicology often summarized as the dose makes the poison. Throughout his life, Paracelsus traveled extensively across Europe, lecturing in German rather than Latin to make medical knowledge accessible. He also wrote on theology and philosophy, advocating a holistic worldview that integrated nature, spirit, and health. Paracelsus died on September 24, 1541, in Salzburg, leaving a profound legacy in medical history.
hugh-jackman: Hugh Michael Jackman is an internationally known Australian actor and singer, born on October 12, 1968, in Sydney, Australia. He gained initial recognition in Australian television and musical theater, including the 1998 London production of Oklahoma!. Jackman achieved global fame with his breakthrough performance as Wolverine in the X-Men film series, playing the character across two decades. Beyond superhero cinema, he has demonstrated versatility in dramatic and musical roles. His performance as Jean Valjean in the film adaptation of Les Misérables earned him a Golden Globe Award and an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. He also starred in the popular musical film The Greatest Showman, as well as dramatic thrillers like The Prestige and Prisoners. On stage, Jackman won a Tony Award for his Broadway leading role in The Boy from Oz. In 2019, he was appointed a Companion of the Order of Australia for his service to the performing arts.
pamela-anderson: Pamela Denise Anderson is a Canadian actress, model, and activist born on July 1, 1967, in Ladysmith, British Columbia. She achieved international fame after being selected as Playboy magazine's Playmate of the Month in February 1990, going on to record the most cover appearances in the publication's history. Anderson gained global recognition on television for her role as C.J. Parker in the action drama series Baywatch, appearing as a main cast member from 1992 to 1997. She subsequently starred as Vallery Irons in the action series V.I.P. from 1998 to 2002 and played title roles in feature films including Barb Wire in 1996. Beyond her entertainment career, Anderson is a prominent advocate for animal rights and a longtime spokesperson for People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. In 2022, she made her Broadway debut playing Roxie Hart in the musical Chicago, and in 2023, she released a memoir. She holds dual Canadian and American citizenship.
alphonse-daudet: Louis Marie Alphonse Daudet was a French novelist, playwright, and poet who became one of the most popular writers of late nineteenth-century France. Born in Nîmes in 1840, he moved to Paris in 1857 to pursue a literary career, initially publishing poetry before turning to prose and drama. Internationally known for his vivid depictions of Provençal life and his humorous, sympathetic characterizations, Daudet achieved lasting fame with his short story collection Letters from My Windmill and the novel Tartarin of Tarascon. His autobiographical novel Le Petit Chose further established his reputation. Associated with the Naturalist movement alongside contemporaries like Émile Zola, Daudet brought a distinctly personal, impressionistic warmth to his realistic portrayals of social conditions and human flaws. His play L'Arlésienne, featuring incidental music by Georges Bizet, remains a celebrated theatrical work. Daudet continued writing prolifically until his death in Paris in 1897, leaving a significant legacy in French literature.
joseph-smith: Joseph Smith Jr., born on December 23, 1805, in Sharon, Vermont, was an American religious leader internationally known as the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement and revered by his followers as a prophet. In the late 1820s, he reported receiving heavenly visions and angelic visitations that led to his translation and publication of the Book of Mormon in 1830. That same year, he formally organized the Church of Christ, attracting thousands of converts who sought to restore early Christianity. Facing local opposition and persecution, he led his followers to establish communities in Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois, where he founded the city of Nauvoo. As mayor and militia commander in Nauvoo, he introduced distinctive theological doctrines, including plural marriage and temple rituals. In June 1844, amid growing political tensions and internal dissension, he was arrested and subsequently killed by an armed mob in Carthage, Illinois, on June 27, 1844.
ferdinand-de-saussure: Ferdinand Mongin de Saussure was an internationally known Swiss linguist and philosopher (1857–1913) whose ideas laid the foundation for major developments in linguistics and semiotics. Born in Geneva, he studied at the University of Leipzig, where he made early contributions to Indo-European philology. Saussure later taught in Paris before returning to teach at the University of Geneva. He is widely considered a founding figure of modern structural linguistics. His theoretical framework distinguished between langue, the abstract system of a language, and parole, the concrete instances of speech. He also emphasized the arbitrary relationship between the signifier and the signified, and introduced the distinction between synchronic and diachronic linguistic analysis. Although he published relatively little during his later career, his former students compiled his lecture notes into the influential volume Course in General Linguistics, which was published posthumously in 1916.
maurice-ravel: Joseph-Maurice Ravel, born on March 7, 1875, in Ciboure, France, was an internationally known French composer, pianist, and conductor. He lived from 1875 to 1937 and became one of the foremost figures of early twentieth-century classical music. Ravel is frequently associated with Impressionism alongside his contemporary Claude Debussy, although he rejected the label. He studied at the Paris Conservatoire under Gabriel Fauré, developing a style characterized by meticulous craftsmanship, inventive harmonies, and masterful orchestral technique. Among his most famous compositions are the hypnotic orchestral piece Boléro, the ballet Daphnis et Chloé, the piano work Pavane pour une infante défunte, and his influential orchestration of Modest Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition. Ravel was also acclaimed for virtuosic piano compositions like Gaspard de la nuit. In his later years, a progressive neurological condition impaired his ability to compose. He died in Paris on December 28, 1937.
christopher-nolan: Christopher Edward Nolan is an internationally known British-American filmmaker born on July 30, 1970, in London, England. Raised in both London and Evanston, Illinois, he studied English literature at University College London, where he began making short films. Nolan gained widespread recognition with his second feature, Memento, in 2000, which highlighted his interest in non-linear narratives and psychological themes. He achieved global commercial success by directing The Dark Knight Trilogy from 2005 to 2012. His subsequent works include blockbuster original science-fiction films such as Inception in 2010 and Interstellar in 2014, as well as historical dramas like Dunkirk in 2017. Nolan often collaborates with his wife, producer Emma Thomas, and is known for using practical effects, large-format film photography, and complex story structures. In 2024, he won the Academy Award for Best Director for the biographical film Oppenheimer. Nolan is widely regarded as one of the most influential directors of his era.
vivien-leigh: Vivien Leigh, born Vivian Mary Hartley, was an internationally acclaimed British actress celebrated for her roles on stage and screen. Born on November 5, 1913, in Darjeeling, British India, she received her formal education in Europe before attending the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London. Leigh gained worldwide fame for her portrayal of Scarlett O'Hara in the epic film Gone with the Wind in 1939, earning her first Academy Award for Best Actress. She won a second Academy Award for her performance as Blanche DuBois in the 1951 film adaptation of A Streetcar Named Desire, a role she had previously performed on the London stage. Throughout her career, Leigh frequently collaborated with her second husband, Laurence Olivier, appearing together in numerous Shakespearean productions and theatrical tours. Despite facing recurrent bouts of chronic tuberculosis and bipolar disorder, she maintained a distinguished acting career until her death on July 8, 1967.
monica-bellucci: Monica Anna Maria Bellucci, born on September 30, 1964, in Città di Castello, Italy, is an internationally acclaimed Italian actress and model. She initially pursued a degree in law at the University of Perugia while modeling to pay her tuition. After signing with Elite Model Management, she became a prominent face for brands like Dolce and Gabbana. Bellucci transitioned to acting in the early 1990s, gaining critical acclaim for her lead role in the 2000 Italian film Malèna. Her international profile expanded with roles in major Hollywood productions, including Persephone in The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, Mary Magdalene in The Passion of the Christ, and Lucia Sciarra in the 2015 James Bond film Spectre. Fluent in Italian, French, and English, she has built a diverse filmography across multiple languages and international cinema markets.
horatio-nelson: Vice Admiral Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson, was a British naval officer who gained international renown for his leadership and tactical brilliance during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Born on September 29, 1758, in Norfolk, England, Nelson entered the Royal Navy at a young age and rose rapidly through the ranks. He was noted for his bold command style, often engaging the enemy at close quarters. Despite suffering severe injuries over his career, including the loss of sight in his right eye and his right arm, he continued to lead major fleet actions. Nelson secured decisive victories at the Battle of the Nile in 1798 and the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801. His most famous victory occurred at the Battle of Trafalgar on October 21, 1805, where he defeated a combined French and Spanish fleet, establishing British naval supremacy. Nelson was mortally wounded during the action and died later that day.
vin-diesel: Mark Sinclair, professionally known as Vin Diesel, is an American actor and filmmaker born on July 18, 1967, in Alameda County, California. He is internationally known for starring in major Hollywood action franchises. Diesel began his creative career in the 1990s, writing, directing, and starring in the short film Multi-Facial and the independent drama Strays. These early works caught the attention of director Steven Spielberg, who cast him in the war film Saving Private Ryan in 1998. Diesel achieved global stardom playing Dominic Toretto in The Fast and the Furious franchise, a series he also produces. He further cemented his action star status by portraying Richard B. Riddick in The Chronicles of Riddick series and Xander Cage in the xXx franchise. Additionally, Diesel provided the voice for the title character in The Iron Giant and Groot in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. He is also the founder of the production company One Race Films.
clara-zetkin: Clara Josephine Zetkin was an internationally known German Marxist theorist, communist activist, and advocate for women's rights. Born Clara Eissner on July 5, 1857, she initially joined the Social Democratic Party of Germany, where she edited its women's newspaper, Die Gleichheit, for twenty-five years. Zetkin was a prominent figure in the international socialist movement and played a crucial role in establishing International Women's Day in 1910 to promote women's suffrage and equal rights. Opposed to World War I, she helped found the revolutionary Spartacus League alongside Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. This group later evolved into the Communist Party of Germany, which Zetkin represented in the Reichstag from 1920 to 1933. She also served as an executive committee member of the Communist International. Following the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi regime, Zetkin went into exile in the Soviet Union, where she died on June 20, 1933.
ayrton-senna: Ayrton Senna da Silva was a Brazilian racing driver born in São Paulo on March 21, 1960. He is widely regarded as one of the most successful drivers in Formula One history. Senna began his career in karting before moving to single-seater racing, making his Formula One debut in 1984 with Toleman. He joined Lotus in 1985, securing his first victory, before moving to McLaren in 1988. Partnered alongside Alain Prost, Senna achieved his greatest success at McLaren, winning three Formula One World Drivers' Championships in 1988, 1990, and 1991. Recognized for his qualifying speed and exceptional performance in wet-weather conditions, he accumulated 41 Grand Prix victories and 65 pole positions throughout his career. In 1994, Senna signed with the Williams team. On May 1, 1994, he died from injuries sustained in a high-speed crash at the San Marino Grand Prix in Imola, Italy.
mitt-romney: Willard Mitt Romney is an American politician and businessman born on March 12, 1947, in Detroit, Michigan. He gained prominence in the private sector as the co-founder of the private equity firm Bain Capital. In 1999, Romney took charge of the Salt Lake Organizing Committee, successfully managing the 2002 Winter Olympics. Entering politics, he served as the 70th governor of Massachusetts from 2003 to 2007, during which he signed a landmark state healthcare reform law. Romney secured the Republican nomination for President of the United States in 2012, ultimately losing the general election to incumbent Barack Obama. In 2018, he was elected to represent Utah in the United States Senate, taking office in January 2019. Throughout his Senate tenure, Romney established a reputation as a moderate conservative, frequently demonstrating political independence within his party on key legislative votes and high-profile congressional proceedings.
georges-bizet: Alexandre César Léopold Bizet, registered at baptism as Georges Bizet, was a French composer of the Romantic era, born in Paris in 1838. Recognized early for his exceptional musical talent, he entered the Conservatoire de Paris at age nine and won the prestigious Prix de Rome in 1857. Bizet composed across various genres, producing orchestral works like his early Symphony in C and incidental music such as L'Arlésienne, as well as operas including Les pêcheurs de perles. His final masterpiece, the opera Carmen, premiered in 1875. Although its initial reception was mixed and distressed the composer, Carmen quickly gained worldwide acclaim shortly after his sudden death. Bizet died of heart failure near Paris in June 1875 at the age of thirty-six. Today, he is internationally celebrated for his brilliant orchestration, expressive melodies, and lasting influence on French operatic music.
viktor-yushchenko: Viktor Andriyovych Yushchenko is a Ukrainian politician who served as the third President of Ukraine from 2005 to 2010. Born on February 23, 1954, in Khoruzhivka, Sumy Oblast, he studied economics and eventually became the Governor of the National Bank of Ukraine in 1993, overseeing the introduction of the national currency, the hryvnia. He served as Prime Minister of Ukraine from 1999 to 2001 under President Leonid Kuchma. Yushchenko gained widespread international recognition as the leader of the democratic opposition during the 2004 presidential election. His campaign was marked by a near-fatal dioxin poisoning that left him severely disfigured. Mass protests against alleged election fraud, known as the Orange Revolution, led to a repeat vote in which Yushchenko won the presidency. During his tenure, he pursued a pro-Western foreign policy, advocating for Ukraine's integration into NATO and the European Union. He was succeeded in 2010 by Viktor Yanukovych.
marquis-de-sade: Donatien Alphonse François, Marquis de Sade, born in Paris in 1740, was a French nobleman, revolutionary politician, philosopher, and writer. He is internationally known for his explicit erotic works, which combined libertine fiction with radical philosophical reflections on materialism, morality, and religion. Sade spent roughly thirty-two years of his life imprisoned in various fortresses and asylums, including the Bastille and Charenton, due to sexual scandals and the provocative nature of his writings. During the French Revolution, he briefly engaged in political life, serving as an elected delegate to the National Convention and aligning himself with revolutionary factions. His most famous works include Justine, The 120 Days of Sodom, and Philosophy in the Bedroom. Sade's literary legacy remains influential and contentious, exploring the extreme boundaries of human behavior and giving rise to the psychological term sadism. He died in Charenton Asylum in 1814 at the age of seventy-four.
robert-a-millikan: Robert Andrews Millikan was an American experimental physicist who made fundamental contributions to modern physics. Born in Morrison, Illinois, Millikan earned his doctorate from Columbia University in 1895. He joined the faculty at the University of Chicago, where he performed his famous oil-drop experiment in 1909. This landmark measurement precisely determined the elementary electric charge of a single electron. Millikan later experimentally verified Albert Einstein's photoelectric equation, providing strong support for the quantum theory of light. For these achievements, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923. In 1921, Millikan moved to the California Institute of Technology, serving as chairman of its executive council until 1945. There, he spearheaded extensive research into extraterrestrial radiation, coining the term cosmic rays. Beyond his research, he played a crucial role in developing Caltech into a leading scientific institution. Millikan died in San Marino, California, in 1953, leaving a lasting legacy in physical science.
emma-stone: Emily Jean Stone, internationally known professionally as Emma Stone, is an American actress and producer. Born on November 6, 1988, in Scottsdale, Arizona, she began acting as a child in youth theater productions. Stone made her feature film debut in the 2007 comedy Superbad and achieved wider recognition with her leading role in Easy A in 2010. Over her career, she has starred in a wide range of critical and commercial successes, including The Help, The Amazing Spider-Man, Birdman, and Cruella. Stone earned widespread acclaim for her performances in musicals and dramas, winning the Academy Award for Best Actress for her roles in La La Land in 2016 and Poor Things in 2023. In addition to her acting achievements, she co-founded the production company Fruit Tree in 2020, producing acclaimed films and television series. Stone remains one of the world's highest-paid and most celebrated contemporary performers.
bram-stoker: Abraham Stoker, internationally known as Bram Stoker, was an Irish novelist and short story writer born on November 8, 1847, in Clontarf, Dublin, Ireland. He graduated from Trinity College Dublin before working as a civil servant and drama critic. In 1878, Stoker relocated to London to become the personal secretary to the renowned actor Sir Henry Irving and the business manager of the Lyceum Theatre, a post he held for twenty-seven years. Alongside his administrative work, Stoker authored fiction, publishing his debut novel, The Snake's Pass, in 1890. He achieved enduring global recognition with his 1897 Gothic horror masterpiece, Dracula. Formatted as an epistolary novel, the story established enduring tropes of vampire mythology and popular culture. Stoker wrote eleven other novels, including The Jewel of Seven Stars, as well as several short story collections. He died in London on April 20, 1912.
salma-hayek: Salma Valgarma Hayek Jiménez, born on September 2, 1966, is a Mexican and American actress and film producer. She began her acting career in Mexico, starring in the successful telenovela Teresa in 1989 and the acclaimed drama film El Callejón de los Milagros in 1995. Transitioning to Hollywood in the mid-1990s, she gained international recognition with prominent roles in films such as Desperado and From Dusk Till Dawn. Hayek achieved major critical acclaim by producing and starring as painter Frida Kahlo in the 2002 biographical film Frida. Her performance earned her an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress, making her the first Mexican actress to be nominated in that category. She has since appeared in a wide variety of genres, including Grown Ups, Puss in Boots, and Eternals. Beyond acting, Hayek works actively as a producer and advocate for women's rights and humanitarian causes worldwide.
jean-baptiste-de-lamarck: Jean-Baptiste Pierre Antoine de Monet, Chevalier de Lamarck, born in 1744, was a French naturalist, soldier, and academic who made foundational contributions to early evolutionary biology. He initially served in the French army before turning to botany and publishing a landmark work on French flora. This achievement secured him a post at the Jardin des Plantes, and he later became a professor of zoology at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle. Lamarck was a key pioneer in the study of invertebrates, coining the term itself and restructuring their classification. In his 1809 work Philosophie Zoologique, he proposed an early theory of biological evolution. His mechanism, known as Lamarckism, suggested that organisms pass on acquired traits to their offspring based on environmental use and disuse. Though later superseded by natural selection, his theories advanced the concept of transmutation and helped formalize biology as a discipline. He died in 1829.
tomas-transtr-mer: Tomas Gösta Tranströmer was an internationally acclaimed Swedish poet, psychologist, and translator who lived from 1931 to 2015. Born in Stockholm, he earned a degree in psychology from Stockholm University in 1956. Throughout his adult life, Tranströmer balanced his literary pursuits with a career as a psychologist, working in juvenile offender institutions and rehabilitation centers. His poetry, translated into more than sixty languages, is widely praised for its vivid metaphors, economy of language, and surrealistic imagery. His works frequently explore nature, memory, isolation, and the underlying mysteries of the human psyche. In 1990, Tranströmer suffered a severe stroke that left him partially paralyzed and impaired his speech, yet he persevered, continuing to write and publish poetry. Recognized as one of Scandinavia's most significant modern literary figures, he received many international honors, culminating in the 2011 Nobel Prize in Literature. He passed away in Stockholm in 2015.
d-h-lawrence: David Herbert Lawrence, born on September 11, 1885, in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, was an influential English writer and poet. His works explored the dehumanizing effects of modern industrial society, focusing on themes of human sexuality, psychological health, and instinct. Lawrence attended University College, Nottingham, and initially worked as a teacher before committing fully to writing. He gained prominence with his autobiographical novel Sons and Lovers in 1913. His later novels, including The Rainbow, Women in Love, and Lady Chatterley's Lover, provoked significant controversy and censorship due to their explicit depictions of sexuality and sharp critiques of Western civilization. Alongside his novels, Lawrence produced numerous short stories, poems, travel books, and literary essays. Following the outbreak of World War I, he and his German wife, Frieda von Richthofen, spent years traveling internationally, a period he called his savage pilgrimage. Lawrence died of tuberculosis on March 2, 1930, in Vence, France, leaving a lasting modernist legacy.
george-v: George V, whose full name was George Frederick Ernest Albert, served as King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 until his death in 1936. Born in London in 1865, he was the second son of Prince Albert Edward, later King Edward VII, and Princess Alexandra of Denmark. George served in the Royal Navy before becoming heir to the throne following the death of his elder brother in 1892. He married Victoria Mary of Teck in 1893. Ascending the throne in 1910, George guided the British monarchy through the First World War. In 1917, he officially renamed the royal house from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor due to anti-German sentiment. His reign saw significant political transformation, including Irish independence and the growth of the Commonwealth. He died in January 1936 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Edward VIII.
rita-hayworth: Margarita Carmen Cansino, known professionally as Rita Hayworth, was an American actress and dancer who achieved international fame during the Golden Age of Hollywood. Born in Brooklyn, New York, on October 17, 1918, she began her career performing as a dancer alongside her father before signing with Fox Film Corporation in 1935. After changing her screen name and hair color, she became Columbia Pictures' top star during the 1940s. Hayworth appeared in 61 films over a 37-year career, earning the moniker "The Love Goddess" for her screen presence. Her most celebrated performances include roles in prominent films such as Cover Girl, Gilda, and The Lady from Shanghai. Beyond her screen career, she was a famous World War II pin-up figure and was married five times, including to director Orson Welles and Prince Aly Khan. Hayworth was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 1980, significantly increasing public awareness of the illness, and died on May 14, 1987.
donald-tusk: Donald Franciszek Tusk is a Polish politician who has served as the Prime Minister of Poland since December 2023, having previously held the position from 2007 to 2014. Born on April 22, 1957, in Gdańsk, Tusk studied history at the University of Gdańsk and became involved in anti-communist student politics and the Solidarity movement during the 1980s. In 2001, he co-founded the liberal-conservative Civic Platform party, which he went on to lead. Following his initial tenure as head of government, Tusk transitioned to international governance, serving as the President of the European Council from 2014 to 2019. He subsequently served as the President of the European People's Party from 2019 until 2022. Tusk re-entered domestic politics to lead the political opposition in the 2023 parliamentary elections, subsequently forming a coalition government that restored him to office.
sylvia-plath: Sylvia Plath was an internationally known American poet, novelist, and short-story writer who lived from 1932 to 1963. Born in Boston, Massachusetts, she displayed an early talent for writing, publishing her first poem at age eight. She attended Smith College and later earned a scholarship to Newnham College, Cambridge, in England. In 1956, Plath married the British poet Ted Hughes, with whom she had two children. She published her first poetry collection, The Colossus and Other Poems, in 1960, followed by her semi-autobiographical novel, The Bell Jar, in early 1963 under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas. Plath struggled with severe clinical depression throughout her adult life and died by suicide in London at thirty years old. Renowned as a pioneer of confessional poetry, her posthumously published collection Ariel cemented her literary legacy. In 1982, Plath became the first person to be posthumously awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry for The Collected Poems.
albert-a-michelson: Albert Abraham Michelson was an American physicist best known for his precise measurements of the speed of light and his pioneering work in optics. Born in Strelno, Prussia, in 1852, his family emigrated to the United States during his infancy. He graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1873 and later studied physics in Europe. Michelson designed the optical interferometer, an instrument that splits light to measure tiny distances. In 1887, along with Edward Morley, he conducted the landmark Michelson-Morley experiment. This test failed to detect the hypothetical luminiferous aether, providing key evidence against its existence and aiding the development of special relativity. In 1907, Michelson became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Physics. He served as a professor at Case School of Applied Science and the University of Chicago, continuing research until his death in 1931.
eugene-oneill: Eugene Gladstone O'Neill was an American playwright who fundamentally transformed the nation's theatre by introducing dramatic realism. Born in New York City on October 16, 1888, O'Neill spent much of his early life traveling with his father, a stage actor. He attended Princeton University briefly before embarking on various maritime jobs, experiences that deeply influenced his writing. O'Neill began writing plays in the 1910s, utilizing vernacular dialogue and exploring tragic, realistic themes involving marginalized characters. His prominent works include Beyond the Horizon, The Hairy Ape, Desire Under the Elms, The Iceman Cometh, and the posthumously published autobiographical masterpiece Long Day's Journey into Night. O'Neill remains the only American playwright to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, awarded in 1936. Additionally, he earned four Pulitzer Prizes for Drama throughout his career. His innovative stylistic techniques and serious subject matter elevated American drama to international standing. O'Neill died in Boston on November 27, 1953.
jeff-bezos: Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor born on January 12, 1964, in Albuquerque, New Mexico. He is best known as the founder of Amazon, the multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. After graduating from Princeton University with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science, Bezos worked on Wall Street before founding Amazon in 1994 as an online bookstore. Under his leadership as chief executive officer, Amazon grew into one of the largest and most influential corporations globally. In addition to Amazon, Bezos founded the aerospace manufacturer and spaceflight services company Blue Origin in 2000, and he purchased the major American newspaper The Washington Post in 2013. Bezos stepped down as chief executive officer of Amazon in 2021 to transition into the role of executive chairman. He consistently ranks among the wealthiest individuals in the world.
whoopi-goldberg: Whoopi Goldberg, born Caryn Elaine Johnson on November 13, 1955, is an internationally known American actress, comedian, author, and television personality. She began her performing career in theater before achieving widespread recognition for her breakthrough film role in The Color Purple in 1985, which earned her a Golden Globe Award. Goldberg subsequently starred in numerous successful films, including Ghost in 1990, for which she won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, becoming the second Black woman to win an acting Oscar. She also starred in the popular comedy Sister Act in 1992 and its sequel. Goldberg is one of few entertainers to achieve EGOT status, having won an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award. Beyond film and stage, she has authored several books for both adults and children. Since 2007, she has served as a co-host and moderator on the daytime talk show The View.
ursula-k-le-guin: Ursula Kroeber Le Guin (1929–2018) was an American author best known for her works of fantasy and science fiction. Born in Berkeley, California, she attended Radcliffe College and Columbia University, studying French and Italian literature. Over a career spanning more than five decades, Le Guin published over twenty novels, alongside short stories, essays, poetry, and children's books. She gained international recognition for her Earthsea fantasy series, beginning with A Wizard of Earthsea in 1968, and her Hainish Cycle science fiction novels, including The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed. Her writing frequently explored themes of anthropology, feminism, Taoism, and political philosophy, significantly influencing modern speculative literature. Le Guin received numerous accolades, including multiple Hugo and Nebula Awards, a National Book Award, and the National Book Foundation Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters. She passed away in Portland, Oregon, in 2018.
gianluigi-buffon: Gianluigi Buffon, born January 28, 1978, in Carrara, Italy, is an Italian former professional footballer who played as a goalkeeper. Widely regarded as one of the greatest goalkeepers of all time, his professional career spanned nearly three decades. Buffon began his senior club career at Parma in 1995, winning the Coppa Italia and the UEFA Cup. In 2001, he transferred to Juventus for a world record transfer fee for a goalkeeper. Across two stints with Juventus, he won ten Serie A titles and reached three UEFA Champions League finals. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain before returning to Parma, where he retired in 2023. Internationally, Buffon earned 176 caps for the Italian national team, making him the most capped player in the squad's history. He played a pivotal role in Italy winning the 2006 FIFA World Cup, keeping five clean sheets during the tournament.
barbra-streisand: Barbara Joan Streisand, born April 24, 1942, is an American singer, actress, director, and producer whose career spans six decades. Internationally known for her achievements in music and cinema, she began performing in nightclubs and Broadway productions during the early 1960s. Her debut musical release, The Barbra Streisand Album, earned two Grammy Awards. Streisand gained film stardom after reprising her Broadway role as Fanny Brice in the musical Funny Girl, winning the Academy Award for Best Actress in 1968. She went on to star in successful films including The Way We Were, A Star Is Born, and Yentl, which she also directed and produced. As one of the best-selling recording artists in history, Streisand has released number-one albums across six consecutive decades. She is among the few performers who have been honored with Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony awards throughout her career.
jeremy-bentham: Jeremy Bentham was an influential English philosopher, jurist, and social reformer who lived from February 15, 1748, to June 6, 1832. Considered the founder of modern utilitarianism, Bentham advocated that actions should be evaluated based on their utility, famously summarized as promoting the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people. Born in London, he studied law at Oxford but chose to pursue legal and social philosophy instead of practicing law. Throughout his life, Bentham proposed extensive legal and institutional reforms. He championed individual rights, freedom of speech, equal rights for women, animal rights, the abolition of slavery, and the decriminalization of homosexual acts. He also designed the Panopticon, an architectural model intended for institutional surveillance, particularly in prisons. Bentham wrote prolifically, with major works including An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation. His ideas profoundly impacted nineteenth-century radical politics, legal philosophy, and social policy globally.
moon-jae-in: Moon Jae-in is a South Korean politician and lawyer who served as the 12th President of the Republic of Korea from May 2017 to May 2022. Born on January 24, 1953, in Geoje, South Korea, to refugees from North Korea, Moon studied law at Kyung Hee University. During his youth, he engaged in pro-democracy student activism and served in the Republic of Korea Army Special Warfare Command. He later established a legal practice specializing in human rights and labor law alongside future president Roh Moo-hyun. Moon entered national politics as Senior Secretary for Civil Affairs and Chief of Staff under Roh. He was elected to the National Assembly in 2012 and led the Democratic Party of Korea. As president, Moon pursued diplomatic engagement with North Korea, culminating in three inter-Korean summits in 2018, promoted clean energy, and managed the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
john-major: Sir John Major is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Leader of the Conservative Party from 1990 to 1997. Born on March 29, 1943, in London, his full name is John Major. He entered Parliament in 1979 as the Member of Parliament for Huntingdon. Before becoming prime minister, he held prominent cabinet positions under Margaret Thatcher, serving as Chief Secretary to the Treasury, Foreign Secretary, and Chancellor of the Exchequer. Major succeeded Thatcher as prime minister in November 1990 and subsequently led his party to a fourth consecutive general election victory in 1992. His tenure was defined by significant events, including the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, internal divisions over European integration, and crucial groundwork for the Northern Ireland peace process through the 1993 Downing Street Declaration. He stepped down after the Conservative defeat in 1997.
mae-west: Mary Jane West, known professionally as Mae West, was an American actress, singer, screenwriter, playwright, and comedian whose entertainment career spanned seven decades. Born on August 17, 1893, in Brooklyn, New York, she began performing in vaudeville during childhood. She gained widespread attention in the 1920s by writing and starring in controversial Broadway plays, including Sex, which led to legal battles over censorship. In the 1930s, West transitioned to Hollywood, becoming one of Paramount Pictures' top box-office attractions. She wrote or co-wrote screenplays for several of her major films, such as She Done Him Wrong and I'm No Angel, both released in 1933. Renowned for her sultry persona, sharp wit, and clever double entendres, West played a significant role in pushing the boundaries of cinematic censorship. She continued performing in theater, radio, television, and film in her later years. West died on November 22, 1980, in Los Angeles, California.
kanye-west: Kanye Omari West is an American rapper, record producer, and fashion designer born on June 8, 1977, in Atlanta, Georgia. Raised primarily in Chicago, Illinois, West first gained widespread recognition in the early 2000s as an in-house producer for Roc-A-Fella Records, crafting signature soul-sampled beats for artists such as Jay-Z. He launched a critically acclaimed solo career with his 2004 debut album, The College Dropout. Over the subsequent decades, West emerged as one of the most influential figures in modern popular music, releasing albums such as Late Registration, Graduation, 808s and Heartbreak, and My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy. His artistic work spans multiple genres, incorporating orchestral arrangements, electronic music, and unconventional production techniques. In addition to his musical output, which has earned him 24 Grammy Awards, West achieved commercial success in the fashion industry through his Yeezy brand. He legally changed his name to Ye in 2021.
edward-vii: Edward VII, born Albert Edward on November 9, 1841, was the eldest son of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Internationally known for serving as King of the United Kingdom from 1901 to 1910, he was the first British monarch of the House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. Before ascending the throne, he served as the Prince of Wales for nearly sixty years, traveling extensively and representing the British monarchy abroad. As king, Edward played a pivotal role in European diplomacy, helping secure the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and fostering peaceful relations across the continent. His reign, termed the Edwardian era, witnessed major reorganizations of the British military, advancements in naval technology, and significant domestic political developments. He married Princess Alexandra of Denmark in 1863, with whom he had six children. Edward died on May 6, 1910, and was succeeded by his son, King George V.
kenzabur-e: Kenzaburō Ōe was a major Japanese novelist and essayist who became a central figure in post-World War II literature. Born on January 31, 1935, in Ehime Prefecture, Ōe studied French literature at the University of Tokyo. He gained early acclaim in 1958 by winning the prestigious Akutagawa Prize for his novella The Catch. Ōe's literary works frequently addressed pacifism, anti-nuclear activism, existential isolation, and the political transformation of post-war Japan. The birth of his son Hikari in 1963 with a brain abnormality profoundly shaped his writing, inspiring landmark novels such as A Personal Matter and The Silent Cry. In 1994, Ōe was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for creating an imagined world where life and myth condenses to form a disconcerting picture of the human predicament today. Throughout his life, he remained a steadfast social critic and peace advocate. Kenzaburō Ōe died on March 3, 2023, at the age of eighty-eight.
joan-mir: Joan Miró i Ferrà was an internationally acclaimed Spanish painter, sculptor, and ceramicist whose work significantly influenced twentieth-century modern art. Born on April 20, 1893, in Barcelona, Spain, Miró began his formal artistic training at a young age before moving to Paris in 1920. There, he allied himself with the Surrealist movement, although he maintained a fiercely independent style. His artistic vocabulary combined dreamlike abstraction, biomorphic shapes, child-like spontaneity, and vibrant color palettes. Beyond painting, Miró made substantial contributions to sculpture, printmaking, and ceramics, frequently collaborating with ceramicist Josep Llorens Artigas on large-scale public murals. Throughout his long career, Miró earned international recognition, receiving numerous awards and establishing the Fundació Joan Miró in his hometown of Barcelona to support contemporary art. He died on December 25, 1983, in Palma, Majorca, leaving behind a profound artistic legacy characterized by poetic imagination and stylistic innovation.
thomas-robert-malthus: Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834) was an influential British political economist and demographer whose work shaped modern understandings of population dynamics and resource management. Born in Surrey, Malthus studied at Jesus College, Cambridge, and was later ordained as an Anglican priest. In 1798, he anonymously published his most famous work, An Essay on the Principle of Population. In this treatise, Malthus argued that human population tends to grow exponentially, whereas food production increases at a slower arithmetic rate. He contended that unchecked population growth would inevitably result in poverty, famine, and disease, phenomena later termed Malthusian catastrophes. To mitigate these risks, he advocated for preventive checks such as delayed marriage and moral restraint. In 1805, Malthus became the first British professor of political economy at the East India Company College in Haileybury. His theories profoundly influenced classical economics, demography, and evolutionary biology, notably inspiring Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace.
svante-august-arrhenius: Svante August Arrhenius (1859–1927) was a Swedish scientist recognized for his foundational contributions to physical chemistry, physics, and astronomy. Born near Uppsala, he studied at Uppsala University and the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Arrhenius is best known for his theory of electrolytic dissociation, which explained how chemical compounds break down into charged ions when dissolved in water. This work earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903, making him the first Swedish Nobel laureate. In physical chemistry, he established the Arrhenius equation, which calculates how temperature affects chemical reaction rates. Beyond laboratory chemistry, Arrhenius pioneered climate science in 1896 by publishing the first quantitative model estimating how increases in atmospheric carbon dioxide contribute to the Earth's greenhouse effect. He also researched astronomical phenomena, promoting the hypothesis of panspermia. Arrhenius later served as the director of the Nobel Institute for Physical Chemistry until his death.
karim-benzema: Karim Mostafa Benzema is a French professional footballer born on December 19, 1987, in Lyon, France. Internationally known for his technical skills, vision, and goalscoring ability, Benzema began his senior club career at his hometown team Olympique Lyonnais, where he won four consecutive Ligue 1 titles. In 2009, he transferred to the Spanish club Real Madrid, where he spent fourteen seasons and achieved widespread acclaim. During his tenure at Real Madrid, Benzema won twenty-five major trophies, including five UEFA Champions League titles and four La Liga titles. He served as team captain and became the second-highest goalscorer in the club's history. In 2022, he received the prestigious Ballon d'Or award. Internationally, Benzema represented the France national football team between 2007 and 2022, winning the UEFA Nations League in 2021. In 2023, he joined the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ittihad.
ursula-von-der-leyen: Ursula Gertrud von der Leyen is a German politician who has served as the President of the European Commission since December 2019. Born on October 8, 1958, in Brussels, Belgium, she studied economics and medicine, later practicing as a physician before entering German politics. A member of the Christian Democratic Union, she held several cabinet positions under Chancellor Angela Merkel, including Minister of Family Affairs from 2005 to 2009 and Minister of Labour and Social Affairs from 2009 to 2013. In 2013, she became Germany's first female Minister of Defence, serving until 2019. As the first woman to lead the European Commission, von der Leyen has spearheaded major policy packages, such as the European Green Deal and the NextGenerationEU recovery plan. Her leadership has also focused on managing the COVID-19 pandemic and coordinating EU support for Ukraine. She was re-elected for a second term in 2024.
jean-sibelius: Johan Julius Christian Sibelius, known internationally as Jean Sibelius, was a Finnish composer and violinist born on December 8, 1865, in Hämeenlinna, Finland. He is widely recognized as Finland's greatest composer, whose music played a crucial role in developing a Finnish national identity during the country's struggle for independence from the Russian Empire. Sibelius studied music in Helsinki, Berlin, and Vienna before gaining international acclaim in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. His most famous works include seven symphonies, the symphonic poem Finlandia, the Violin Concerto in D minor, Valse triste, and the Lemminkäinen Suite. His distinct musical style combined late Romantic orchestrations with evocative structures inspired by Finnish folklore, particularly the national epic, the Kalevala. Sibelius largely retired from public composition in the late 1920s, spending his remaining decades at his home, Ainola. He died on September 20, 1957, in Järvenpää, Finland, leaving a lasting legacy in orchestral music.
dua-lipa: Dua Lipa is an internationally known British singer and songwriter. Her full name is Dua Lipa, born on August 22, 1995, in London, England, to Kosovo Albanian parents.
