After working briefly as a model, she signed with Warner Music Group in 2015 and released her self-titled debut studio album in 2017. The album featured successful singles such as Be the One and New Rules, the latter reaching number one on the UK Singles Chart. In 2019, she won the Grammy Award for Best New Artist. Her second studio album, Future Nostalgia, released in 2020, received widespread critical acclaim and earned her the Grammy Award for Best Pop Vocal Album. The record produced major hit singles including Don't Start Now and Levitating. Beyond her music career, Lipa has expanded into acting, appearing in the 2023 film Barbie, for which she also recorded the hit single Dance the Night.
larry-sanger: Lawrence Mark Sanger is an American Internet project developer, philosopher, and former college professor born on July 16, 1968. He is best known as the co-founder of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia alongside Jimmy Wales. Before Wikipedia, Sanger served as the editor-in-chief of Nupedia, a peer-reviewed web encyclopedia launched in 2000. Recognizing the need for a more open model to generate content quickly, he proposed using a wiki interface, which led directly to the creation of Wikipedia in January 2001. Sanger coined the project's name and formulated many of its foundational policies, including its neutral point of view policy. After leaving Wikipedia in 2002, he became a critic of the platform's accuracy and governance. He subsequently established several alternative web projects, including Citizendium in 2007, which emphasized expert oversight. Sanger earned a doctorate in philosophy from Ohio State University and has taught at higher education institutions.
umm-kulthum: Umm Kulthum, whose full name was Fatima Ibrahim al-Sayyid al-Beltagi, was a renowned Egyptian singer and actress who lived from 1904 to 1975. Born in the village of Tamay e-Zahayra, she began her musical career singing religious songs in her youth before moving to Cairo in the 1920s to pursue a professional career. Often referred to as the Star of the East, she became one of the most celebrated and influential musical figures in the Arab world. Her powerful, expressive vocal range and mastery of traditional Arabic music styles earned her international acclaim. Throughout her career, she released over three hundred songs, acted in several prominent films during the 1930s and 1940s, and held regular monthly live radio broadcasts that captivated millions of listeners across the region. She died in Cairo on February 3, 1975, leaving behind a profound cultural legacy that continues to resonate throughout the Middle East and globally.
nancy-reagan: Nancy Davis Reagan, born Anne Frances Robbins on July 6, 1921, was an American actress who served as the First Lady of the United States from 1981 to 1989. Raised in New York and Maryland, she pursued an acting career in the 1940s and 1950s under the name Nancy Davis, starring in several Hollywood films. In 1952, she married fellow actor Ronald Reagan. She became the First Lady of California during her husband's tenure as governor from 1967 to 1975. As First Lady of the United States, she championed social causes, most notably founding the Just Say No drug awareness campaign to discourage youth drug abuse. She also exerted significant influence within the White House, particularly regarding personnel and presidential scheduling. Following her husband's Alzheimer's diagnosis in 1994, she became an advocate for stem cell research and Alzheimer's awareness. She died on March 6, 2016.
dick-cheney: Richard Bruce Cheney, born January 30, 1941, is an American politician and businessman who served as the 46th vice president of the United States from 2001 to 2009 under President George W. Bush. Raised in Wyoming, Cheney began his public career in the Nixon and Ford administrations, eventually serving as White House Chief of Staff from 1975 to 1977. He represented Wyoming in the United States House of Representatives from 1979 to 1989 and was appointed Secretary of Defense by President George H. W. Bush, directing Operation Desert Storm during the 1991 Gulf War. Between political offices, he served as chairman and chief executive officer of Halliburton from 1995 to 2000. As vice president, Cheney was widely regarded as one of the most influential vice presidents in United States history, exerting substantial influence over foreign policy, national security, and the response to the September 11 attacks, including the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
marjorie-estiano: Marjorie Dias de Oliveira, known professionally as Marjorie Estiano, is a Brazilian actress and singer born on March 8, 1982, in Curitiba, Paraná. She gained widespread national recognition in 2004 for her breakout role as Natasha in the popular teen soap opera Malhação, which simultaneously launched her successful musical career. Estiano released her self-titled debut studio album in 2005, followed by Flores, Amores e Blábláblá in 2007 and O.O.O. in 2014. As an actress, she has starred in prominent television series and telenovelas, including Duas Caras, Lado a Lado, and Império. Estiano achieved significant international acclaim for her starring performance as Dr. Carolina in the medical drama series Sob Pressão, earning an International Emmy Award nomination for Best Actress in 2019. Her film credits include notable performances in critically praised movies such as Good Manners. Throughout her career, she has established herself as a versatile Brazilian artist.
jens-stoltenberg: Jens Stoltenberg is a Norwegian politician who has served in major national and international leadership roles. Born in Oslo on March 16, 1959, Stoltenberg earned a degree in economics from the University of Oslo before entering public service. A prominent member of the Labour Party, he served as Norway's Minister of Finance from 1996 to 1997. Stoltenberg later became the Prime Minister of Norway, holding office for two separate terms, first from 2000 to 2001 and again from 2005 to 2013. During his tenure as prime minister, he focused on economic stability, public sector reform, and environmental issues. In October 2014, Stoltenberg was appointed Secretary General of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). He led the military alliance for a decade, navigating significant geopolitical crises including the Russian invasion of Ukraine, until stepping down in October 2024. Throughout his career, Stoltenberg gained international recognition for his diplomatic approach and commitment to multilateral cooperation.
louis-xv-of-france: Louis XV, whose full name was Louis de Bourbon, served as King of France and of Navarre from 1715 until his death in 1774. Born on February 15, 1710, at the Palace of Versailles, he succeeded his great-grandfather, Louis XIV, at age five. His early reign was governed by a regency council under Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, followed by the chief ministry of Cardinal Fleury until 1743. Initially popular and known as The Well-Beloved, Louis XV supported significant cultural projects during the French Enlightenment. However, his later rule saw severe foreign policy setbacks, including defeat in the Seven Years' War, which forced France to yield vast colonial territories in North America and India to Great Britain. His lifestyle and relationships with royal mistresses like Madame de Pompadour further damaged his reputation. He died on May 10, 1774, leaving a financially strained kingdom to his grandson, Louis XVI.
maria-montessori: Maria Tecla Artemisia Montessori, an Italian physician and educator, was born on August 31, 1870, in Chiaravalle, Italy, and died on May 6, 1952, in Noordwijk, Netherlands. She became one of Italy's first female medical doctors after graduating from the University of Rome in 1896. Initially working in psychiatry, Montessori developed a deep interest in child development and educational theory. In 1907, she opened the Casa dei Bambini, a childcare center in Rome, where she tested and refined her innovative teaching philosophy. Her approach emphasized child-centered learning, self-directed activity, mixed-age classrooms, and specialized instructional materials. Known globally as the Montessori method, this pedagogical system gained international acclaim and revolutionized early childhood education. Montessori spent her later years lecturing worldwide, publishing books, and training teachers, including a significant period in India during World War II. She was nominated three times for the Nobel Peace Prize for her advocacy of education and peace.
ben-affleck: Benjamin Géza Affleck-Boldt, known professionally as Ben Affleck, is an American film actor, director, screenwriter, and producer born on August 15, 1972, in Berkeley, California. He began his acting career as a child before gaining international fame for co-writing and starring in the 1997 drama Good Will Hunting, which earned him the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay. Affleck subsequently starred in major studio features including Armageddon, Pearl Harbor, and Gone Girl, as well as portraying Batman in several superhero films within the DC Extended Universe. In addition to acting, he established a successful directing career with critically acclaimed films such as Gone Baby Gone, The Town, and Argo. His work as a producer and director on Argo earned him the Academy Award for Best Picture in 2013. Outside of filmmaking, Affleck co-founded the Eastern Congo Initiative, a non-profit advocacy and grant-making organization.
pablo-escobar: Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria was a Colombian drug lord born on December 1, 1949, in Rionegro, Colombia. He became internationally known as the founder and leader of the Medellín Cartel, an organization that dominated the international cocaine trade during the 1980s and early 1990s. Through vast illegal operations, Escobar accumulated immense wealth, ranking among the world's richest individuals. In Colombia, he cultivated popular support by constructing homes, sports complexes, and funding local civic projects. However, his rise was accompanied by extreme violence, including bombings, kidnappings, and the assassinations of politicians, judges, and law enforcement officials. His actions led to severe violent conflict between the cartel, rival criminal organizations, and the state. Following a prolonged manhunt conducted by Colombian authorities with assistance from the United States, Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria (1949–1993) was shot and killed on a Medellín rooftop on December 2, 1993.
imelda-marcos: Imelda Remedios Visitacion Trinidad Romualdez Marcos, born July 2, 1929, is a Philippine politician who served as First Lady of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986. Married to President Ferdinand Marcos, she wielded significant political power during his presidency, holding key official roles such as Governor of Metropolitan Manila and Minister of Human Settlements. Globally, she gained fame for her opulent lifestyle, extensive art patronship, and vast personal collection of footwear and jewelry, which became symbols of extravagance. Following the 1986 People Power Revolution, her family was ousted and fled into exile in Hawaii. Marcos returned to the Philippines in 1991 after her husband died, subsequently resuming her political career. She served multiple terms as a member of the Philippine House of Representatives. Despite facing long-standing legal battles over allegations of corruption and ill-gotten wealth, she maintained public influence, eventually witnessing her son, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., assume the presidency in 2022.
keira-knightley: Keira Christina Knightley is an internationally known British actress recognized for her roles in both independent films and major blockbuster franchises. Born on March 26, 1985, in Teddington, London, she began acting as a child, making her feature film debut in 1995. Knightley gained widespread public attention with her breakout role in the sports comedy Bend It Like Beckham in 2002. She achieved international stardom portraying Elizabeth Swann in the Pirates of the Caribbean fantasy franchise. Renowned for her work in period dramas, Knightley received Academy Award nominations for her performances as Elizabeth Bennet in Pride & Prejudice in 2005 and Joan Clarke in the historical drama The Imitation Game in 2014. Her other prominent films include Atonement, Anna Karenina, and Colette. Beyond film, she has performed in theatrical productions on Broadway and the West End. In 2018, Knightley was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire for her services to drama and charity.
pierre-joseph-proudhon: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was a French politician, philosopher, mutualist economist, and writer who lived from 1809 to 1865. He is internationally recognized as one of the most influential theorists of anarchism and socialism. Proudhon was the first person to declare himself an anarchist, famously proclaiming in his 1840 work What Is Property? that property is theft. Born in Besançon, he initially worked as a printer before devoting himself to political literature and activism. Following the French Revolution of 1848, he was elected to the French Constituent Assembly. Proudhon advocated for mutualism, a system based on labor-backed currency and credit unions, which sought to replace state authority and capitalism with voluntary associations. His 1846 publication, The System of Economical Contradictions, drew a famous response from Karl Marx. Proudhon spent several years imprisoned and in exile for opposing Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte. His ideas significantly shaped European labor movements, federalism, and libertarian socialist thought.
madeleine-albright: Madeleine Korbel Albright, born Marie Jana Korbelová on May 15, 1937, in Prague, Czechoslovakia, was an American diplomat and political scientist who served as United States Secretary of State from 1997 to 2001. Nominated by President Bill Clinton, she was the first woman to hold the position, making her the highest-ranking woman in the history of the United States government at that time. Her family fled Europe during World War II and settled in the United States in 1948. Albright earned a doctorate from Columbia University and served as the United States Ambassador to the United Nations from 1993 to 1997. As Secretary of State, she advocated for NATO expansion into Eastern Europe and played a central role in shaping American policy in the Balkans. After leaving office, Albright taught at Georgetown University and authored several books. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 and died on March 23, 2022.
elie-wiesel: Eliezer Elie Wiesel was a Romanian-born American writer, professor, political activist, Nobel laureate, and Holocaust survivor who lived from 1928 to 2016. Born in Sighet, Romania, Wiesel was deported to the Auschwitz concentration camp in 1944 with his family during World War II. He survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald, though his parents and younger sister died during the Holocaust. Following the war, Wiesel studied in France before moving to the United States, where he became a naturalized citizen. He authored over fifty books, most famously his 1960 memoir Night, which detailed his harrowing experiences in Nazi concentration camps. Wiesel served as a professor of humanities at Boston University and was an international advocate for human rights, speaking out against hatred, violence, and genocide worldwide. In 1986, he received the Nobel Peace Prize for his lifelong commitment to fighting injustice and promoting peace. He died in New York City at age eighty-seven.
ray-charles: Ray Charles Robinson was an American singer, pianist, and songwriter who became one of the most influential figures in popular music. Born in Albany, Georgia, on September 23, 1930, he lost his sight in early childhood but pursued music while attending the Florida School for the Deaf and the Blind. During the 1950s, Charles pioneered soul music by blending rhythm and blues, gospel, and blues styles, scoring groundbreaking hits such as I've Got a Woman and What'd I Say. His 1962 album Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music successfully integrated country music into mainstream pop, yielding classic recordings like Georgia on My Mind. Over his six-decade career, he earned 17 Grammy Awards, received the Kennedy Center Honors, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Charles continued to record and perform internationally until his death on June 10, 2004, in Los Angeles.
larry-page: Lawrence Edward Page is an American computer scientist and Internet entrepreneur born on March 26, 1973, in Lansing, Michigan. He is best known as the co-founder of Google, one of the world's largest technology companies. Page earned a Bachelor of Science in engineering from the University of Michigan and later attended Stanford University to pursue a doctorate in computer science. At Stanford, he met fellow graduate student Sergey Brin in 1995. Together, they developed PageRank, a search engine algorithm that ranked web pages based on link structures. In 1998, Page and Brin incorporated Google. Page served as Google's chief executive officer from 1998 to 2001 and again from 2011 to 2015. He later became the inaugural chief executive officer of Alphabet Inc., holding the position from 2015 until stepping down in December 2019, while remaining a board member and controlling shareholder.
chinua-achebe: Albert Chinualumogu Achebe was a Nigerian novelist, poet, professor, and critic whose work profoundly shaped modern African literature. Born on November 16, 1930, in Ogidi, Nigeria, Achebe gained international acclaim with his debut novel, Things Fall Apart, published in 1958. The book examined traditional Igbo society and the disruptive effects of European colonialism, becoming one of the most widely read African novels in history. Over his career, Achebe authored several additional novels, including Arrow of God and Anthills of the Savannah, alongside essays, poetry, and children's literature. His influential 1975 essay on Joseph Conrad challenged prevailing Western perspectives on Africa. Achebe served as a professor at universities in Nigeria and the United States, including Bard College and Brown University. He received many honors, including the Man Booker International Prize in 2007. Achebe died on March 21, 2013, leaving a monumental cultural and literary legacy.
alphonse-de-lamartine: Alphonse Marie Louis de Prat de Lamartine was a French author, poet, and statesman who lived from 1790 to 1869. Internationally known for his foundational role in French Romantic poetry and his key political actions, he first gained fame with his 1820 collection, Poetic Meditations. His literary achievements were complemented by an active career in public service. During the Revolution of 1848, Lamartine served as the Minister of Foreign Affairs and effective head of the provisional government. In this position, he played a central role in founding the French Second Republic, championing democratic rights, the abolition of slavery, and the end of the death penalty for political offenses. After losing the 1848 presidential election to Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, he withdrew from public office. Lamartine devoted his later years to writing historical texts, essays, and novels to pay off debts, remaining a respected literary figure until his death in Paris.
edgar-de-wahl: Edgar von Wahl, universally known as Edgar de Wahl, was a Baltic German schoolteacher, mathematician, and linguist born on August 23, 1867, in Olviopol, Russian Empire. He spent much of his life in Tallinn, Estonia, where he taught physics and mathematics at various secondary schools. De Wahl is internationally renowned as the creator of Occidental, a naturalistic constructed international auxiliary language published in 1922 and later renamed Interlingue. Before developing Occidental, he was an active proponent of Volapük and an early pioneer of Esperanto, collaborating with its creator, L. L. Zamenhof, before departing due to disagreements over language reforms. Throughout his career, de Wahl contributed extensively to linguistics and interlinguistics, authoring numerous articles and publications. He remained in Tallinn during the Soviet and Nazi occupations of Estonia in World War II, living his final years in a sanatorium. Edgar de Wahl died on March 9, 1948.
jacques-offenbach: Jacques Offenbach, born Jacob Offenbach, was a German-born French composer, virtuoso cellist, and impresario who became one of the most influential figures in nineteenth-century European musical theater. Born in Cologne, Prussia, in 1819, he moved to Paris in 1833 to study cello at the Paris Conservatoire. He initially earned acclaim as a concert cellist before turning his talents toward composition and theater management. In 1855, Offenbach founded the Theatre des Bouffes-Parisiens, where he pioneered the modern operetta, blending sharp satirical humor, catchy melodies, and lively theatricality. His stage works captured the spirit of Second Empire France and gained widespread international popularity. Among his nearly one hundred operettas, his most famous creations include Orpheus in the Underworld, featuring the famous Infernal Galop, La Belle Helene, and La Vie parisienne. Near the end of his life, he composed his masterpiece, the grand opera The Tales of Hoffmann, which remained unfinished at his death in Paris in 1880.
imre-kert-sz: Imre Kertész was a Hungarian author and translator who received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2002. Born in Budapest on November 9, 1929, he was deported to the Auschwitz concentration camp in 1944 at age fourteen and later transferred to Buchenwald before liberation in 1945. His experiences during the Holocaust profoundly shaped his literary work. Kertész worked as a journalist and translator in postwar Hungary, translating major German-language authors such as Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud, and Franz Kafka into Hungarian. His debut novel, Fatelessness, published in 1975, drew heavily on his wartime experiences to explore the absurdities and alienation of totalitarian systems. It became the first part of a trilogy that included Fiasco and Kaddish for an Unborn Child. Recognized globally for writing that upholds the fragile experience of the individual against history, Kertész died in Budapest on March 31, 2016.
guillaume-apollinaire: Guillaume Apollinaire, born Wilhelm Albert Włodzimierz Apolinaris Kostrowicki, was a French poet, playwright, short story writer, novelist, and art critic of Polish descent. Born in Rome in 1880, he grew up to become one of the most important literary figures of the early twentieth century and a passionate champion of avant-garde movements. Apollinaire gained international renown as a groundbreaking poet through his innovative techniques, notably eliminating all punctuation from his celebrated 1913 collection Alcools. He also pioneered graphic poetry in Calligrammes, published in 1918, in which words are arranged visually to create thematic designs. As an influential art critic, he actively defended Cubist painters and coined the term surrealism in 1917. Apollinaire served in the French army during World War I and suffered a critical head wound in 1916. Weakened by his injuries, he died during the Spanish flu pandemic in Paris in November 1918 at age thirty-eight.
fernando-pessoa: Fernando António Nogueira Pessoa was a Portuguese poet, writer, and philosopher who lived from 1888 to 1935. Born in Lisbon, he spent much of his youth in Durban, South Africa, gaining fluency in English and Portuguese. Pessoa is internationally known as one of the most significant literary figures of the twentieth century. His defining contribution was the creation of a complex heteronymic system through which he invented dozens of distinct alter egos. Far beyond simple pseudonyms, these heteronyms possessed complete biographies, distinct writing styles, physical traits, and unique philosophical beliefs. Among his most prominent heteronyms were the pastoral poet Alberto Caeiro, the neoclassical doctor Ricardo Reis, the modernist engineer Álvaro de Campos, and the assistant bookkeeper Bernardo Soares, credited with writing the prose masterpiece The Book of Disquiet. Although Pessoa published relatively little during his lifetime, his posthumously discovered writings established his enduring international stature in modern literature.
